meta.notes: Each question supports two views. The default view explains why the key is correct: 'takeaway' is the clinical rule and each option carries its own rationale. The strategy view uses 'elimination', which names the test-taking strategies in play, walks the options out one at a time, and ends with the verdict. Both views describe the same question, so a student who is short on content can still reason to the answer. All fields are plain text with no markup, so render 'strategy' in italic with CSS rather than expecting tags.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate absolutes
optionStrategies.cue: always, never, all, none, only, every
optionStrategies.note: Absolutes are usually wrong because medicine rarely deals in certainties.

optionStrategies.name: Favor qualifiers
optionStrategies.cue: usually, generally, often, may, approximately, most
optionStrategies.note: Qualifiers make a statement realistic. Not automatically right, but worth a second look against an absolute.

optionStrategies.name: Opposite pair, look closely
optionStrategies.cue: increase vs decrease, before vs after
optionStrategies.note: Often one of the pair is correct. Sometimes both are distractors, so treat it as a flag for attention.

optionStrategies.name: Global or umbrella option
optionStrategies.cue: one option covers two or more others
optionStrategies.note: If one option encompasses the others it is often the most complete answer.

optionStrategies.name: Patient-centered option
optionStrategies.cue: asks, involves, or respects the patient
optionStrategies.note: Options that involve the patient beat options that decide for them.

optionStrategies.name: Duplicate facts
optionStrategies.cue: a wrong fact shared by two or more options
optionStrategies.note: One shared wrong fact eliminates several options at once.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
optionStrategies.cue: don't worry, it's nothing, most people are fine
optionStrategies.note: Therapeutic communication reflects feelings and invites more.

optionStrategies.name: Odd man wins
optionStrategies.cue: three options share an idea, one stands apart
optionStrategies.note: When most options point one way, the different one is often correct.

optionStrategies.name: Negative polarity
optionStrategies.cue: avoid, except, not, least, contraindicated, requires further teaching
optionStrategies.note: You are hunting the wrong option. Identify polarity before reading the choices.

optionStrategies.name: Priority key word
optionStrategies.cue: priority, immediate, first, best, most, least
optionStrategies.note: More than one option may be true. The key word decides how to choose among them.

optionStrategies.name: Apply the ABCs
optionStrategies.note: In ordering and priority questions, airway, breathing, and circulation come first, then safety, then comfort.

optionStrategies.name: Assessment before intervention
optionStrategies.cue: assess, check, determine versus administer, apply, notify
optionStrategies.note: When the stem asks what comes first and an assessment option is present, assessment usually precedes action.

optionStrategies.name: Treat each option as true or false
optionStrategies.note: Work each option independently. Partial credit means a wrong selection costs you, so only select what the scenario supports.

questions.stem: A nurse with four years on a medical unit is asked by a provider to insert a device she has never placed. He offers to talk her through it. Two colleagues say they have done it here before. The hospital policy manual does not mention the procedure. Which factors determine whether she may legally perform it? Select all that apply.

options.text: The patient consenting to the procedure being performed
options.rationale: Consent decides whether the procedure happens, not who is allowed to do it. A patient cannot authorize a nurse into a task the law keeps outside her scope.

options.text: Agency policy and procedure
options.rationale: Policy can narrow what the practice act allows but never widen it. The manual saying nothing is a reason to check before she starts, not permission to go ahead.

options.text: Her demonstrated competence to perform it safely
options.rationale: The act allowing a task does not mean she can safely do it today. Competence is hers to judge, and she has never placed one of these.

options.text: That other nurses on the unit have done it
options.rationale: Common practice is not permission. Every one of those colleagues could be working outside their scope without anyone having noticed.

options.text: The provider offering to supervise her
options.rationale: Supervision feels like cover and gives her no legal authority. She answers for what her own hands do, watched or not.

options.text: Her state nurse practice act
options.rationale: State law sets the outer limit of what any nurse there may do. If the procedure sits outside it, nothing else on this list makes it lawful.

questions.takeaway: Three things decide scope and they stack: the practice act sets the limit, policy may narrow it, and competence is yours to declare.
questions.strategy: More than one option describes something reassuring. Reassurance is not legal authority.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The state practice act, and nothing overrides it.

elimination.verdict: B, C, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that four patients over two weeks received their scheduled 0800 insulin after 0930. She reported each delay to the charge nurse and each time was told the unit was short-staffed. Which action best reflects a Standard of Professional Performance?

options.text: Continue reporting each late dose to the charge nurse as it happens
options.rationale: She has already done this four times and nothing changed. Repeating a step that has not worked is not what the standard asks of her.

options.text: Stay past her shift to give the insulin herself when the unit is short
options.rationale: This is the kind answer and the worst one. It gets tonight's insulin given and hides the pattern, so the data that would force a fix never exists.

options.text: Bring the pattern to the unit practice council with a proposed change
options.rationale: Quality of practice is a Standard of Professional Performance. Four late doses is a pattern, and a pattern belongs where practice actually gets changed.

options.text: Ask the provider to move the insulin to a later administration time
options.rationale: Moving the order makes the prescription fit the staffing problem. The insulin is not the thing that is broken.

questions.takeaway: Standards of Professional Performance cover how you conduct yourself as a professional, including quality of practice.
questions.strategy: One option is what she has already tried. One is kind and conceals the problem. Ask which one changes anything.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reporting, four times, with no change.
Fixes one shift and hides the pattern.
Adjusts the prescription to a staffing problem.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the practice council: take the pattern where practice changes.

questions.stem: A nurse administers a dose of heparin that a colleague drew up and left at the bedside during a busy round. The syringe held five times the ordered dose and the patient bleeds. The colleague states she drew it correctly, and leaving prepared syringes is routine on this unit. Which statement describes the administering nurse's position?

options.text: The colleague is accountable, because she prepared the dose
options.rationale: The colleague does answer for drawing it up wrong. That takes nothing away from the nurse who pushed it.

options.text: She is accountable, because the nurse who gives a medication answers for it
options.rationale: Preparing a drug and giving it are two separate acts, and each nurse answers for her own. Once she picked up that syringe, verifying it became her job.

options.text: Both share accountability equally, because both handled the syringe
options.rationale: Accountability is not split between them like a bill. Each one answers in full for what she personally did.

options.text: This is a system failure, because the unit routinely leaves syringes out
options.rationale: Leaving syringes at the bedside is a real system problem, and it still does not excuse giving a drug nobody verified.

questions.takeaway: Accountability follows administration. It does not transfer to whoever prepared the dose, or to the system that made the error likely.
questions.strategy: Three options name something genuinely true. Only one describes her own position.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the shared and transferred options

steps.detail: Real, and it does not erase what she did.

elimination.verdict: That leaves her own accountability for administering it.

questions.stem: A nurse finds a systematic review supporting mobilization within 12 hours of abdominal surgery. Her patient, six hours post-operative, reports a fall at home last month, is frightened of falling again, and declines to get up. Which action best reflects evidence-based practice?

options.text: Document the refusal and try again tomorrow
options.rationale: Waiting a day respects his wish and throws out the evidence. Immobility after abdominal surgery carries real risk, so tomorrow is not a neutral choice.

options.text: Follow the review and mobilize him today as the evidence directs
options.rationale: This is the research without the patient. Strong evidence applied over someone's stated refusal is not evidence-based practice, it is protocol.

options.text: Ask the provider for an order requiring ambulation
options.rationale: An order does not touch the fear that is actually stopping him. It also hands a nursing decision to someone who is not in the room.

options.text: Explore what is behind the fear and adapt how mobility is introduced
options.rationale: Evidence-based practice is the research, your judgment and what matters to the patient, together. His fear is data, and the plan has to bend around it.

questions.takeaway: Evidence-based practice needs all three legs: research, clinical expertise, and what matters to the patient.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option keeps one leg of the triad and drops another. The fall last month is what makes his refusal reasonable rather than obstinate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hands the decision to someone else.

elimination.verdict: That leaves exploring the fear and adapting the plan.

questions.stem: For each action, indicate which professional role the nurse is performing.

rows.text: Weighs him and assesses for peripheral edema
rows.rationale: This is hands-on care delivered straight to the patient, which is the caregiver role.

rows.text: Arranges a meeting so he can put his questions about the catheterization to the provider
rows.rationale: She is creating the opening for his questions to reach the person making the decision.

rows.text: Reassigns the assistive personnel so the two heaviest patients are not bathed at the same hour
rows.rationale: She is organizing people, time and workload so the shift is safe, which is management.

rows.text: Shows him how to read a food label for sodium
rows.rationale: She is building a skill he will use after discharge, and teaching is the educator role.

rows.text: States his wish not to proceed clearly during the team discussion
rows.rationale: She carries his stated position into a room he is not in. Advocacy is not a single action.

questions.takeaway: Five roles: caregiver, educator, communicator, advocate, manager. Autonomy and accountability run underneath all five rather than forming a sixth.
questions.strategy: Two rows are both advocate. Advocacy is anything that keeps the patient's own position in play, whether or not he is present.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two rows protect his stated position.
One is hands-on, one is teaching, one is workload.

elimination.verdict: Caregiver, educator, advocate, manager, advocate.

questions.scenario: A nurse cares for a patient newly diagnosed with heart failure across one shift. The patient is alert, anxious about a recommended cardiac catheterization, with a spouse at the bedside.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews her unit's fall rate for the past quarter, finds it at 4.2 per 1,000 patient days against a benchmark of 3.4, trials an hourly rounding protocol for 60 days, and re-measures at 2.9. Which QSEN competency does this best demonstrate?

options.text: Safety
options.rationale: Falls are a safety issue, so safety is in the room. The question asks what she did, and what she did was run an improvement cycle.

options.text: Informatics
options.rationale: She used data, and informatics is about the systems that hold information. That is not the method she used here.

options.text: Evidence-based practice
options.rationale: Hourly rounding is evidence-based, so this is true as well. It explains where the intervention came from, not what she did with it.

options.text: Quality improvement
options.rationale: She measured against a benchmark, changed something, and measured again. That closed loop is what quality improvement means.

questions.takeaway: Quality improvement is the measure, change, re-measure cycle. The subject matter of a project is not the competency.
questions.strategy: More than one competency is genuinely involved. Choose the one that names what she actually did.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The topic of the project, not the method.
One is the source of the intervention, one is the systems.

elimination.verdict: That leaves quality improvement.

questions.stem: A patient in a rural clinic needs hypertension managed, medication adjusted, and ongoing follow-up over the coming year. No physician is on site four days a week. Which advanced practice role is prepared to manage this care independently, including diagnosing and prescribing?

options.text: Certified nurse-midwife
options.rationale: Nurse-midwives practice independently, but within pregnancy, birth and women's health. Ongoing hypertension management falls outside that population.

options.text: Clinical nurse specialist
options.rationale: The expertise is real, but a clinical nurse specialist works through staff and systems rather than carrying patients. Nobody is left seeing this patient the other four days.

options.text: Nurse practitioner
options.rationale: Nurse practitioners diagnose, prescribe and carry their own patients over time. That is the whole job this clinic needs covered.

options.text: Certified registered nurse anesthetist
options.rationale: Nurse anesthetists are advanced practice, and their scope is anesthesia. No part of it covers managing blood pressure across a year.

questions.takeaway: Four APRN roles: clinical nurse specialist, nurse practitioner, certified nurse-midwife, certified registered nurse anesthetist.
questions.strategy: All four are advanced practice. Ask which one manages a general caseload over time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Consults to practice rather than carrying patients.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the nurse practitioner.

questions.stem: A preceptor discusses scope with a new graduate in her third month. Which statement by the new graduate indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If the provider writes the order, the responsibility for giving it rests with him."
options.rationale: A written order does not hand the responsibility to the prescriber. The nurse who gives the drug answers for having given it.

options.text: "My state nurse practice act sets the outer limit of what I may legally do."
options.rationale: This is accurate. The practice act is the outer boundary, and nothing else widens it.

options.text: "Agency policy can narrow my practice but cannot widen it beyond the act."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it is why a permissive employer cannot authorize something the act excludes.

options.text: "Competence is my own responsibility, so I should say when I have not done something before."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Saying when you have never done something is what protects both the nurse and the patient.

questions.takeaway: An order authorizes the drug. It does not transfer answerability for administering it.
questions.strategy: Three statements are correct as written. The one needing correction moves responsibility off the person who acts.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the statement handing responsibility to the provider.

questions.stem: A nurse moves to a neighboring state and is told a wound procedure she performed routinely is outside her scope there. She holds the same national certification she held before. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Scope is set by each state's practice act, not certification
options.rationale: Certification proves expertise inside a scope, and the state decides what that scope contains. Crossing a state line changes what the same credential lets her do.

options.text: The certification lapses when practising in a different state
options.rationale: Certification is national and travels with her. What changed is the legal boundary drawn around it.

options.text: Employer approval is needed before the procedure returns to scope
options.rationale: An employer can narrow her scope and can never widen it past the practice act.

options.text: The procedure requires an additional state-specific credential
options.rationale: Adding a credential does not help when the act itself excludes the procedure. There is nothing to certify her into.

questions.takeaway: Licensure permits practice and is state-governed. Certification demonstrates expertise and does not widen scope.
questions.strategy: Every distractor offers a way to get the procedure back. Ask who defines scope in the first place.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the state act, with certification not expanding it.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel tells a nurse she gave eye drops routinely at her previous hospital and offers to give a patient's drops now. The nurse has watched her work all week and considers her careful. Which consideration determines the answer?

options.text: Whether the previous employer permitted it
options.rationale: What another employer allowed has no authority in this state. It is the same mistake as a nurse assuming her old scope came with her.

options.text: Whether the patient consents to the assistive personnel giving the drops
options.rationale: Consent decides whether the care happens, not who may lawfully give it. A patient cannot place a task inside someone's scope.

options.text: Whether the nurse has observed her perform the task competently
options.rationale: Competence is one of the five rights of delegation, and it only matters once the task is delegable. This one may not be.

options.text: What the state practice act permits assistive personnel to perform
options.rationale: State law decides what unlicensed staff may do. Being careful and having done it elsewhere cannot move a task inside a scope the act excludes.

questions.takeaway: Check whether a task may be delegated before asking whether this person can do it. Scope first, competence second.
questions.strategy: Two options describe genuine considerations that come later. Ask what has to be true before any of them matter.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: May it be delegated, then can she do it.
Both matter only after scope allows it.

elimination.verdict: That leaves what the state act permits.

questions.stem: A unit adopts an artificial intelligence tool that flags patients at risk of deterioration. It alerts on a patient whose pulse has risen from 74 to 108 and whose blood pressure has fallen to 94/56. The nurse had already noticed both changes. Which statement about her responsibility is accurate?

options.text: The tool assumes responsibility for identifying deterioration once implemented
options.rationale: Technology supports judgment and cannot hold it. Installing a tool does not move accountability off the nurse.

options.text: She remains accountable for her own assessment and for acting on her findings
options.rationale: A tool can surface a pattern in the numbers. It cannot assess the patient, and it cannot answer for what happens next.

options.text: Alerts from the tool may be documented in place of nursing assessment
options.rationale: An alert records what an algorithm noticed, not what a nurse found. The two are not interchangeable in the chart.

options.text: She should defer to the tool when her assessment disagrees with it
options.rationale: Her assessment comes first. When the tool disagrees with her, that is a reason to look harder, not to stand down.

questions.takeaway: Emerging technology supports clinical judgment. Accountability for assessment and action stays with the nurse.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you she had already noticed. Ask what the tool actually changed about her obligations.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She had seen both changes herself.
Her assessment is the primary source.

elimination.verdict: That leaves her own accountability, unchanged by the tool.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
Three weeks after a stroke, a patient enters a facility for daily physical and occupational therapy with the goal of going home. This is [[1]].

A 34-year-old with no chronic conditions sees a family nurse practitioner for a sore throat and to discuss contraception. This patient is receiving [[2]].

An 84-year-old with advanced dementia lives in a residential facility receiving help with all activities of daily living. The condition is not expected to improve. This is [[3]].

A 58-year-old is admitted directly to intensive care after a myocardial infarction, needing continuous monitoring and intravenous medication. This patient is receiving [[4]].

options.text: tertiary care
options.rationale: Tertiary names specialization, not the recovery of function. The specialized part is behind him.

options.text: restorative care
options.rationale: He lost function and it is expected to come back. Restorative care exists to recover exactly that.

options.text: acute care
options.rationale: The acute event was three weeks ago and he is medically stable, so acute care is finished.

options.text: continuing care
options.rationale: Continuing care supports needs that are not expected to change. His are expected to improve.

options.text: secondary care
options.rationale: Secondary care is hospital treatment for an acute episode, not a clinic visit for a sore throat.

options.text: tertiary care
options.rationale: Tertiary care is the highly specialized end of treatment, for complex conditions. A sore throat is not that.

options.text: preventive care
options.rationale: Preventive care reduces risk before disease appears. She arrived with a symptom, so something is already wrong.

options.text: primary care
options.rationale: This is first contact for a routine problem, with no specialist involved and a relationship that continues. That is primary care.

options.text: continuing care
options.rationale: Her needs are ongoing and are not expected to improve, and that is what continuing care is for.

options.text: preventive care
options.rationale: Nothing here is aimed at stopping a disease before it starts.

options.text: restorative care
options.rationale: This is the near miss. Both happen in facilities, and only restorative expects the patient to improve.

options.text: secondary care
options.rationale: No acute episode is being treated, so secondary does not fit.

options.text: restorative care
options.rationale: Restorative care recovers function that has been lost. He is still in the middle of the acute event.

options.text: primary care
options.rationale: Primary care is first contact and continuity, which an intensive care admission is not.

options.text: secondary care
options.rationale: This is the near miss. Secondary is admission for an acute episode, and intensive care is the specialized level above it.

options.text: tertiary care
options.rationale: Intensive care is the specialized end of hospital treatment, and that is what tertiary names.

questions.takeaway: Six levels: preventive, primary, secondary, tertiary, restorative, continuing. Restorative and continuing are separated by the trajectory, not the setting.
questions.strategy: Two pairs get confused. Secondary versus tertiary is how specialized; restorative versus continuing is whether function is expected to return.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what is expected to happen
steps.detail: Improvement, or a stable ongoing need.
Admission is secondary; intensive care is tertiary.
Recovery is restorative; permanent need is continuing.

elimination.verdict: Primary, tertiary, restorative, continuing.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes has not filled his insulin prescription for two months, and his A1C has risen from 7.4% to 10.2%. He works two jobs, has no car, and the pharmacy is a 40-minute bus ride each way with one change. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Reinforce teaching about the consequences of untreated diabetes
options.rationale: This is a correct nursing action that assumes the barrier is knowledge. Nothing says he misunderstands; he cannot physically get to the pharmacy.

options.text: Ask the provider to simplify the insulin regimen
options.rationale: Simplifying makes sense for a complicated regimen. It changes nothing about a prescription he cannot collect.

options.text: Document nonadherence to the medication regimen
options.rationale: This feels like doing something and it is only a label. Nonadherent puts the failure on him and closes a question the stem already answered.

options.text: Explore the transportation and pharmacy options available to him
options.rationale: The rising A1C shows the problem is real and getting worse. Two jobs, no car and a 40-minute bus ride name the obstacle, and the obstacle is what you can act on.

questions.takeaway: When a patient is not doing what the plan asks, the plan usually met a barrier it cannot pass. Find the barrier.
questions.strategy: One option names him rather than the obstacle. Labels close a problem instead of solving it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two jobs, no car, 40 minutes each way.
Assumes a knowledge gap the stem does not show.
One labels him, one changes a prescription he cannot collect.

elimination.verdict: That leaves exploring transport and pharmacy options.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is discharged after abdominal surgery needing a daily dressing change for 14 days. The wound is 6 cm with moderate serous drainage. He lives alone, has never changed a dressing, and his daughter works weekdays. Which actions belong in the discharge plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Arrange home health services before discharge
options.rationale: His daughter works weekdays and he has never done this before. Someone skilled has to cover the days nobody is there.

options.text: Provide written instructions in plain language
options.rationale: He needs something to read on day nine, when the teaching session is a memory.

options.text: Document that the discharge teaching was completed
options.rationale: This records what the nurse did, not what he can do. It does not get a single dressing changed.

options.text: Reassure the patient that the wound will most likely be healed before the fourteen days are up
options.rationale: False reassurance about a 6 cm wound with moderate drainage, and it gives him a reason to skip the plan.

options.text: Verify the patient can actually obtain the supplies
options.rationale: A perfect teaching session is worth nothing if the dressings never arrive.

options.text: Confirm by return demonstration that whoever will perform it can
options.rationale: Watching the skill performed is the only way to know it can be done. Saying you understand is not evidence.

questions.takeaway: Discharge planning asks four things: who will do it, can they demonstrate it, is the information usable, and are the supplies in place.
questions.strategy: Two options are reasonable things to do, and neither makes the dressing change happen tomorrow morning.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask who does it on day one
steps.detail: Not him, and not his daughter on a weekday.
Records your action, not his capability.
Thirteen days too late for the first change.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E, and F are selected.

questions.scenario: A 79-year-old is admitted with a wound infection. It is a third admission in four months, each for the same wound. The patient reports changing the dressing without help because the home health visits stopped when the insurance changed. There is no car, and an adult child visits at weekends.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Teach the dressing change again before discharge
options.rationale: This is a correct nursing action aimed at the wrong problem. He has been doing the dressing for months, so teaching it again changes nothing.

options.text: Refer to social work for insurance and home health options
options.rationale: The visits stopped for an administrative reason, and social work is who untangles insurance and home health.

options.text: Document that he has been changing the dressing himself
options.rationale: This records the finding without doing anything about it, and he comes back a fourth time.

options.text: Confirm who will perform the dressing change at home and verify they can
options.rationale: Three admissions say nobody competent is doing this at home. Naming who will do it, and checking they can, is what breaks the cycle.

options.text: Nonadherence to the wound care regimen
options.rationale: This blames him for something he did not choose. He has been doing it himself because nobody is coming.

options.text: Lack of family support
options.rationale: Closer, and still wrong. His daughter does visit; what is missing is skilled care on weekdays.

options.text: Interrupted access to skilled care after an insurance change
options.rationale: He tells you the cause outright. The visits stopped when the insurance changed, which is administrative rather than clinical.

options.text: Knowledge deficit about wound care
options.rationale: Nothing suggests he misunderstands the dressing. Assuming a knowledge gap is what produces the wrong action.

options.text: Whether he can name the signs of infection
options.rationale: This is measurable, and it evaluates teaching that nobody identified as the problem.

options.text: Whether the wound is smaller at the next visit
options.rationale: A smaller wound is a real outcome, and it does not tell you whether the access problem got solved.

options.text: Whether home health visits have actually restarted
options.rationale: This measures whether the referral actually worked, which is the thing you changed.

options.text: Whether he is readmitted within 30 days
options.rationale: Readmission is the outcome the whole plan exists to prevent, and the pattern that brought him in.

questions.takeaway: Access failures look like nonadherence. When a patient tells you why the plan stopped working, that is the problem statement.
questions.strategy: Two problem options blame the patient. Evaluate the thing you actually changed, not a related outcome that would move anyway.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The visits stopped when the insurance changed.
You referred and you verified, so measure those.

elimination.verdict: Refer and verify, for interrupted access, evaluated by restarted visits and readmission.

questions.stem: A nurse manager audits the unit after complaints that decisions were made without patients. Which staff actions reflect person-centered care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Completing the plan before the admission interview to save the patient's time
options.rationale: This sounds considerate and produces a plan made without him, which is the complaint that started the audit.

options.text: Involving the patient in decisions about the plan of care
options.rationale: Respecting the patient's values, preferences and expressed needs is the first of the eight dimensions.

options.text: Including the family the patient designates in discussions
options.rationale: This brings in family on the patient's terms rather than on the institution's definition of family.

options.text: Sharing information in a form the patient can use
options.rationale: Information the patient cannot use has not really been shared. The form it takes is part of the sharing.

options.text: Applying the same standardized plan to every patient with the diagnosis
options.rationale: A standard plan is efficient and evidence-based, and it is the opposite of individualized.

options.text: Asking what matters most to the patient about this admission
options.rationale: Asking what matters surfaces the preferences the rest of the plan has to fit around.

questions.takeaway: Person-centered care: respect for values, coordination, information, physical comfort, emotional support, family involvement, continuity, and access.
questions.strategy: One distractor uses efficiency as the reason for excluding the patient, dressed as courtesy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Produces exactly the complaint being audited.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A hospital preparing a Magnet application must show how it measures the quality of nursing care specifically. Its dashboard reports 30-day readmission after myocardial infarction, surgical site infection after colorectal surgery, time from emergency arrival to provider, and fall rate with injury. Which measure serves the application?

options.text: Fall rate with injury
options.rationale: Falls come down when nurses assess risk, round on schedule, keep toileting predictable and clear the path to the bathroom. Change the nursing care and the number changes with it.

options.text: Surgical site infection after colorectal surgery
options.rationale: Infection rates matter, but this one is mostly decided in the operating room. Surgical technique and antibiotic timing drive it, not what nursing does on the unit.

options.text: Thirty-day readmission after myocardial infarction
options.rationale: Readmission depends mostly on the medical plan and whether the patient can get to follow-up. Nursing affects it through teaching, but too many other causes crowd the number.

options.text: Time from emergency arrival to provider evaluation
options.rationale: This measures how fast the department moves patients through, which is staffing and bed availability. It says nothing about the care nurses give once the patient is seen.

questions.takeaway: A nursing-sensitive outcome is one that changes when nursing care changes. Falls, pressure injuries and line infections are the classic three.
questions.strategy: All four are real measures the hospital reports. The test is simple: would this number move if nursing care got better or worse?

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Does this number move when nursing care moves?

steps.action: Cut the medical and surgical measures

elimination.verdict: That leaves fall rate with injury.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a community group about where to go for different needs. Several participants describe using the emergency department for routine problems. Which statement by a participant indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "An immunization clinic is preventive care, because it stops me getting ill."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Preventive care reduces risk before any disease appears.

options.text: "The emergency department is the same as seeing a primary provider."
options.rationale: The emergency department treats acute episodes. It offers no continuity, no prevention and no ongoing relationship, which is the whole point of primary care.

options.text: "Rehabilitation after a stroke is restorative care, because the goal is getting function back."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it is why restorative care sits apart from continuing care.

options.text: "Being admitted for intravenous antibiotics is secondary care."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Secondary care is hospital treatment for an acute episode.

questions.takeaway: Primary care is first contact plus continuity and prevention. An emergency department provides none of the last three.
questions.strategy: Three statements are accurate as spoken. The fourth is the behavior the session set out to change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Treating the emergency department as a provider.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the emergency department statement.

questions.stem: A nurse manager presents to the board on the challenges facing nursing over the next decade. Which set of factors matches what the profession identifies?

options.text: An aging patient population, rising costs, and falling patient satisfaction scores
options.rationale: Cost and satisfaction are real problems in health care delivery. They follow from the workforce shortage rather than causing it.

options.text: Physician shortages, expanded advanced practice scope, and growth in telehealth
options.rationale: This names one real factor and pairs it with two things that relieve workforce pressure rather than create it.

options.text: An aging population, physician shortage, nurse retirements, and health care reform
options.rationale: Demand and supply move against each other. The boomers reach their heaviest years of health care use just as the nurses who would care for them retire.

options.text: Nurse retirements, competency concerns, and variation in prelicensure preparation
options.rationale: Retirements belong on the list. Competency and variation in prelicensure preparation are separate professional debates.

questions.takeaway: Four challenges: the aging baby boomer generation, physician shortage and uneven distribution, the rate of nurse retirements, and uncertainty over health care reform.
questions.strategy: Every distractor contains at least one true factor. Ask which set names drivers rather than consequences.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Costs and satisfaction result from the shortage.
Expanded scope and telehealth ease pressure.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the four the profession names.

questions.nursesNote: 1015: Patient is 71, discharged home four days ago after a hip replacement. Lives alone in a two-story house with the bathroom upstairs. An adult child visits at weekends. Reports not having been able to shower since coming home and sleeping in a downstairs chair. Physical therapy was arranged twice weekly but no visit has taken place. Says eating 'whatever is easy to reach'. Wound is clean and dry with no redness. Pain is 3 of 10 and controlled with acetaminophen. Temperature 36.8 C, blood pressure 128/76.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate the discharge plan has failed.

segments.text: Physical therapy arranged twice weekly but no visit has taken place
segments.rationale: Arranging a service is not the same as the service happening. Nobody verified it started.

segments.text: Has not been able to shower since coming home
segments.rationale: A direct consequence of the environment, and an unmet basic need four days in.

segments.text: Sleeping in a downstairs chair
segments.rationale: She has no accessible bed. This raises risks for skin, sleep and further deconditioning.

segments.text: An adult child visits at weekends
segments.rationale: A fact about her support, and it was known before discharge. It is context rather than a failure.

segments.text: Wound is clean and dry with no redness
segments.rationale: The wound is the one part going well. A clean, dry incision with no redness is an expected finding.

segments.text: Eating whatever is easy to reach
segments.rationale: Nutrition has become a function of what she can physically get to, which is a mobility problem presenting as a dietary one.

segments.text: Pain is 3 of 10 and controlled with acetaminophen
segments.rationale: Controlled pain on a simple analgesic four days after joint replacement is an expected finding.

segments.text: Lives alone in a two-story house with the bathroom upstairs
segments.rationale: The environment was never matched to her mobility. She cannot reach her own bathroom.

questions.takeaway: Discharge planning fails at the point where the plan meets the home. Arranging a service is not the same as confirming it happened.
questions.strategy: Three findings are normal or expected and they are there to be left alone. Ask which findings describe a plan that did not survive contact with her house.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate the clinical from the situational
steps.detail: The wound and the pain are fine.
That she could reach a bathroom and that therapy would start.
The daughter's schedule was known beforehand.

elimination.verdict: s1, s2, s3, s6, and s8: missing therapy, hygiene, sleep, reachable food, and the environment.

questions.stem: A nurse is named in a review after a patient deteriorated overnight. The record shows vital signs charted at every scheduled interval, a documented change in level of consciousness at 0300, no further assessment after that entry, and no contact with the provider until 0600. Measured against the ANA Standards of Practice, which standard was most directly breached?

options.text: Assessment, by not obtaining the vital signs
options.rationale: The vital signs were taken on schedule. The failure came after the data existed, not in collecting it.

options.text: Diagnosis, by not naming an active nursing problem
options.rationale: Naming the problem is the weaker charge here. A change was recognized and recorded, and then nothing was done with it.

options.text: Evaluation, by not reassessing after the change
options.rationale: Evaluation is the standard that makes you look again after something shifts. A charted change with no reassessment and no call is that loop left open for three hours.

options.text: Planning, by not writing measurable patient outcomes
options.rationale: Measurable outcomes matter. A missing outcome statement is not what let this patient slide for three hours.

questions.takeaway: The six Standards of Practice are the nursing process. Charting a change and not reassessing is an evaluation failure, not an assessment failure.
questions.strategy: Three options name a standard that was met. Find the point in the sequence where the nurse stopped.

strategies: Walk the nursing process in order

steps.action: Match that point to its standard
steps.detail: Looking again after a change is evaluation.

elimination.verdict: Evaluation is the answer.

questions.stem: A nurse wants two things: the state's nurse-to-patient staffing legislation amended, and a credential in her own clinical specialty. A colleague says the board of nursing handles both. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: A professional association, then a specialty organization
options.rationale: Associations advocate and lobby; specialty organizations credential. Two goals, two different bodies.

options.text: The state board of nursing for both of them
options.rationale: The board regulates and disciplines. It does not lobby for legislation and it does not grant specialty credentials.

options.text: A professional association for both of them
options.rationale: Associations do advocate, and the certification comes from the specialty organization rather than the association.

options.text: The state board, then a professional association
options.rationale: This is backwards on both counts. The board enforces law rather than shaping it, and certification is not an association function.

questions.takeaway: Professional associations advocate and set standards. Specialty organizations certify. Boards of nursing license and discipline. Those three roles do not overlap.
questions.strategy: Ask what each body is empowered to do, not what it is interested in.

strategies: Identify the body with the authority

steps.detail: A board enforces; an association persuades.

steps.action: Cut every option putting the board in a lobbying role
steps.detail: That is not a regulatory function.
Credentials come from the specialty body.

elimination.verdict: A professional association, then a specialty organization.

questions.stem: A patient with a blood pressure of 168/98 mm Hg has missed three clinic appointments. She has active insurance, a current prescription on file, and lives four blocks from the clinic. She holds two hourly jobs with no paid leave, and the clinic closes at 1600. Which barrier to access does this describe?

options.text: Health and health care, through no insurance coverage
options.rationale: This is the pull of the question. It is an access problem, and her insurance is active, so coverage is not what is blocking her.

options.text: Neighborhood and built environment, through poor transit
options.rationale: She lives four blocks away. Distance and transport are not the barrier here.

options.text: Economic stability, through unpaid time away from work
options.rationale: Going to the clinic costs her wages. When the clinic's open hours and her paid hours are the same hours, the barrier is economic even though the door is open.

options.text: Social and community context, through weak family support
options.rationale: Nothing in the history points to isolation. Inventing a support deficit is how this option gets picked.

questions.takeaway: Access is not only insurance and distance. Lost wages, shift work, and clinic hours exclude patients who are nominally covered and nearby.
questions.strategy: The question hands you three facts that rule options out. Use them before reaching for the familiar answer.

strategies: Let the given data eliminate

steps.detail: Unpaid hours, which is economic stability.

elimination.verdict: Economic stability is the barrier.

questions.stem: A patient is admitted at 0200 for a three-day course of intravenous antibiotics. On rounds the charge nurse asks about discharge planning. A new nurse answers that it is too early to say, with discharge still days away. Which correction is accurate?

options.text: Planning begins once the provider writes the order
options.rationale: The order is the end of planning, not the start. By the time it is written there is no time left to arrange anything.

options.text: Planning begins at admission and continues throughout
options.rationale: You start the day the patient arrives, because the things that hold up a discharge take days: home support, equipment, transport, a pharmacy that stocks the drug.

options.text: Planning begins when the patient is medically stable
options.rationale: Stability tells you discharge is close. It does not tell you when to start getting ready for it.

options.text: Planning begins the day before the anticipated discharge
options.rationale: One day is not enough for durable equipment, a home health intake or a prior authorization.

questions.takeaway: Discharge planning starts at admission. Everything that commonly delays a discharge takes longer to arrange than the notice you get.
questions.strategy: Three options tie planning to an event late in the stay. The exam answer is always the earliest one.

strategies: Look for the earliest defensible point

steps.action: Reject the order as a trigger
steps.detail: That is the end of the process.

steps.action: Reject stability and the day before
steps.detail: Both arrive too late to arrange services.
Planning runs the length of the stay.

elimination.verdict: Planning begins at admission.

questions.stem: A nurse with five years on a medical unit enters a room, says the patient does not look right before any vital signs are taken, and asks the provider to assess him. Vitals taken minutes later are normal. Six hours later he meets sepsis criteria. Which stage of Benner's model does this illustrate?

options.text: Advanced beginner, recognizing recurring aspects of care
options.rationale: An advanced beginner needs the findings to be there before the picture registers. This nurse read the room before any data existed.

options.text: Competent, planning care against long-range goals
options.rationale: Competence shows up as deliberate planning, usually around two to three years in. It is organized rather than perceptive.

options.text: Proficient, perceiving the situation as a whole
options.rationale: A proficient nurse takes in the whole situation and notices when it does not look the way it usually does. Normal vital signs did not reassure her, and that is the clue.

options.text: Expert, no longer relying on analytic principles
options.rationale: This is the near miss, and the tiebreak is what she did next. An expert acts on the grasp; this nurse recognized something was off and handed it on to be analyzed.

questions.takeaway: Proficient means you take in the whole situation and notice when it does not look right. Expert means you act on that without working through the rules.
questions.strategy: Two options are defensible. What tips it is whether the nurse acted on the perception or escalated it.

strategies: Separate the near-miss stages

steps.detail: Both need the data to be visible first.

steps.action: Use the escalation as the tiebreak

elimination.verdict: Proficient is the answer.

questions.stem: A nurse reviewing the record finds that assistive personnel charted a full set of vital signs at 0800 for a patient the nurse knows was off the unit at that time. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Assess the patient and obtain the vital signs
options.rationale: The chart holds numbers nobody measured, so right now nobody knows how this patient is. Everything else can wait ten minutes; real vital signs cannot.

options.text: Report the assistive personnel to the nurse manager
options.rationale: It will need reporting, and it does nothing for the patient in the next ten minutes. The pull is that it feels like the serious response.

options.text: Correct the entry and note the time discrepancy
options.rationale: This is documenting instead of acting. The record gets corrected after the patient has been assessed.

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to repeat the measurement
options.rationale: This sends the person who falsified the first set to produce the second. The nurse needs data she can trust.

questions.takeaway: Falsified data means the patient is unassessed. Assess first, then address the record and the person.
questions.strategy: Three options act on the chart or the staff member. One acts on the patient.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.action: Cut the reporting and charting options

elimination.verdict: Assess the patient.

questions.stem: A patient is leaving with a new anticoagulant. The nurse notices his printed discharge summary lists 5 mg daily while the final prescriber order reads 2.5 mg daily. Transport is waiting. Which action takes priority?

options.text: Teach from the order and note the discrepancy in the record
options.rationale: This leaves a document in his hands that says twice the dose. Teaching correctly does not cancel a written instruction he will read at home.

options.text: Clarify the dose with the prescriber before the patient leaves
options.rationale: Two written doses exist and the nurse does not know which is current. An anticoagulant at double the dose is a bleed, and the window to sort it closes when transport leaves.

options.text: Give both documents and explain which one to follow
options.rationale: This hands the patient the job of settling a prescribing conflict. Comprehension under pressure is not a safety plan.

options.text: Send the summary to the primary care provider for review
options.rationale: This is the right action answering the wrong question. That review happens days from now, and he takes a dose tonight.

questions.takeaway: Two conflicting written doses is an unresolved order, not a documentation problem. Resolve it before the patient leaves with either number.
questions.strategy: A deadline in the stem is there to make a premature option attractive. Transport waiting is not a reason to discharge on an unclarified dose.

strategies: Resolve the ambiguity before acting

steps.action: Notice there are two written doses
Cut the options that discharge anyway
steps.detail: All three leave the conflict live.
The only one that resolves it.

elimination.verdict: Clarify the dose first.

chapters.title: Older Adults
chapters.subtitle: Geriatric syndromes, expected change versus disease, polypharmacy, falls, delirium, dementia, depression, and elder mistreatment

sources.title: Concepts of Care for Older Adults
sources.label: Iggy Ch. 4 · Concepts of Care for Older Adults

questions.stem: A 91-year-old woman admitted two days ago for a urinary tract infection is oriented in the morning and cannot say where she is by evening. Her daughter reports that she manages the household finances at home. Which finding most strongly supports delirium?

options.text: Her age of 91, which makes confusion expected
options.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis. Confusion is never an expected finding, at any age.

options.text: The acute onset with attention that fluctuates through the day
options.rationale: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and marked by inattention. Waxing and waning within one day is what separates it from the other two.

options.text: The gradual loss of her ability to manage daily activities
options.rationale: Gradual decline over months to years points to dementia. Her daughter describes her managing finances until now.

options.text: Long-standing memory impairment noted on previous admissions
options.rationale: Chronic and stable memory loss describes dementia, and nothing in the stem reports it.

questions.takeaway: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, and inattentive. Dementia is progressive and chronic. Depression brings mood change and withdrawal.
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe a slow decline and one blames her age. Ask how fast this appeared and whether it holds steady.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Oriented this morning, disoriented by evening.

elimination.verdict: That leaves acute onset with fluctuating attention.

questions.scenario: A nurse completes an annual assessment on an 84-year-old who lives alone.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected age-related change or a red flag requiring further assessment.

rows.text: Needs more light to read than she did five years ago
rows.rationale: Changes in sensory perception are expected, and they raise fall risk, which is assessed separately.

rows.text: Stopped attending her weekly card group and snaps at her daughter
rows.rationale: A new significant change in behavior is a red flag, and withdrawal with irritability may point to depression.

rows.text: Has fallen twice in the past month with no clear explanation
rows.rationale: New unexplained falls are a red flag. A fall is a clinical clue, not an event to record and move past.

rows.text: Became disoriented to place over the past two days
rows.rationale: Sudden confusion is a red flag. Think delirium and look for the cause.

rows.text: Takes slightly longer to respond when asked a question
rows.rationale: Slower reaction time is a normal age-related change and does not indicate impairment.

rows.text: Reports food tastes blander than it used to
rows.rationale: Decreased taste and smell is expected, and it matters because it can lead to poor intake.

questions.takeaway: Expected: slower reaction time, sensory change, gradual mobility change. Red flags: sudden confusion, sudden functional decline, new unexplained falls, new behavior change.
questions.strategy: The word that sorts them is sudden. Gradual and mild belongs to aging; abrupt and unexplained belongs in an assessment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Three expected, three requiring assessment.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman is admitted after a fall at home. The nurse reviews her home medication list: lisinopril, metformin, furosemide, zolpidem at night, ibuprofen most days for knee pain, a herbal sleep supplement, and a multivitamin. Which concerns should the nurse identify? Select all that apply.

options.text: Taking a multivitamin indicates the patient is not eating adequately
options.rationale: A supplement is not evidence of poor intake. Intake is assessed by asking about eating, not by counting bottles.

options.text: The over-the-counter items may not be on the provider's list
options.rationale: Over-the-counter drugs and supplements are not regulated like prescriptions and are frequently omitted when patients list what they take.

options.text: A sedative in a patient who has fallen needs review
options.rationale: Medications are one of the named fall risk factors, and a hypnotic in an older adult who is already falling is the clearest example.

options.text: The zolpidem and the herbal sleep supplement may duplicate each other
options.rationale: Duplicate therapy is a named polypharmacy concern, and two sedating products together raise her fall risk further.

options.text: The number of prescribers is what defines polypharmacy
options.rationale: Multiple prescribers is a real risk for duplication, and polypharmacy is defined by the number of medications, not the number of providers.

options.text: The patient meets the definition of polypharmacy
options.rationale: Five or more medications at once, and the count includes over-the-counter drugs and supplements.

questions.takeaway: Polypharmacy is five or more medications at once, counting over-the-counter drugs and supplements. Concerns include the number, duplicates, difficult dosing, and unregulated products.
questions.strategy: One distractor redefines polypharmacy by prescribers. One reads a vitamin as evidence about her diet.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A bottle is not a dietary assessment.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, and F are selected.

questions.stem: An 86-year-old woman moved into her daughter's home three weeks ago after living in the same house for 40 years. She is tearful, has stopped her daily morning walk, and is disoriented to place in the evenings. Her cognition was intact at her last clinic visit. She has no fever, her medications are unchanged, and her attention is steady through the day. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep her usual daily routines where possible and involve her in decisions
options.rationale: Relocation stress comes from lost surroundings, lost routines, and lost control. Restoring the routine and the control addresses the cause.

options.text: Request a cognitive screening tool to establish the degree of impairment
options.rationale: Steady attention and no acute cause makes this relocation rather than a new cognitive problem. Screening now measures the upheaval, not her baseline.

options.text: Reassure the daughter that confusion is expected after a move at this age
options.rationale: Normalizes a red flag. Confusion is never expected, and calling it so means nobody looks for what is driving it.

options.text: Arrange a referral for placement in an assisted living facility
options.rationale: This is a second relocation for a woman whose problem is the first one. Moving her again repeats the cause rather than treating it.

questions.takeaway: Relocation stress produces anxiety, confusion, and withdrawal. Maintain routines, include the patient in decisions, and promote orientation.
questions.strategy: One option measures the problem, one normalizes it, one repeats it. Ask what changed three weeks ago.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She moved after 40 years in one house.
One normalizes a red flag, one moves her again.

elimination.verdict: That leaves keeping her routines and including her in decisions.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old woman has lost 6 kg over four months. The nurse asks her to describe what a typical day's eating looks like. Which response reflects the best nursing approach?

options.text: Teach her the importance of adequate protein and calorie intake
options.rationale: This is correct nutritional teaching that assumes the barrier is knowledge. Telling someone to eat more does nothing until you know why she stopped.

options.text: Explore what is making eating difficult before offering any solution
options.rationale: Poor intake in an older adult has many possible causes: taste changes, dentures, constipation, fatigue, cost, and loneliness among them. The cause decides the intervention.

options.text: Request an order for a high-calorie oral supplement
options.rationale: Treats the weight loss without finding its cause, and a supplement she also cannot chew or afford changes nothing.

options.text: Document the weight loss and recheck at the next visit
options.rationale: This records a significant change and then waits. Six kilograms in four months is a finding to act on now, not at the next visit.

questions.takeaway: Poor intake is a symptom with many causes. Find out why before deciding what to do about it.
questions.strategy: Two options intervene before assessing. Ask what you would need to know to choose between a supplement, a dental referral, and help with groceries.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Taste, teeth, constipation, fatigue, cost, loneliness.

steps.action: Cut the teaching and supplement options
steps.detail: Both act before knowing the cause.
A 6 kg loss is already the finding.

elimination.verdict: That leaves exploring what is making eating difficult.

questions.nursesNote: 1400: A 77-year-old attends clinic with an adult grandchild who manages the finances and answers most questions directed at the patient. Weight is down 9 kg since the last visit four months ago. The antihypertensive was last filled in March. The patient flinches when the grandchild moves toward the chair. There is bruising on both upper arms. Clothing is soiled and there is a sacral pressure injury. When asked how the day is spent, the patient looks at the grandchild before answering. A hearing aid is worn in the left ear. Blood pressure 158/94, pulse 88.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that raise concern for abuse or neglect.

segments.text: The grandchild manages the finances
segments.rationale: Managing money for a relative is common and lawful. It becomes a concern only when her needs go unmet because of it, which the other findings establish.

segments.text: Lost 9 kg since the last visit four months ago
segments.rationale: Unmet basic needs over time. Unintentional weight loss of this size is a core indicator of neglect.

segments.text: Flinches when the grandchild moves toward the chair
segments.rationale: Fearfulness of a specific person is a red flag and is not explained by any medical finding here.

segments.text: Bruising on both upper arms
segments.rationale: Bruising in a location consistent with being gripped, unexplained, is an unexplained injury.

segments.text: Wears a hearing aid in the left ear
segments.rationale: A device she uses. Sensory change is expected with aging and this is being managed.

segments.text: Antihypertensive last filled in March
segments.rationale: Withheld medication is neglect, and it raises the question of where the money went when someone else manages her finances.

segments.text: Blood pressure 158/94, pulse 88
segments.rationale: An elevated pressure explained by the unfilled prescription. It is a consequence of the neglect rather than a separate red flag.

segments.text: The grandchild answers most questions directed at the patient
segments.rationale: A caregiver controlling communication is a named red flag, and it means she cannot disclose in his presence.

segments.text: Clothing is soiled and there is a sacral pressure injury
segments.rationale: Poor hygiene and a pressure injury together point to prolonged unmet care needs.

questions.takeaway: Red flags: unexplained injuries, poor hygiene, unmet basic needs, fearfulness, sudden behavior change, financial concerns, inconsistent explanations, and a caregiver controlling communication.
questions.strategy: Two findings describe an arrangement rather than a finding, and one is a consequence of another finding you have already selected.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She flinches, and she checks his face before answering.

elimination.verdict: s2, s3, s4, s6, s8, and s9: weight, fear, bruising, medication, communication, and hygiene with skin.

questions.stem: A nurse caring for a 77-year-old woman admitted for pneumonia finds her disoriented on day three, having been oriented on admission. Her oxygen saturation is 88% on room air and her temperature is 38.4 C. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Request an order for a sedative to settle her overnight
options.rationale: Medications are themselves a contributing factor for delirium, and sedating a hypoxic patient makes the oxygenation worse.

options.text: Document the confusion and report it at handover
options.rationale: Communicates the change on a timescale that does not match a saturation of 88%.

options.text: Address the oxygenation and temperature as likely causes of the delirium
options.rationale: Hospital-acquired delirium appears around day two or three, and poor oxygenation, fever, and infection are all named contributing factors. The confusion is a symptom of something treatable.

options.text: Reorient her and place a bed alarm for safety
options.rationale: Reorienting her and adding an alarm are reasonable supportive steps. Neither one raises her oxygen saturation or treats the fever behind the confusion.

questions.takeaway: Hospital-acquired delirium appears around days two to three. Look for infection, fever, poor oxygenation, medications, and acute illness.
questions.strategy: Three options manage the confusion. Ask what the saturation and the temperature are telling you about why it happened.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Worsens both the delirium and the hypoxia.

elimination.verdict: That leaves treating the oxygenation and the fever.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses fall risk for an 81-year-old woman admitted after tripping at home. She takes seven medications including a nightly sedative, has cataracts, and fell once last year, and her daughter reports she eats very little and drinks few fluids. Which findings increase her risk of falling? Select all that apply.

options.text: Being 81 years old
options.rationale: Age itself is not a risk factor. The age-related changes that come with it are, and the stem names them separately.

options.text: A fall in the past year
options.rationale: A previous fall is the strongest single predictor of the next one. One fall last year puts her in the highest risk group before you look at anything else.

options.text: Poor fluid intake
options.rationale: Too little fluid leaves her dizzy and confused, and both of those come before a fall. Dehydration is a fall risk, not just a hydration problem.

options.text: Living with a daughter who checks on her
options.rationale: Having a daughter who checks on her lowers risk rather than raising it. Support is protective here.

options.text: Cataracts
options.rationale: Vision problems are a named risk factor. She cannot avoid a hazard she cannot see.

options.text: Seven medications including a nightly sedative
options.rationale: Five or more is polypharmacy, and a sedative adds drowsiness and slowed reactions on top of the count.

questions.takeaway: Fall risk factors: age-related changes, chronic conditions, vision problems, cognitive impairment, previous falls, nutritional deficiency, and dehydration.
questions.strategy: One distractor is protective and one is age itself. Age is not a diagnosis and it is not a risk factor.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Medications, cataracts, a previous fall, poor intake.
Not a risk factor on its own.

elimination.verdict: B, C, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse admits an 88-year-old woman for an elective hip replacement. Her daughter reports that she has become much more forgetful over the past three years and now needs prompting to dress. Her attention is steady throughout the interview. Which condition does this pattern suggest?

options.text: Dementia
options.rationale: Progressive, chronic cognitive decline over years, with attention intact. That combination is dementia.

options.text: Delirium
options.rationale: Delirium is acute and fluctuating with inattention. Three years is not acute and her attention is steady.

options.text: Depression
options.rationale: Depression brings mood change, withdrawal, and loss of interest. The stem describes function and memory, not mood.

options.text: Expected age-related memory change
options.rationale: Needing prompting to dress is a functional decline, and functional decline is not an expected change.

questions.takeaway: Dementia is progressive and chronic. Delirium is acute and fluctuating. Depression centers on mood and withdrawal.
questions.strategy: The two things that decide it are the timeline and whether attention holds steady.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Needing prompting to dress is decline.

elimination.verdict: That leaves dementia.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old woman tells the nurse she has three glasses of wine most evenings, the same as for the past thirty years, and adds that it now feels far stronger than it used to. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Tolerance has increased over thirty years of regular use
options.rationale: This reverses what she is describing. Tolerance would mean feeling it less, and she says the same wine now hits harder.

options.text: Three glasses is within safe limits for an adult of any age
options.rationale: Limits are lower for older adults because of the metabolic change, and the interaction with her medications matters too.

options.text: Alcohol use typically resolves on its own as people age
options.rationale: Substance use does not disappear with age. It is described as an invisible epidemic because it goes unrecognized.

options.text: Aging slows alcohol metabolism, so the same amount hits harder
options.rationale: Changes in metabolism and excretion mean the same dose behaves differently. The same drug and the same dose does not mean the same response.

questions.takeaway: Aging slows the breakdown of alcohol and drugs, so effects come on faster and last longer at the same dose.
questions.strategy: She has told you the finding herself. Ask what changed, given the amount has not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Thirty years at the same amount.

steps.action: Cut tolerance and the safe-limit option
steps.detail: One reverses her report, one ignores age.

elimination.verdict: That leaves slowed metabolism with age.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
An 84-year-old is admitted from home. The nurse uses two frameworks to organize the assessment.

Asking whether the patient has been sleeping, eating, staying continent, becoming confused, falling, or developing skin breakdown uses the [[1]] framework.

Asking what the patient wants recovery to look like addresses the [[2]] element of the 4 Ms.

Reviewing the seven home medications addresses the [[3]] element.

New confusion on day three belongs to the [[4]] element.

options.text: STEADI
options.rationale: STEADI is the fall framework: screen, assess the modifiable risks, intervene and teach. It covers falls, not these six areas.

options.text: BMAT
options.rationale: A mobility assessment tool, and it covers movement rather than these six areas.

options.text: SPICES
options.rationale: Sleep, Problems with eating, Incontinence, Confusion, Evidence of falls, Skin breakdown. The six areas named are the acronym.

options.text: the 4 Ms
options.rationale: The 4 Ms are What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility. Four elements, not six.

options.text: Medication
options.rationale: Medication covers what she takes and whether it is safe. It is not about what she wants out of this admission.

options.text: What Matters
options.rationale: The patient's own goals and preferences, and the element that anchors the rest of the plan.

options.text: Mobility
options.rationale: Mobility covers function and safe movement. Her goals for recovery sit somewhere else.

options.text: Mentation
options.rationale: Mentation covers delirium, dementia and depression. Her preferences are not a cognitive finding.

options.text: What Matters
options.rationale: What Matters is about her goals, not her prescriptions. Seven drugs is a medication question.

options.text: Mentation
options.rationale: Mentation is cognition rather than pharmacy, even though medications are a common cause of cognitive change.

options.text: Mobility
options.rationale: Mobility is about function and movement. Reviewing a drug list is not that.

options.text: Medication
options.rationale: Medication safety and review, which at seven items is also a polypharmacy assessment.

options.text: Mobility
options.rationale: Mobility is movement and function, and confusion will affect both. The finding itself is cognitive.

options.text: Medication
options.rationale: A medication may well be causing the confusion, and the element the finding belongs to is mentation.

options.text: Mentation
options.rationale: Mentation covers delirium, dementia and depression, and new confusion on day three points to delirium.

options.text: What Matters
options.rationale: What Matters is her preferences, which you still ask about even when she is confused. New confusion is not a preference.

questions.takeaway: SPICES: Sleep, Problems eating, Incontinence, Confusion, Evidence of falls, Skin breakdown. The 4 Ms: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility.
questions.strategy: Count the elements. Six areas is SPICES, four is the 4 Ms, and the fall-specific one is STEADI.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A drug may cause the confusion, and the finding is still mentation.

elimination.verdict: SPICES, What Matters, Medication, Mentation.

questions.stem: A 90-year-old woman who walked independently on admission has needed two people to transfer since day four. She is medically improving and her infection has resolved. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The decline is expected with hospitalization at her age
options.rationale: Hospital-associated decline is common and often does not reverse on its own, so you assess for it rather than accept it.

options.text: The functional decline needs investigating, because it is not explained by her improving illness
options.rationale: A decline of this speed signals something treatable. Deconditioning from bed rest, a new medication, or an unrecognized problem all need excluding.

options.text: Function should be reassessed once she is fully recovered from the infection
options.rationale: Sensible-sounding, and it loses the window in which the decline can be reversed.

options.text: The decline reflects her age, since function naturally declines after 90
options.rationale: Age is not a diagnosis. Function does not fall from independent to two-person assist in four days because of a birthday.

questions.takeaway: A rapid decline in function is a symptom, not aging. Mobility is independence, and deconditioning starts within days.
questions.strategy: Each distractor offers a reason to wait. Ask what four days of immobility does on its own.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Independent to two-person assist in four days.
Age does not explain the rate.

elimination.verdict: That leaves investigating the decline.

questions.stem: A nurse performs medication reconciliation for an 80-year-old woman on admission. Which errors is this process designed to prevent? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dangerous interactions between home medications and new orders
options.rationale: Comparing her home list against the new orders is exactly what reconciliation exists to catch. An interaction found on paper never reaches the patient.

options.text: Incorrect administration technique by the nurse giving it
options.rationale: Technique is a medication administration concern. Reconciliation compares lists rather than watching a dose being given.

options.text: Omissions, where a home medication is not continued
options.rationale: A drug she has taken for years disappearing from the list is one of the three named errors.

options.text: Duplications, where two products do the same thing
options.rationale: Particularly likely when several prescribers are involved and over-the-counter products are in use.

options.text: Nonadherence with the regimen after returning home
options.rationale: Adherence is affected by many things and reconciliation addresses the accuracy of the list, not whether she takes it.

questions.takeaway: Medication reconciliation compares the current list against newly ordered drugs to prevent omissions, duplications, and dangerous interactions.
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe real medication problems that a list comparison cannot catch.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse plans care for a 76-year-old woman admitted with a hip fracture. Which approach best reflects patient-centered care for an older adult?

options.text: Apply the standard hip fracture pathway, which is evidence-based
options.rationale: The pathway is evidence-based and identical for every patient who walks in. That sameness is what makes it the opposite of individualized care.

options.text: Ask her daughter what goals would be realistic for a woman of her age
options.rationale: Substitutes the family's judgment for hers, and anchors the plan to her age rather than her function.

options.text: Set a goal of returning to her prior level of function in all activities
options.rationale: A reasonable-sounding goal set without her, and it may be neither what she wants nor achievable.

options.text: Ask what she wants her recovery to look like and build the plan from her answer
options.rationale: What Matters is the first of the 4 Ms, and patient-centered independence means having control over decisions and keeping the highest possible level of function.

questions.takeaway: Patient-centered care for older adults starts with What Matters: her goals and preferences, not her diagnosis or her age.
