options.rationale: It is not conditional on agreement, comfort, or the nurse's own views. The obligation attaches to every patient.

options.text: State law protects patients from discrimination in health care settings
options.rationale: Real and binding, and it comes from the legislature rather than from the profession.

options.text: Affirming care improves patient satisfaction survey scores
options.rationale: This is true and it is the wrong basis. Dignity is not owed to a patient because respecting it scores well on a survey.

questions.takeaway: The Code of Ethics: compassion, respect for dignity, and the worth of every patient. Not conditional and not variable by jurisdiction.
questions.strategy: Three options name real reasons to do it. Ask which one is the professional obligation rather than an external requirement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the Code of Ethics.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse prepares to care for a transgender patient.

Gender-affirming care is the treatment for a diagnosis of [[1]].

A nurse who examines her own assumptions before an encounter is practicing [[2]].

Adding pronoun fields to the intake form is an example of [[3]].

Deciding what screening a patient needs is based on [[4]].

options.text: gender dysphoria
options.rationale: Gender-affirming care treats a diagnosis of gender dysphoria. Dysphoria is the distress, and it is what gets treated.

options.text: sexual orientation
options.rationale: Sexual orientation is who a person is attracted to. It is not a diagnosis and it is unrelated to gender identity.

options.text: gender expression
options.rationale: Gender expression is how someone presents outwardly. It is not a diagnosis either.

options.text: gender identity
options.rationale: Identity is who a person is. It is not a diagnosis and does not require treatment.

options.text: self-reflection
options.rationale: Self-reflection means examining your own biases and holding yourself accountable for them. That is inward work.

options.text: affirming communication
options.rationale: Affirming communication is what happens out loud in the conversation. This describes something the nurse does in her own head.

options.text: prioritizing patient needs
options.rationale: Prioritizing the patient means listening, respecting and asking for feedback. It is directed at the patient rather than at yourself.

options.text: educating yourself
options.rationale: Educating yourself is learning terminology and health issues. It points outward at the content, not inward at your assumptions.

options.text: affirming communication
options.rationale: The near-miss. Pronouns are used in communication, and changing the form changes the space rather than the conversation.

options.text: self-reflection
options.rationale: Self-reflection is inward work on your own assumptions. Changing a form is not that.

options.text: fostering an inclusive environment
options.rationale: Updating policies and building identity fields into the record is how the environment itself becomes inclusive.

options.text: educating yourself
options.rationale: Educating yourself is training and terminology. This describes changing the system rather than changing what you know.

options.text: the sex recorded at birth
options.rationale: Closer, and still wrong after surgery. What matters is what is there now.

options.text: the patient's gender identity
options.rationale: Gender identity does not tell you which organs are present. Screening follows anatomy, not the marker in the chart.

options.text: whether the patient takes hormone therapy
options.rationale: Hormone therapy changes physiology and removes nothing. A patient on testosterone who still has a cervix still needs screening.

options.text: the organs the patient has
options.rationale: Screening follows anatomy. A transgender man with a cervix still needs cervical screening.

questions.takeaway: Gender dysphoria is the diagnosis. Identity, expression and orientation are not diagnoses. Screening follows anatomy.
questions.strategy: Blank 3 has a genuine near-miss: pronouns belong to communication, and putting a field on a form changes the environment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The nurse, the words, or the space.

elimination.verdict: Gender dysphoria, self-reflection, inclusive environment, organs present.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews why LGBTQ+ health matters specifically to nursing. Which reason is most accurate?

options.text: Nurses are often the first contact, which shapes whether patients return
options.rationale: First point of contact, better outcomes and ethical responsibility are the three reasons, and the first is what makes the other two possible.

options.text: Nurses are responsible for prescribing gender-affirming hormone therapy
options.rationale: Outside the registered nurse's scope. The nurse's role is assessment, support, education, and advocacy.

options.text: Nurses must document sexual orientation for every patient on admission
options.rationale: Incorporating identity into records is a system practice, and it is not a mandatory field for every patient.

options.text: Nurses should refer LGBTQ+ patients to specialist clinicians where possible
options.rationale: Reasonable-sounding and it routes patients away from the care in front of them, which is how needs get overlooked.

questions.takeaway: Three reasons: nurses are the first point of contact, they improve health outcomes, and they hold an ethical responsibility.
questions.strategy: One distractor exceeds nursing scope. One routes the patient elsewhere, which is the opposite of the point.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves being the first point of contact.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse she has put off a mammogram for three years, because at her last visit staff repeatedly asked questions about her partner. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Reassure her that staff attitudes have improved since then
options.rationale: A promise the nurse cannot keep and that asks her to trust an institution that has already failed her.

options.text: Document that the patient declined screening for three years
options.rationale: This records the gap without doing anything about it, and declined misstates what happened. She was driven away, not asked and refused.

options.text: Explain the importance of regular screening and the risks of delay
options.rationale: This is correct teaching that assumes the barrier is knowledge. She knows why screening matters; she is avoiding the experience of getting it.

options.text: Acknowledge what happened and arrange the screening with the concern addressed
options.rationale: The barrier is the previous encounter. Naming it and changing what happens this time is what makes the screening possible.

questions.takeaway: Avoidance after a bad encounter is an access problem. Address what happened before addressing the screening.
questions.strategy: One option teaches, one documents, one reassures. None of them changes what she is afraid will happen again.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves acknowledging it and arranging the screening differently.

questions.scenario: A 68-year-old is admitted for a scheduled procedure. She lives with the woman she calls her partner of 30 years, who is not listed anywhere in the record. During admission she asks twice whether her partner will be allowed to stay, and says a previous hospital sent her partner home at the end of visiting hours while family members of other patients remained. She has not had a primary care visit in four years.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Confirm with her what the visiting arrangements are and tell the team
options.rationale: Answers the question she has now asked twice, and makes the arrangement known to the people who will enforce it.

options.text: Ask who she wants documented as her support person and record it where staff will see
options.rationale: Records that assume a family structure are what produced the exclusion last time. Writing down the support person she names is what stops it repeating.

options.text: Reassure her that this hospital does not discriminate
options.rationale: A promise the nurse cannot enforce, offered instead of the documentation and communication that would actually secure it.

options.text: Document that the patient appears anxious about visiting policy
options.rationale: This records her anxiety as a finding and leaves the cause of it untouched. She will be just as anxious with it charted.

options.text: Knowledge deficit regarding hospital visiting policy
options.rationale: Frames it as not knowing the rules. She knows what happened last time; the issue is whether it happens again.

options.text: Lack of family support during hospitalization
options.rationale: She has support. The risk is that the institution will not recognize it.

options.text: Anxiety related to the upcoming procedure
options.rationale: This is plausible and it is not what she asked about. Both of her questions were about her partner, not the operation.

options.text: Anticipated exclusion of her partner, based on a previous experience
options.rationale: She has asked twice and told you why. The problem is a reasonable expectation built from what happened before.

options.text: Whether her vital signs remain stable before the procedure
options.rationale: Stable vital signs are a real parameter and they evaluate nothing you changed. Nothing in the plan was aimed at her blood pressure.

options.text: Whether she can state the hospital's visiting policy
options.rationale: Tests recall of a rule. The problem was never that she did not know one.

options.text: Whether her partner is recorded and treated as her support person by all staff
options.rationale: This measures whether the documentation actually changed how staff behaved, which is the only thing that matters to her.

options.text: Whether she raises the question again
options.rationale: She asked twice. If she stops asking, the question has been answered to her satisfaction.

questions.takeaway: Lack of affirmation discourages people from using services. A partner unrecognized by the record is how that exclusion happens in practice.
questions.strategy: Two problem options relocate the issue into her, as anxiety or as not knowing. She told you it is about what happened last time.

strategies: Match each part to what the stem gives

steps.detail: Twice, about her partner, with a reason.

steps.action: Cut the options that relocate it

steps.detail: You documented and you told the team.

elimination.verdict: Document and communicate, for anticipated exclusion, evaluated by staff behavior and whether she asks again.

questions.stem: A clinic schedules every patient for a 15-minute visit and sends every patient home with the same printed handout. A nurse points out that patients who need an interpreter receive less information in that time than patients who do not. Which principle supports the concern?

options.text: Health equity, matching resources to patient need
options.rationale: Equity asks what a patient needs to reach the same outcome. The interpreted visit needs more minutes to deliver the same teaching, so identical scheduling produces unequal care.

options.text: Health equality, giving every patient the same thing
options.rationale: The emotionally satisfying answer and the wrong one. Equality is exactly what the clinic is already doing, and it is what created the gap.

options.text: Beneficence, acting in the patient's best interest
options.rationale: This is true of the nurse's motive and too broad to name the problem. Beneficence does not explain why giving everyone the same thing fails here.

options.text: Cultural competence, learning about patient groups
options.rationale: Knowledge about groups would not add the minutes back. The barrier is structural rather than informational.

questions.takeaway: Equality gives everyone the same. Equity gives each patient what it takes to reach the same outcome. Identical treatment can produce unequal care.
questions.strategy: When an option restates the policy that caused the problem, it is the distractor.

strategies: Name what the policy already does

steps.action: Notice the clinic is treating everyone alike
Choose the principle that accounts for need

elimination.verdict: Health equity is the answer.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman is admitted to a long-term care facility. The record lists her partner of 40 years as a friend. She asks the nurse not to mention the relationship to the rest of the staff. Which nursing action best addresses the concern behind that request?

options.text: Correct the record so the relationship is listed accurately
options.rationale: Accuracy serves the patient only when the patient wants it. Overriding the request hands out information the patient deliberately withheld.

options.text: Document the request and hold the limits the patient set
options.rationale: Disclosure belongs to the patient. Older LGBTQ+ patients entering congregate care often return to concealment because they expect worse treatment, and the nurse's job is to make the limit hold rather than test it.

options.text: Reassure the patient that staff here are trained to be inclusive
options.rationale: A promise the nurse cannot verify, and it answers a fear with optimism instead of control.

options.text: Encourage disclosure so the partner can be fully involved
options.rationale: Well meant pressure is still pressure. It asks the patient to accept a risk for the nurse's idea of better care.

questions.takeaway: Disclosure is the patient's to control. Entering a facility is exactly when an older LGBTQ+ patient is most likely to re-conceal, and the nurse protects that choice rather than correcting it.
questions.strategy: Options that make the patient more visible feel like advocacy. Ask who carries the risk if they are wrong.

strategies: Ask who owns the information

steps.action: Cut the options that widen disclosure
steps.detail: Correcting the record and encouraging it both do.

elimination.verdict: Document the request and hold the limit.

questions.stem: A patient who is transgender is admitted for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. While taking the surgical history, the nurse considers how to ask about previous gender-affirming surgery. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Ask about prior abdominal and pelvic surgeries only
options.rationale: Ask what bears on this operation. Previous abdominal or pelvic surgery of any kind raises the chance of adhesions, and that is a surgical fact rather than a question about gender.

options.text: Ask about all gender-affirming surgeries for completeness
options.rationale: Completeness is the stated reason and curiosity is the usual one. A chest reconstruction has no bearing on a gallbladder.

options.text: Avoid the surgical history entirely to protect privacy
options.rationale: Avoidance is not respect. Skipping relevant history puts the patient at risk in the operating room.

options.text: Review the record instead of asking the patient directly
options.rationale: Records are frequently incomplete or wrong on this. The patient is the better source, and this question is clinically relevant to an abdominal operation.

questions.takeaway: Ask about anatomy and procedures that affect the care in front of you. Gender-affirming surgery is relevant when the site is relevant, and not otherwise.
questions.strategy: Two options sound protective. Neither gets the clinical information this operation requires.

strategies: Tie each question to this admission

steps.action: Ask what affects a laparoscopic approach

elimination.verdict: Ask about abdominal and pelvic surgeries.

questions.scenario: Maria is 68 with well-controlled hypertension. She takes her medication daily, gardens, volunteers at her church, and says she feels healthy and happy despite occasional knee pain.
questions.stem: For each model of health, indicate whether it would judge Maria healthy or not healthy.

rows.text: Clinical model
rows.rationale: Health is the absence of disease. She has a diagnosis and knee pain, so this model calls her unhealthy regardless of how she lives.

rows.text: Role performance model
rows.rationale: She fulfills her roles: she gardens and volunteers. Function is what this model measures.

rows.text: Adaptive model
rows.rationale: She has adapted to a chronic condition and manages it daily. Adaptation is the measure.

rows.text: Eudaimonistic model
rows.rationale: She reports meaning and satisfaction through her gardening and volunteering, and self-actualization is what this model measures.

questions.takeaway: Only the clinical model says a person with a chronic condition cannot be healthy. The other three judge function, adaptation, or fulfillment.
questions.strategy: One model disagrees with the other three, and the reason is that it looks only at the diagnosis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only one is looking at her blood pressure.
She functions, adapts, and finds meaning.

elimination.verdict: Clinical says no. The rest say yes.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has stopped attending the choir he sang with for twenty years, because of breathlessness. He manages his inhalers correctly and says he no longer feels like himself. Which model of health best captures what he has lost?

options.text: Clinical, because his lung disease is progressing
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem says the disease has worsened. He describes a loss that the clinical model cannot see.

options.text: Adaptive, because he has failed to adjust to his diagnosis
options.rationale: He uses his inhalers correctly and has changed his activity. That is adaptation, not failure to adapt.

options.text: Role performance, because he cannot perform his usual activities
options.rationale: The near-miss, and singing in a choir is not a societal or work role. What he lost was meaning rather than function.

options.text: Eudaimonistic, because meaning and life satisfaction have gone
options.rationale: He is managing the disease and performing daily tasks. What has gone is the thing that made his life feel like his own.

questions.takeaway: Eudaimonistic health is self-actualization: satisfaction, meaning, and growth. It is the model that sees what the others miss.
questions.strategy: Two options describe things he is actually doing well. The near-miss turns a source of meaning into a role.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what he is still doing

steps.detail: A choir is meaning, not a societal role.

elimination.verdict: That leaves eudaimonistic.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses two patients with the same diagnosis and the same severity whose management of it differs greatly. Which variables influence health? Select all that apply.

options.text: Genetics and age
options.rationale: Genetics and age both shape health and neither one can be changed. You assess them to decide how hard to screen and teach.

options.text: The severity of the diagnosis itself
options.rationale: The stem holds severity constant between the two patients, so it cannot explain the difference between them.

options.text: Environment and lifestyle
options.rationale: Environment and lifestyle are two of the seven, and they are the ones nursing intervention actually reaches.

options.text: Culture and socioeconomic status
options.rationale: Culture shapes what health means to a person; socioeconomic status shapes what is available to them.

options.text: Access to health care
options.rationale: The last of the seven. A plan a patient cannot reach does not work.

options.text: The nurse's own health beliefs
options.rationale: They shape the encounter and are not a variable influencing the patient's health.

questions.takeaway: Seven variables influence health: genetics, age, environment, lifestyle, culture, socioeconomic status, and access to health care.
questions.strategy: The stem holds two things constant on purpose. Anything that does not vary cannot explain a difference.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It cannot explain a difference it does not vary with.
About the nurse, not the patient.

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man develops crushing chest pain while mowing the lawn. He sits down, tells his wife it is indigestion, and takes an antacid. Which stage of illness behavior does this represent?

options.text: Assumption of the sick role
options.rationale: Stage two, where a person accepts being ill and seeks relief from usual duties. He is minimizing rather than accepting.

options.text: Medical care contact
options.rationale: Medical care contact is stage three, and he has contacted nobody. He is still explaining the pain to himself.

options.text: Symptom experience
options.rationale: Stage one. He has noticed something is wrong and is interpreting it, which is exactly what this stage is.

options.text: Dependent patient role
options.rationale: Stage four, where the person accepts care from others. He has not entered the system at all.

questions.takeaway: Five stages: symptom experience, assumption of the sick role, medical care contact, dependent patient role, recovery and rehabilitation.
questions.strategy: Every distractor is a later stage. Ask how far into the sequence he has actually travelled.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Noticed a symptom and named it something harmless.
He has told nobody and accepted nothing.

elimination.verdict: That leaves symptom experience.

questions.stem: A self-employed builder has had a persistent cough for six weeks. He tells the nurse he has been calling it a chest cold because he cannot afford to lose a week of work. Which concept explains his delay in seeking care?

options.text: Assumption of the sick role
options.rationale: Stage two, where a person accepts being ill. He is doing the opposite.

options.text: Illness behavior
options.rationale: Illness behavior is how a person monitors, interprets, and responds to symptoms. Calling a six-week cough a chest cold is the interpretation; not seeking care is the response.

options.text: Perceived severity
options.rationale: A Health Belief Model construct about how serious he judges it to be. It is one input into illness behavior rather than the concept itself.

options.text: The dependent patient role
options.rationale: Stage four, where care from others is accepted. He has not entered care.

questions.takeaway: Illness behavior is influenced by culture, family, education, and past experiences.
questions.strategy: Three options name a specific stage or construct. Ask which term covers the whole pattern of interpreting and responding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Interpreting a symptom and deciding not to act.
He has neither accepted the sick role nor entered care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves illness behavior.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse plans care for a community with a high rate of cardiovascular disease.

Running a cardiac rehabilitation group for people who have had a myocardial infarction is [[1]].

Running a school program that teaches children never to start smoking is [[2]].

Teaching a patient with diabetes how to inspect the feet is [[3]].

Offering blood pressure checks at a community event is [[4]].

options.text: tertiary prevention
options.rationale: The heart attack has already happened. Rehabilitation limits further damage and loss of function, which is tertiary.

options.text: primary prevention
options.rationale: This is far too late for primary prevention, which acts before any disease exists.

options.text: secondary prevention
options.rationale: Detection is behind them. The diagnosis is established, so there is nothing left to find early.

options.text: restorative care
options.rationale: Restorative care is a level of care rather than a level of prevention. The question asks about prevention.

options.text: secondary prevention
options.rationale: Secondary prevention looks for disease that is already present but has not caused symptoms yet. Nothing has started here.

options.text: health promotion
options.rationale: The near-miss. Health promotion is broad and aimed at wellbeing; this targets one specific disease, which makes it prevention.

options.text: tertiary prevention
options.rationale: Tertiary prevention limits complications in someone who already has the disease. These children do not.

options.text: primary prevention
options.rationale: This acts before any disease exists, in people who are currently well. That is what primary prevention means.

options.text: primary prevention
options.rationale: The disease is already present, so nothing here prevents it occurring.

options.text: health education
options.rationale: It is health education, and the question asks which level of prevention it serves.

options.text: secondary prevention
options.rationale: This is the near-miss. He is looking for early skin changes in a disease he already has, which makes it a complication rather than detection of something new.

options.text: tertiary prevention
options.rationale: He already has diabetes, and checking his feet exists to stop an ulcer becoming an amputation. That is tertiary prevention.

options.text: tertiary prevention
options.rationale: Tertiary prevention manages a disease that has already been diagnosed. Screening happens before any diagnosis exists.

options.text: secondary prevention
options.rationale: Screening finds disease early, before symptoms bring anyone in. That is secondary prevention, even in people who feel fine.

options.text: secondary care
options.rationale: A level of the health care system, not a level of prevention. Same word, unrelated systems.

options.text: primary prevention
options.rationale: Primary prevention acts before the disease occurs. A screening is looking for disease that may already be there.

questions.takeaway: Primary prevents disease occurring. Secondary detects it early. Tertiary limits complications once it exists.
questions.strategy: Ask one question of each: does the person have the disease yet? No is primary, maybe is secondary, yes is tertiary.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Secondary prevention is screening; secondary care is hospital treatment.

elimination.verdict: Primary, secondary, tertiary, tertiary.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old smoker whose father died of lung cancer at 60 tells the nurse, I know smoking is dangerous, but it is not going to happen to me. Which Health Belief Model construct does this reflect?

options.text: Low perceived severity
options.rationale: Severity is how serious he judges the outcome to be. He watched his father die of it, so he is unlikely to underrate its seriousness.

options.text: Low perceived benefits
options.rationale: Benefits concern whether he thinks quitting would help. He has not said quitting would not work.

options.text: Low perceived susceptibility
options.rationale: He accepts the risk exists and does not accept it applies to him. That gap is susceptibility.

options.text: High perceived barriers
options.rationale: Barriers are what stands in the way, such as cost or withdrawal. He has named none.

questions.takeaway: Health Belief Model: perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits, perceived barriers.
questions.strategy: The family history is placed to rule one option out. Someone who watched a parent die of a disease knows how serious it is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That it will happen to him.

elimination.verdict: That leaves low perceived susceptibility.

questions.stem: A nurse works with a patient who wants to lose weight and has not managed to change anything in six months. Which barriers should the nurse assess in him? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fear about what change might involve
options.rationale: Fear is a named barrier, and it includes the fear of trying and failing again after six months of not managing it.

options.text: His motivation to change
options.rationale: Motivation is one of the four requirements for change, not a barrier. The stem already tells you he wants to.

options.text: Health literacy
options.rationale: Named. A plan he cannot read or interpret is not a plan he can follow.

options.text: His genetic predisposition to weight gain
options.rationale: A non-modifiable risk factor. It affects the difficulty of the goal rather than standing between him and starting.

options.text: Time available to make the change
options.rationale: Named, and it is why plans built for someone with free evenings fail.

options.text: Cost of the changes involved
options.rationale: A named barrier, and gym fees or fresh food can make a plan unreachable.

questions.takeaway: Change requires motivation, knowledge, resources, and support. Barriers include cost, time, fear, and health literacy.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a requirement for change rather than a barrier, and the stem has already established it is present.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He wants to; that is given.
Non-modifiable, and not a barrier to starting.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse plans a program for a workplace. Which activity is health promotion rather than illness prevention?

options.text: An on-site influenza vaccination clinic
options.rationale: A flu clinic is illness prevention: one named disease, one intervention aimed at stopping it.

options.text: Mammography screening arranged for eligible staff
options.rationale: Mammography targets one disease and looks for it early. That is prevention, and specifically the secondary kind.

options.text: A campaign encouraging seatbelt use in company vehicles
options.rationale: Illness prevention. It targets a specific harm before it happens, which puts seatbelts under primary prevention.

options.text: A stress management and exercise program open to all staff
options.rationale: Health promotion is broad and aimed at increasing wellbeing and maximizing health potential. It targets no single disease.

questions.takeaway: Health promotion improves wellness and has a broad focus. Illness prevention targets a specific disease or harm.
questions.strategy: Three options name one disease or one harm each. Ask which one has no particular target.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the one with no target

elimination.verdict: That leaves the stress and exercise program.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a 52-year-old man's risk factors: 20 cigarettes a day, heavy weekend drinking, a sedentary routine, a body mass index of 34, a father who died of myocardial infarction at 55, and an ethnicity carrying raised cardiovascular risk. Which of his risk factors are modifiable? Select all that apply.

options.text: Heavy alcohol use
options.rationale: Alcohol use is modifiable, and weekend drinking at this level is one of the things he can change.

options.text: His father's death from myocardial infarction at 55
options.rationale: Family history is genetics, and genetics is non-modifiable. It raises the urgency of changing the others.

options.text: Being sedentary
options.rationale: Activity level can be changed, which makes a sedentary routine modifiable and a reasonable place to start.

options.text: Smoking 20 cigarettes a day
options.rationale: Smoking is modifiable, and it is the single change on this list with the largest effect on his risk.

options.text: A body mass index of 34
options.rationale: Weight is modifiable, though it moves slowly and usually follows changes in diet and activity rather than leading them.

options.text: His ethnicity
options.rationale: Ethnicity is non-modifiable. It tells you how aggressively to screen, and it is never itself a target.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable: smoking, diet, alcohol and drug use, weight. Non-modifiable: age, genetics, biological sex, ethnicity.
questions.strategy: Two of his risk factors are real and cannot be changed. They alter how urgent the others are, not whether they are targets.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what he could change tomorrow

elimination.verdict: A, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse on a busy oncology unit finds herself irritable with colleagues, dreading her shifts, and no longer moved by patients' distress. She has worked twelve-hour shifts without a break for three months. Which is she most likely experiencing?

options.text: Compassion fatigue
options.rationale: Emotional and physical exhaustion from prolonged caregiving. The decreased empathy alongside irritability and cynicism is the recognizable picture.

options.text: A normal adjustment to a demanding specialty
options.rationale: This normalizes a recognized syndrome, and normalizing it is how the problem goes unaddressed.

options.text: Ineffective coping with the patients' diagnoses
options.rationale: Closer, and it locates the problem in her response to individual patients rather than in cumulative exposure.

options.text: An underlying mood disorder requiring referral
options.rationale: Possible, and the occupational pattern and timing point first to compassion fatigue. Assessment precedes that conclusion.

questions.takeaway: Compassion fatigue: emotional exhaustion, irritability, cynicism, decreased empathy, burnout. Prevention is boundaries, self-care, peer support, mindfulness, debriefing, and counselling when needed.
questions.strategy: One option normalizes it. One reaches for a diagnosis before assessing. Ask what the three months of unbroken shifts adds.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Irritability, dread, lost empathy, no breaks.
These are named findings, not adjustment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves compassion fatigue.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with well-controlled hypertension and osteoarthritis gardens daily, volunteers twice a week, and describes feeling well. A new nurse says she cannot be called healthy with two chronic diagnoses. Which definition of health contradicts that view?

options.text: Health means the absence of any diagnosed disease
options.rationale: The clinical model, and the narrowest definition on the list. It makes anyone with a diagnosis permanently unhealthy, which is exactly what the new nurse just did.

options.text: Health is the ability to perform paid work roles
options.rationale: The role performance model. It would call this patient healthy for the wrong reason, and it would call a retired person unhealthy.

options.text: Health becomes a fixed state once disease appears
options.rationale: Reverses the point. Health is dynamic, and a person moves along a continuum rather than losing health permanently at the moment of diagnosis.

options.text: Health is complete physical, mental and social wellbeing
options.rationale: This is broader than the absence of disease, and that is the part that matters. A patient with two managed diagnoses who functions well and feels well fits it.

questions.takeaway: WHO: complete physical, mental, and social wellbeing, not just the absence of disease. Six dimensions: physical, emotional, intellectual, social, spiritual, environmental.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are models of health offered as the definition. One contradicts the continuum.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Not merely the absence of disease.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the WHO definition.

questions.nursesNote: 1100: Patient is 61, attends for a routine review. Reports sleeping four to five hours most nights since being moved to night shifts six months ago. Has gained 8 kg in that time. Says meals come from vending machines at work because nothing else is open. Blood pressure 152/94, up from 128/80 a year ago. Smokes 15 a day, unchanged for 20 years. Walks a dog twice daily. Says friends are no longer seen because the hours no longer match theirs. Temperature 36.6 C. Attends the annual review every year without fail.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that represent modifiable risks the nurse can address.

segments.text: Eats from vending machines because nothing else is open
segments.rationale: Diet is modifiable, and he has named the barrier himself, which is what makes it addressable.

segments.text: Attends the annual review every year without fail
segments.rationale: A health-seeking behavior and another strength. It is why you are able to catch this at all.

segments.text: Sleeping four to five hours most nights
segments.rationale: Sleep hygiene is named under health promotion, and short sleep affects weight, blood pressure and mood.

segments.text: Blood pressure 152/94, up from 128/80 a year ago
segments.rationale: A change from his own baseline, and it is the consequence the other findings are producing.

segments.text: Gained 8 kg in six months
segments.rationale: Weight is a named modifiable risk factor, and the rate of gain makes it recent and reversible.

segments.text: Has stopped seeing friends because the hours no longer match theirs
segments.rationale: Social isolation affects the social dimension of health and removes the support systems that behavior change requires.

segments.text: Smokes 15 a day
segments.rationale: Smoking is the first named modifiable risk factor. Unchanged for years does not mean unchangeable.

segments.text: Temperature 36.6 C
segments.rationale: A normal temperature. Nothing here needs addressing.

segments.text: Walks a dog twice daily
segments.rationale: Something he is already doing well. It is a strength, not a risk.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable risks are the ones nursing can act on. Strengths matter too, and they are not risks.
questions.strategy: Two findings describe things he is doing right, and one is normal. A strength offered among risk factors is there to be left alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The dog walk and the attendance are strengths.
Night shifts changed sleep, food, weight and pressure.

elimination.verdict: s1, s3, s4, s5, s6, and s7: diet, sleep, pressure, weight, isolation, and smoking.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares discharge teaching for a patient newly diagnosed with heart failure. Which content is the priority before he goes home?

options.text: The pathophysiology of how heart failure develops
options.rationale: Interesting and it does not change what he does on Tuesday when his weight is up two kilograms.

options.text: When to notify the provider and how to recognize the signs that matter
options.rationale: Health education exists so patients can make informed decisions. Knowing when to seek help is what prevents the readmission.

options.text: A complete list of his medication side effects
options.rationale: Medication instruction is named content, and an exhaustive list without priorities is not usable at home.

options.text: The names and roles of the team members who cared for him
options.rationale: Knowing the team's names is courteous and it prevents nothing. He needs to know which symptoms mean call tonight.

questions.takeaway: Health education asks what the patient needs to know before discharge to stay healthy and prevent complications. When to seek help sits at the top.
questions.strategy: Three options contain real information. Ask which one he will act on at home.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what he does with each
Cut the exhaustive list and the team names

elimination.verdict: That leaves when to notify the provider.

questions.stem: A patient with a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes attends a follow-up. He has learned to adjust his meals, check his glucose, and plan around his work shifts, and says it has become routine. Which model of health evaluates him most favorably?

options.text: The clinical model, because his glucose is being monitored
options.rationale: The clinical model measures absence of disease. He has diabetes, so this model does not judge him healthy.

options.text: The adaptive model, because he has adjusted to the change
options.rationale: Adaptive health is the ability to adapt flexibly. Coping with a new diagnosis is her own example of it.

options.text: The role performance model, because he keeps working
options.rationale: This is plausible, and the stem is about how he adjusted rather than which roles he still fills. Working is evidence, not the model being described.

options.text: The eudaimonistic model, because he has found meaning
options.rationale: He describes routine, not meaning or growth. This model would need more than competent management.

questions.takeaway: Adaptive health is resilience and flexible adjustment. Her examples are coping with a new diagnosis and adjusting after an amputation.
questions.strategy: The stem emphasizes one particular thing about him. Ask what word describes what he did.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Adjusted his life around a new condition.
One is function, one needs meaning.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the adaptive model.

questions.stem: A nurse works with a community where many residents have no supermarket within three miles, limited bus services, and high unemployment. Rates of diabetes are well above the national average. Which concept explains the link?

options.text: Social determinants of health
options.rationale: Non-medical conditions where people live, learn, work and age, which shape daily wellbeing and life expectancy. Transportation, food security and employment are her examples.

options.text: Non-modifiable risk factors
options.rationale: Genetics, age, sex and ethnicity. The conditions described are features of a place, and places can change.

options.text: Illness behavior
options.rationale: How individuals monitor and respond to symptoms. The stem describes conditions before anyone becomes symptomatic.

options.text: The clinical model of health
options.rationale: A way of defining health, not an explanation of why a population's rates differ.

questions.takeaway: Social determinants of health are non-medical conditions with major effects on health, daily wellbeing, and life expectancy.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats a feature of a neighborhood as though it were fixed like genetics.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut illness behavior and the clinical model
steps.detail: One is about symptoms, one is a definition.

elimination.verdict: That leaves social determinants of health.

questions.stem: A nurse joins a county initiative that measures the gap in infant mortality between neighborhoods and sets a ten-year target to close it. Which national framework does this work follow?

options.text: Healthy People 2030, which sets population health objectives
options.rationale: Its aims are to improve health and wellbeing, eliminate disparities, promote healthy environments, and increase health equity. Closing a neighborhood gap in infant mortality is that work exactly.

options.text: The Joint Commission's accreditation standards for organizations
options.rationale: The Joint Commission accredits organizations against clinical and safety standards. It sets no ten-year population targets.

options.text: The ANA Scope and Standards of Professional Practice
options.rationale: The ANA standards describe what nurses do and how they perform. They set no population health objectives for a county.

options.text: The state nurse practice act and its implementing regulations
options.rationale: A practice act governs who may practise and within what limits. It sets no health targets for a population.

questions.takeaway: Healthy People 2030: improve health and wellbeing, eliminate disparities, promote healthy environments, increase health equity.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name real functions performed by other bodies entirely.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what kind of document it is

elimination.verdict: That leaves the four aims.

questions.stem: A nursing student discusses health and wellness with her preceptor. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Someone with a chronic illness can still be healthy under most models."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Only the clinical model would call Maria unhealthy, and three of the four models call her healthy.

options.text: "Health sits on a continuum rather than being present or absent."
options.rationale: This is accurate. The continuum runs from high-level wellness through neutral health and illness to death, and people move along it.

options.text: "Learning to manage my blood pressure now counts as primary prevention."
options.rationale: Managing a diagnosed condition is tertiary prevention. Primary acts before disease exists, and hers already does.

options.text: "Illness affects the family as well as the patient."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Caregiver burden, lost income, shifted roles and emotional strain all land on the family.

questions.takeaway: Primary prevents disease occurring. Secondary detects it early. Tertiary manages an established condition to limit complications.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her key takeaways correctly. The fourth misplaces a level of prevention.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Chronic illness, continuum, family impact. All accurate.
Management of an existing condition is tertiary.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the primary prevention statement.

questions.scenario: A 44-year-old attends a follow-up three months after being told the diagnosis is prediabetes. The exercise plan has not started and the diet has not changed. The patient says the reasons are understood, works two cleaning jobs with a two-hour commute, and that the recommended gym costs more than a week of food. Weight is unchanged and fasting glucose has risen from 112 to 119 mg/dL.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Build a plan around activity that costs nothing and fits her existing day
options.rationale: Cost and time are the two barriers she has named. A plan that avoids both is one she can actually start.

options.text: Connect her with community food and activity resources she can reach
options.rationale: Advocating for resources is part of the nursing role in risk reduction, and it addresses the barrier rather than the behavior.

options.text: Re-teach the risks of progressing from prediabetes to diabetes
options.rationale: This is correct teaching aimed at the wrong problem. She has already told you she understands why it matters.

options.text: Document that she has not adhered to the recommended plan
options.rationale: This records the outcome and calls it her failure. The stem has already told you what stood in the way.

options.text: Non-modifiable risk factors driving her rising glucose
options.rationale: Her risks here are diet and activity, both modifiable. Naming them fixed would end the intervention.

options.text: Lack of motivation to change her health behaviors
options.rationale: This blames her for a plan that never fit her life. Nothing suggests she does not want to change.

options.text: Knowledge deficit about diabetes prevention
options.rationale: She states she understands. Assuming a knowledge gap is what produces more teaching and no change.

options.text: Barriers of cost and time preventing a plan she is motivated to follow
options.rationale: Motivation and knowledge are both present. What is missing is resources and time, which are two of the four requirements for change.

options.text: Her fasting glucose at the next visit
options.rationale: The outcome the whole intervention exists to move, and it is already trending the wrong way.

options.text: Whether she can state three complications of diabetes
options.rationale: Tests knowledge she already has, and it evaluates teaching nobody identified as the problem.

options.text: Whether she attends her next appointment
options.rationale: Attendance is worth noticing, and showing up does not tell you whether the plan was usable.

options.text: Whether she has started and sustained any of the agreed activity
options.rationale: This measures whether the redesigned plan actually worked in her week, which is the thing you changed.

questions.takeaway: Change requires motivation, knowledge, resources, and support. When the first two are present and nothing happens, look at the last two.
questions.strategy: Two problem options blame her motivation or her knowledge. She has told you she has both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Motivation yes, knowledge yes, resources no, time no.
Knowledge deficit and lack of motivation.
You redesigned the plan, so measure whether she started.

elimination.verdict: Redesign and connect resources, for cost and time barriers, evaluated by uptake and glucose.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from pneumonia says, I am not sick anymore but I am not back to normal either. The nurse documents that she is somewhere between illness and wellness. Which model of health does that reflect?

options.text: The health-illness continuum, where health shifts along a range
options.rationale: Health is constantly changing, and the same person occupies different points at different times. Between illness and wellness is a described position on it.

options.text: The health belief model, which predicts preventive action
options.rationale: The health belief model explains why people do or do not take preventive action. It does not describe moving between states of health.

options.text: The basic human needs model, ranking needs by urgency
options.rationale: Maslow ranks needs by urgency so you know what to address first. It says nothing about where a person sits between illness and wellness.

options.text: The holistic health model, which treats mind and body
options.rationale: The holistic model addresses the whole person rather than the disease. It describes the scope of care, not a position along a range of health.

questions.takeaway: The continuum runs from high-level wellness through neutral health to illness and death, and a person moves along it in both directions.
questions.strategy: Two distractors treat health as a fixed state. One invents a direction of travel.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves movement along the continuum.

questions.stem: A nurse on an oncology unit has begun avoiding conversations with families, feels blank during report, and dreads the drive in. The workload and staffing have not changed in a year. Which description fits this pattern?

options.text: Compassion fatigue from sustained exposure to suffering
options.rationale: Look at who the numbness is aimed at. Compassion fatigue blunts feeling toward patients and families, and it comes from the caring itself rather than the hours.

options.text: Burnout from excessive workload and short staffing
options.rationale: The reflex answer, and the stem rules it out. Workload and staffing are unchanged, so the cause lies elsewhere.

options.text: Moral distress from being unable to act rightly
options.rationale: Requires a known right action the nurse is blocked from taking. Nothing here describes one.

options.text: Lateral violence within the nursing team
options.rationale: Nothing in the history involves colleagues. The withdrawal is from patients and families.

questions.takeaway: Compassion fatigue comes from absorbing suffering and shows up as numbness toward patients. Burnout comes from the job's conditions and shows up as exhaustion with the work.
questions.strategy: One line in the stem exists only to kill an option. Here it is the unchanged workload.

strategies: Use the detail that rules something out

steps.action: Ask what the numbness points at
Cut moral distress and lateral violence

elimination.verdict: Compassion fatigue.

questions.stem: At a community health fair a 55-year-old man has a blood pressure of 168/102 mm Hg on two readings ten minutes apart. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day, has a body mass index of 33, and has no primary care provider. Which action takes priority?

options.text: Provide smoking cessation resources and a referral
options.rationale: Addresses the largest long-term risk and the wrong timescale. Cessation changes the next decade.

options.text: Teach about sodium reduction and weight loss
options.rationale: Teaching about salt and weight is appropriate health promotion. It is not what a pressure of 168/102 needs in the next hour.

options.text: Arrange evaluation of the blood pressure today
options.rationale: Two readings at that level is an unevaluated finding in someone with no provider. The point of screening is the follow-up, and without it the reading changes nothing.

options.text: Schedule a repeat pressure check in one month
options.rationale: Treats the reading as surveillance rather than a finding. A month is a long time at 168/102.

questions.takeaway: A screening finding only helps if it connects to evaluation. Health promotion sits behind an abnormal result that is not yet being managed.
questions.strategy: Every option is good health promotion. The question is which one is time-critical.

strategies: Acute before chronic

steps.detail: Cessation and weight are not today's problem.

elimination.verdict: Arrange evaluation today.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman arrives at urgent care with 40 minutes of crushing substernal pain. She is diaphoretic, says it is indigestion, and asks for an antacid so she can leave. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Obtain a 12-lead electrocardiogram without delay
options.rationale: Forty minutes of crushing substernal pain with diaphoresis is a cardiac presentation whatever the patient calls it. The electrocardiogram is the time-critical step and it does not wait on the patient agreeing with the concern.

options.text: Explain the risks of leaving before an evaluation
options.rationale: Necessary conversation and it comes while the workup is running, not instead of it.

options.text: Document that the patient attributes the pain to indigestion
options.rationale: Recording the patient's interpretation while the heart is the question. Documenting is not acting.

options.text: Offer an antacid and reassess in thirty minutes
options.rationale: This accepts what the patient said at face value and buys thirty minutes of myocardium. It is the option that looks responsive.

questions.takeaway: A patient minimizing symptoms does not lower the risk. Crushing substernal pain with diaphoresis gets an electrocardiogram before anything is negotiated.
questions.strategy: When a patient supplies a benign explanation in the stem, it will be one of the options. Treat it as a finding about the patient, not as data about the diagnosis.

strategies: ABCs and acute before chronic

steps.action: Read the findings, not the patient's label

steps.detail: Delays the only test that answers the question.

elimination.verdict: Get the electrocardiogram.

sources.title: Caring in Nursing Practice
sources.label: Potter Ch. 7 · Caring in Nursing Practice

questions.stem: Two nurses complete identical admission assessments on a patient with pneumonia. The first works quickly, says little, and leaves. The second introduces herself, sits at eye level, explains each step, and asks what worries the patient most today. Both assessments are clinically complete. What distinguishes the second nurse's care?

options.text: The second nurse gathered more assessment data before acting
options.rationale: Identical assessments. Asking what worries her is presence rather than an extra data point, though it may well produce one.

options.text: The second nurse was more clinically competent at the task
options.rationale: The stem states both assessments were complete. Competence is not what separates them.

options.text: How the care was delivered, not only what was done
options.rationale: Caring involves both what nurses do and how they do it. The assessment data is identical; the experience of being assessed is not.

options.text: The second nurse spent more minutes with the patient
options.rationale: Time is a consequence rather than the distinction. Sitting at eye level and introducing yourself cost seconds.

questions.takeaway: Caring is what nurses do and how they do it. Two technically identical encounters can differ entirely in whether the patient feels cared for.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you both were competent and both were complete. Whatever separates them is not clinical.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves how the care was delivered.

questions.stem: A hospital reviews patient comments to learn which nursing behaviors patients describe as caring. Which behaviors do patients most often name? Select all that apply.

options.text: Listening carefully
options.rationale: The behavior patients name most, and the one that costs nothing but attention.

options.text: Treating them with dignity
options.rationale: This is named, and it runs through both the bathing and the hygiene examples.

options.text: Completing tasks without disturbing the patient
options.rationale: This is efficient, and it is the nurse who does the assessment and leaves. Not disturbing someone is not the same as caring for them.

options.text: Explaining procedures
options.rationale: Named directly, and it turns something done to a patient into something done with them.

options.text: Responding promptly
options.rationale: Patients name this constantly. A call light answered quickly says something before anyone has spoken.

options.text: Protecting privacy
options.rationale: Patients name privacy, and protecting it is what makes an exposing task tolerable rather than humiliating.

options.text: Withholding difficult information until the patient seems ready
options.rationale: Protective in intention and closer to false reassurance than to caring. Patients name honesty and explanation.

questions.takeaway: Patients name: listens carefully, explains procedures, treats with dignity, responds promptly, shows kindness, includes family, protects privacy, advocates.
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe things a nurse might do out of consideration. Ask whether patients actually name them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Listen, explain, dignity, promptness, kindness, family, privacy, advocacy.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A patient with a new cancer diagnosis says, I have no idea how to tell my children. The nurse has six other patients and a medication round due. Which response demonstrates presence?

options.text: Offer to arrange a referral to the social worker
options.rationale: An appropriate referral, and offered now it moves her distress to someone else instead of meeting it.

options.text: Say you will come back after the medication round and follow through
options.rationale: Better than dismissing her, and it still asks a frightened woman to hold it for an hour. Presence is a few minutes now.

options.text: Tell her many families find a way and she will too
options.rationale: False reassurance. It is meant kindly and it closes the conversation she has just opened.

options.text: Sit down, put the tasks aside for a few minutes, and let her talk
options.rationale: Presence means full attention. Sitting signals you are not about to leave, and sometimes the most therapeutic intervention is simply being present.

questions.takeaway: Presence: sit at eye level, make eye contact, minimize distractions, listen without interrupting, validate feelings.
questions.strategy: Three options are things a considerate nurse might genuinely say. Ask which one meets her now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both move it elsewhere or later.

elimination.verdict: That leaves sitting down with her.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure has not been taking his diuretic. Which question reflects Caritas Coaching?

options.text: "Would it help if I explained how the medication works?"
options.rationale: This offers teaching before you know whether teaching is what he needs. It also answers a question he did not ask.

options.text: "What makes taking the water tablet difficult?"
options.rationale: Opens with the obstacle and assumes he has a reason. Caritas Coaching partners rather than instructs, and it helps patients find their own solutions.

options.text: "Do you understand why the water tablet matters?"
options.rationale: Checks knowledge and implies the problem is his understanding. It also invites a defensive yes.

options.text: "Did you take your medication this week?"
options.rationale: Her own example of the closed question Caritas Coaching replaces. It produces a yes or no and stops there.

questions.takeaway: Caritas Coaching listens first, asks open-ended questions, encourages reflection, supports the patient's goals, builds confidence, and partners.
questions.strategy: One distractor is the exact question this one is meant to be contrasted with. Ask which one cannot be answered with a single word.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Test each for a one-word answer
steps.detail: Three can be answered yes or no.
Assumes the gap before finding it.

elimination.verdict: That leaves asking what makes it difficult.

questions.scenario: A nurse cares for a patient admitted with pneumonia over one shift.
questions.stem: For each statement the nurse makes, indicate whether it is therapeutic or a communication block.

rows.text: "Everything will be fine."
rows.rationale: False reassurance. It is meant kindly and it tells him the subject is closed.

rows.text: Finishing his sentence when he pauses to catch his breath
rows.rationale: Interrupting, and in a breathless patient it also takes away the time he needs to speak.

rows.text: "I can see this is difficult."
rows.rationale: Validates the feeling without judging it, and it invites him to say more.

rows.text: "Try not to worry about it."
rows.rationale: Dismisses the worry rather than exploring it, and it asks him to manage his feeling alone.

rows.text: "Tell me more."
rows.rationale: The shortest way to keep someone talking, and it commits the nurse to listening.

rows.text: "What concerns you the most today?"
rows.rationale: This is open-ended and it hands him the agenda. He gets to say what the problem is rather than confirming yours.

questions.takeaway: Therapeutic: I can see this is difficult, tell me more, what concerns you most, how can I help. Blocks: false reassurance, don't worry, interrupting.
questions.strategy: The blocks all sound kind. Ask whether the statement opens the conversation or ends it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Does he say more, or stop?
Fine and don't worry both close it.

elimination.verdict: Three therapeutic, three blocking.

questions.stem: A nursing student says caring means being kind to patients. Which response by the preceptor is most accurate?

options.text: Caring includes competence, so warmth without skill is not caring
options.rationale: The definition names compassion, respect, presence, empathy and competence together. Professional competence and caring work together.

options.text: Kindness is the central element and the skills follow from it
options.rationale: This reverses the relationship between the two. Neither one produces the other, and caring requires both.

options.text: Kindness matters most with patients who are frightened or distressed
options.rationale: Makes caring conditional on the patient's state, and it applies to every interaction.

options.text: Caring is an attitude, while competence is a separate professional obligation
options.rationale: This separates two things that belong together. Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction.

questions.takeaway: Caring is intentional concern for wellbeing through compassion, respect, presence, empathy, and competence. Competence is part of it, not a separate track.
questions.strategy: Three options treat caring and competence as two different things. Ask what the definition actually contains.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Caring is not reserved for distress.

elimination.verdict: That leaves competence being part of caring.

questions.stem: A nurse performs a bed bath for a patient who is embarrassed about needing help. Which actions demonstrate caring during this skill? Select all that apply.

options.text: Close the door and the curtain before starting
options.rationale: Privacy is one of the caring behaviors patients name most. Closing the door costs nothing and changes the whole encounter.

options.text: Keep him covered except for the area being washed
options.rationale: Draping protects privacy and dignity at the same time. Expose what you are washing and nothing else.

options.text: Tell him there is nothing to be embarrassed about
options.rationale: Dismisses the feeling rather than validating it. His embarrassment is real whether or not it is necessary.

options.text: Work quickly so the embarrassing part is over sooner
options.rationale: This sounds considerate and produces the efficient, silent nurse. Speed is not the same as kindness here.

options.text: Ask what he would prefer to do himself
options.rationale: Asking what he wants to do himself preserves the independence he still has and makes him a participant rather than an object.

options.text: Explain each step before doing it
options.rationale: Turns something done to him into something he can anticipate and consent to.

questions.takeaway: Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction. For bathing, that means privacy and dignity specifically.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are kindly meant. One rushes, one tells him how to feel.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, E, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse administering an intravenous antibiotic explains what it is for, what side effects to report, and answers the patient's questions while the infusion runs. Which principle does this demonstrate?

options.text: Caring behaviors are most important during invasive procedures
options.rationale: This ranks the skills, and vital signs, medication, bathing and wound care all count alike.

options.text: Medication administration requires verbal consent for each dose
options.rationale: Explaining is not the same as obtaining consent, and no such requirement is described.

options.text: Patient education should be scheduled separately from procedures
options.rationale: This reverses the point. Teaching while you administer is the example, not a mistake to correct.

options.text: Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction
options.rationale: Caring is not a separate activity performed when there is time. The medication round became teaching and presence without adding a task.

questions.takeaway: Caring should be present during every skill. Vital signs, medication, bathing and wound care are all opportunities.
questions.strategy: One distractor makes caring a separate scheduled activity. One reserves it for the invasive tasks.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nothing, other than how she did it.
Teaching while administering is the example.

elimination.verdict: That leaves every skill being a caring interaction.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse reflects on her practice after a shift.

Sitting at eye level and listening without interrupting demonstrates [[1]].

Asking a patient what makes taking the medication difficult, rather than whether it was taken, is [[2]].

Saying "don't worry, everything will be fine" is an example of [[3]].

According to Watson, caring is best described as [[4]].

options.text: advocacy
options.rationale: Advocacy is acting on his behalf with other people. This describes what the nurse does in the room with him.

options.text: empathy
options.rationale: The near-miss. Empathy is understanding what he feels; presence is the behavior that makes room for him to say it.

options.text: competence
options.rationale: Competence is the skill to perform the care safely. It is necessary and it is not what is described here.

options.text: presence
options.rationale: This is full attention given deliberately: sitting down, eye contact, distractions cut, no interrupting. That is presence.

options.text: Caritas Coaching
options.rationale: Partnering instead of instructing, and helping him find his own solution. Her exact contrast.

options.text: therapeutic silence
options.rationale: Silence gives someone time to think. This is an open question, which is a different move.

options.text: motivational reassurance
options.rationale: This is not a named technique, and reassurance is one of the things coaching deliberately avoids.

options.text: health teaching
options.rationale: Teaching supplies information. This question supplies none and asks for his instead.

options.text: validating feelings
options.rationale: Validating names the feeling and stays with it. This statement dismisses the feeling instead.

options.text: false reassurance
options.rationale: This is false reassurance, named alongside don't worry and interrupting as a communication block.

options.text: offering self
options.rationale: Offering self is being available. This tells him not to feel what he feels.

options.text: giving information
options.rationale: No information is given here. It is a prediction that nobody is in a position to make.

options.text: the essence of nursing, and both an art and a science
options.rationale: Watson's position, and the art and science pairing is why competence sits inside caring.

options.text: an additional skill applied once clinical tasks are complete
options.rationale: This reverses the point. Every skill is itself a caring interaction, not a task you finish before caring starts.

options.text: a personality trait some nurses have and others do not
options.rationale: Makes caring innate rather than practised, which would make the whole theory pointless.

options.text: the emotional component of care, separate from the technical
options.rationale: This separates what Watson joins. Mind, body and spirit are treated as one thing, not as a clinical half and an emotional half.

questions.takeaway: Presence is the behavior. Caritas Coaching is the partnership. False reassurance is the block. Watson calls caring the essence of nursing, art and science together.
questions.strategy: Blank 1 has a real near-miss: empathy is the understanding, presence is what you visibly do.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Empathy is internal; presence is visible.
An open question that asks for his reason.

elimination.verdict: Presence, Caritas Coaching, false reassurance, essence of nursing.

questions.stem: A nurse asks a patient what has been hardest about managing his diet since his diagnosis. He describes his shift pattern and the food available at work. Together they agree he will eat his main meal before his shift rather than during it. Which describes what the nurse has done?

options.text: Negotiated a compromise between preference and the plan
options.rationale: Closer, and nothing was traded away. The dietary goal is unchanged; only the timing moved.

options.text: Partnered so the patient could find a workable solution
options.rationale: Caritas Coaching helps patients discover their own strengths and solutions. The plan came from his information, not from a leaflet.

options.text: Assessed adherence to the prescribed regimen
options.rationale: Adherence assessment asks whether he is doing it. She asked what was in the way, which is a different question.

options.text: Provided health teaching about dietary management
options.rationale: She supplied no dietary information at all. The solution came out of his description of his own shifts.

questions.takeaway: Caritas Coaching: listen first, ask open questions, encourage reflection, support the patient's goals, build confidence, partner.
questions.strategy: The near-miss calls it a compromise. Check whether anything clinical was actually given up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask where the plan came from

steps.detail: She supplied nothing and checked nothing.

elimination.verdict: That leaves partnering so he found the solution.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews what professional caring includes beyond compassion. Which elements are part of it? Select all that apply.

options.text: Emotional involvement in each patient's situation
options.rationale: Empathy is understanding what a patient feels. Becoming emotionally involved is not a professional element and it leads toward compassion fatigue.

options.text: Ethical practice
options.rationale: Ethical practice is part of professional caring, and it is what keeps caring from sliding into personal preference.

options.text: Confidentiality
options.rationale: Confidentiality belongs here, and protecting privacy is one of the behaviors patients name themselves.

options.text: Advocacy
options.rationale: Named, and it appears in both the professional caring list and the behaviors patients value.

options.text: Emotional detachment to preserve clinical objectivity
options.rationale: The mirror image of over-involvement and wrong in the same way. Professional caring is presence with boundaries, not distance.

options.text: Cultural sensitivity
options.rationale: Cultural sensitivity is part of it, and it is how respect for the whole person actually gets delivered.

options.text: Accountability
options.rationale: Accountability is named directly, and it is why caring cannot exist without competence behind it.

questions.takeaway: Professional caring: compassion, respect, accountability, cultural sensitivity, confidentiality, advocacy, ethical practice.
questions.strategy: One distractor sounds like the most caring option on the list and is the one that harms the nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Compassion, respect, accountability, sensitivity, confidentiality, advocacy, ethics.
Not on the list, and not sustainable.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse taking a patient's vital signs enters, applies the cuff, records the readings, and leaves without speaking. The readings are accurate. Which principle has been missed?

options.text: The readings should be verified with the patient before recording
options.rationale: There is no such requirement, and verification is not what was missing. What was missing was any human contact.

options.text: Caring should be present during every skill, including routine ones
options.rationale: Her example for vital signs is to introduce yourself and explain what you are doing. The task was done and the interaction was not.

options.text: Vital signs should be explained because patients have a right to their results
options.rationale: This is a reasonable position but not the principle here, which is about the interaction rather than the disclosure.

options.text: Routine tasks may be delegated so the nurse can focus on caring
options.rationale: This treats caring as something that happens elsewhere, when it is happening right here.

questions.takeaway: Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction. For vital signs, introduce yourself and explain what you are doing.
questions.strategy: One distractor suggests delegating the routine work so caring can happen separately, which inverts the whole principle.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the results and verification options

steps.detail: Moves caring away from the task.

elimination.verdict: That leaves caring during every skill.

questions.nursesNote: 1430: Patient is 54, admitted three days ago with pancreatitis. Sitting on the edge of the bed facing the window. Answers questions in single words. Has not touched the lunch tray. Says 'fine' when asked, then adds that a spouse has not visited since admission. Wound site clean and dry. Pain reported as 2 of 10. Declines to discuss discharge planning, saying there is no point. Vital signs stable. Ambulated in the corridor this morning with the physiotherapist.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate a need for therapeutic presence.

segments.text: Declines to discuss discharge planning, saying there is no point
segments.rationale: There is no point is a statement about hopelessness rather than about discharge. It needs exploring, not rescheduling.

segments.text: Pain reported as 2 of 10
segments.rationale: Controlled pain, and it rules out discomfort as the explanation for the withdrawal.

segments.text: Wound site clean and dry
segments.rationale: A clean, dry wound is a normal finding. The physical recovery is the part going well.

segments.text: Answers questions in single words
segments.rationale: Withdrawal from conversation, and it is the finding that tells you asking more questions will not work.

segments.text: Says 'fine', then adds that a spouse has not visited since admission
segments.rationale: He offered something after saying he was fine. That second sentence is an opening, and it is the one to stay with.

segments.text: Has not touched the lunch tray
segments.rationale: A change in a basic behavior, and in this context it belongs with the withdrawal rather than with his pancreatitis.

segments.text: Sitting on the edge of the bed facing the window
segments.rationale: Turned away from the room and from people. Nonverbal behavior is part of what you assess.

segments.text: Ambulated in the corridor this morning with the physiotherapist
segments.rationale: He is participating in his physical care. A strength, included to be left alone.

questions.takeaway: Presence is indicated when a patient is saying something the clinical findings cannot explain. Listen for the sentence that comes after 'I'm fine'.
questions.strategy: Three findings are normal or positive, and one of them actively rules out the easy explanation. If his pain is 2 of 10, the withdrawal is not about pain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Wound, pain and ambulation are fine.
It rules out discomfort as the cause.
He volunteered the part about his wife.

elimination.verdict: s1, s4, s5, s6, and s7: no point, single words, the spouse, untouched tray, and posture.

questions.stem: A nurse hears a colleague tell a frightened preoperative patient that there is nothing to worry about and the surgeon is the best in the hospital. What is the problem with this response?

options.text: It gives the patient unrealistic expectations of the surgical outcome
