options.rationale: Well-being is one of the standards, and it covers nurse satisfaction and moral distress.

options.text: Cost containment per patient day
options.rationale: A real organizational concern and not among the Magnet standards. The standards concern how nursing is practised and supported.

options.text: Leadership
options.rationale: Named, and it reflects how a unit is led affecting outcomes and burnout.

options.text: Nurse-to-patient ratios fixed by state statute
options.rationale: A staffing law in some states and not a Magnet standard. Magnet measures how a unit is led and how its nurses practise.

options.text: Safety
options.rationale: Safety is one of the six standards, and it is measured rather than asserted.

questions.takeaway: Magnet standards: shared decision-making, leadership, safety, quality, well-being, and professional development.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a legitimate hospital priority that is not one of the six.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shared decision-making, leadership, safety, quality, well-being, professional development.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A unit adopts a Professional Practice Model built around patient- and family-centered care. Which set of elements defines it?

options.text: Communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, and mutual support
options.rationale: The TeamSTEPPS pillars, which concern how the team works rather than how patients are engaged.

options.text: Respect and dignity, information sharing, participation, and collaboration
options.rationale: Her four core elements of patient- and family-centered care within the practice model.

options.text: Values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teamwork
options.rationale: These are the four interprofessional competencies. They describe how a team works, not the practice model.

options.text: Responsibility, autonomy, authority, and accountability
options.rationale: This is the decision-making framework. It describes an individual nurse's standing, not a practice model.

questions.takeaway: Patient- and family-centered care: respect and dignity, information sharing, participation, collaboration. The practice model drives the nursing care delivery model.
questions.strategy: All four options are real sets of four from this chapter. Ask which set is about patients rather than about staff.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves respect, information sharing, participation, collaboration.

questions.stem: A nurse executive introduces a program inviting staff nurses to propose and trial changes to unit practice, with protected time to do so. Which characteristic of an empowered nursing team does this support?

options.text: Compliance with regulatory standards for nursing practice
options.rationale: Regulation sets the floor. Empowerment is about what a unit does above that floor.

options.text: Standardization of nursing care across the organization
options.rationale: This points the other way. The program invites variation on purpose so that improvements can be tested.

options.text: Clear separation between management and clinical decision-making
options.rationale: Decentralization and shared governance blur that line deliberately. Staff nurses making practice decisions is the point.

options.text: An environment that supports risk-taking, innovation, and professional growth
options.rationale: Named directly as what empowering environments do, and protected time is what turns the invitation into something real.

questions.takeaway: Empowering environments support risk-taking, innovation, and professional growth. A culture of autonomy, quality and collaboration raises satisfaction and lowers moral distress.
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe control rather than empowerment. Ask what protected time to trial a change actually enables.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Trying something that might not work.

elimination.verdict: That leaves risk-taking and innovation.

questions.stem: A nurse wants staff on the unit to have real authority over how admissions are scheduled, not just to be asked afterward. Which structure provides that?

options.text: A manager who consults staff before announcing decisions
options.rationale: Consultation is better than none and it keeps the decision in one place. Governance means staff hold part of it.

options.text: An annual satisfaction survey distributed to staff nurses
options.rationale: A survey collects views without handing anyone a decision. Being asked afterwards is exactly what she is trying to move past.

options.text: A unit council of staff nurses that decides care delivery
options.rationale: Decentralization and shared governance mean decisions move toward the people doing the work.

options.text: A central committee writing policy applied to every unit
options.rationale: A central committee writing policy for every unit is centralization, which is the thing shared governance moves away from.

questions.takeaway: Decentralization and shared governance move decision-making toward the staff who deliver the care.
questions.strategy: Two distractors gather opinions without transferring any decision. Ask who actually decides in each.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both inform a decision held elsewhere.

elimination.verdict: That leaves staff sitting on the deciding council.

questions.stem: A nurse participates in interprofessional rounds with a physician, a pharmacist, a physical therapist and a social worker. Which interprofessional competencies are being exercised? Select all that apply.

options.text: Values and ethics for interprofessional practice
options.rationale: Values and ethics underlie the mutual respect that makes a round work at all, and it is one of the four competencies.

options.text: Interprofessional communication
options.rationale: Communication is the visible activity of a round, and it is one of the four competencies by name.

options.text: Roles and responsibilities
options.rationale: Roles and responsibilities is one of the four, and rounds only work when everyone knows what each discipline brings.

options.text: Delegation of tasks across disciplines
options.rationale: Delegation operates within nursing to appropriate personnel. Coordinating with other disciplines is collaboration rather than delegation.

options.text: Teams and teamwork
options.rationale: Teams and teamwork is one of the four, and it is what turns four disciplines into a single plan.

questions.takeaway: Four interprofessional competencies: values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teams and teamwork.
questions.strategy: One distractor applies a nursing-specific concept to interdisciplinary work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Values and ethics, roles, communication, teamwork.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.nursesNote: 0730: Charge nurse reviewing the shift. Unit has four registered nurses, one licensed practical nurse, and two assistive personnel for 28 patients. One registered nurse is orienting on her second shift. Three patients are scheduled for transfer to a step-down unit today. A patient in room 14 was admitted overnight with chest pain and has not yet been assessed this shift. The assistive personnel were told to 'do the vitals' with no reporting parameters given. A newly admitted patient in room 22 needs discharge teaching for a new insulin regimen, and this has been assigned to an assistive personnel. Two patients are stable and awaiting routine morning care.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that the charge nurse must address before the shift proceeds.

segments.text: Discharge teaching for a new insulin regimen assigned to assistive personnel
segments.rationale: Patient education cannot be delegated. This fails right task before any other consideration.

segments.text: Three patients scheduled for transfer to a step-down unit
segments.rationale: Three planned transfers need coordinating. That is expected work rather than a safety problem.

segments.text: A registered nurse orienting on her second shift
segments.rationale: Right person applies to assignments as well as to delegation. A nurse two shifts in needs an assignment matched to her competence and support.

segments.text: Assistive personnel told to 'do the vitals' with no reporting parameters
segments.rationale: This is the right directions and communication missing. Without parameters, an abnormal reading can sit unreported for hours.

segments.text: Four registered nurses, one licensed practical nurse and two assistive personnel for 28 patients
segments.rationale: The staffing she has. It shapes every decision she makes and is not itself a finding she can correct this morning.

segments.text: Two stable patients awaiting routine morning care
segments.rationale: Routine care on stable patients. This is the work the shift exists to do.

segments.text: A patient admitted overnight with chest pain, not yet assessed this shift
segments.rationale: An unassessed patient with chest pain is the one nobody has laid eyes on this shift. Right now nobody knows his status.

questions.takeaway: Delegation errors and unassessed patients come first. Staffing constraints shape the plan rather than being a correctable finding.
questions.strategy: One finding is the constraint she is working inside rather than a problem to solve. Two describe expected work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The staffing number is the constraint.
No parameters, and teaching assigned to AP.

elimination.verdict: s1, s3, s4, and s7: the orientee, the unassessed patient, and two delegation errors.

questions.stem: During a staffing huddle, a nurse explains how accountability works once a task has been delegated. Which statement needs correcting?

options.text: "Once I delegate a task, the person performing it becomes accountable for the outcome."
options.rationale: Accountability stays with the delegating nurse. The task transfers and the answerability does not.

options.text: "A task that is usually delegable may not be, if the patient is unstable."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it is the right circumstance. Instability takes a delegable task off the table.

options.text: "I need to tell them what to report back and when."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Saying what to report and when is the right directions and communication.

options.text: "I cannot delegate assessment, teaching or evaluation."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Assessment, teaching and evaluation need nursing judgment and stay with the nurse.

questions.takeaway: Delegation transfers the task. Accountability for the outcome stays with the nurse who delegated it.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate the rights correctly. The fourth moves accountability with the task.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the statement transferring accountability.

questions.stem: A unit reports rising nurse turnover, frequent reports of moral distress, and falling patient satisfaction. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Recruitment should be the priority before addressing unit culture
options.rationale: Recruiting into a unit people are leaving addresses the symptom and refills a leaking bucket.

options.text: The findings reflect individual nurses' resilience and coping skills
options.rationale: Locates a unit-level pattern in individual character, which is the misreading that leaves the culture unchanged.

options.text: How a unit is led affects outcomes, satisfaction, and burnout
options.rationale: Her first key takeaway. These are not three separate problems, and leadership is the common factor.

options.text: Turnover and satisfaction are unrelated to clinical quality measures
options.rationale: They move together, so Magnet treats well-being as a standard alongside quality rather than a perk.

questions.takeaway: Leadership shapes care quality. Patient outcomes, nurse satisfaction and burnout move together rather than separately.
questions.strategy: One distractor turns a unit pattern into a personal shortcoming. Ask what the three findings have in common.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: All three sit on one unit.

steps.action: Cut the unrelated and recruitment options
steps.detail: One denies the link, one treats the symptom.

elimination.verdict: That leaves leadership affecting all three.

questions.scenario: A nurse reports to the provider that a patient's blood pressure has fallen from 132/78 to 94/56 over three hours, the pulse has risen from 78 to 118, and urine output has been 15 mL/hr for two hours. She uses a structured report. The provider says to continue monitoring and recheck in two hours. She remains concerned.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem this represents, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Notify the charge nurse and prepare to move up the chain of command
options.rationale: Her authority includes questioning an order and escalating. Preparing the next step is not going over anyone's head prematurely.

options.text: Recheck in two hours as instructed and document the conversation
options.rationale: Following an instruction that does not match the findings, and documenting it does not make two hours safe.

options.text: Escalate using graded language: concerned, uncomfortable, this is a safety issue
options.rationale: CUS exists for exactly this moment. She reported once and the response did not match the findings, so the next step is language that cannot be filed away.

options.text: Repeat the same structured report to the same provider
options.rationale: The report was already given clearly. Repeating the tool that did not work is unlikely to change the response.

options.text: A communication failure requiring a clearer handover
options.rationale: She communicated clearly using a structure. The failure is in the response, not in the report.

options.text: A deteriorating patient whose concern has not been acted on
options.rationale: Three parameters moving together in one direction, and a response that does not match them. Both halves are the problem.

options.text: An expected postoperative variation in vital signs
options.rationale: Falling pressure with rising pulse and oliguria is not expected variation in any context.

options.text: A conflict between the nurse and the provider
options.rationale: Frames a patient safety issue as an interpersonal one, which is how escalation gets delayed.

options.text: The provider's response to being escalated
options.rationale: Concerns the relationship rather than the patient, and escalation is judged by whether the patient was assessed.

options.text: Whether a provider has assessed the patient in person
options.rationale: This measures whether the escalation actually worked. A verbal instruction over the phone is not an assessment.

options.text: Whether the incident report has been completed
options.rationale: Administrative follow-up. It records what happened and does not evaluate whether he is safe now.

options.text: Blood pressure, pulse and urine output at short intervals
options.rationale: The three parameters that defined the deterioration, measured frequently enough to catch the next change.

questions.takeaway: SBAR reports and CUS escalates. When the response does not match the findings, the graded language is the next tool, and the chain of command is behind it.
questions.strategy: Two distractors frame this as a communication or relationship problem. Three numbers are moving together, which makes it a patient problem.

strategies: Match each part to what the stem gives

steps.detail: Pressure down, pulse up, output 15 mL/hr.
Not a handover failure, not a conflict.

elimination.verdict: Escalate with CUS and prepare the chain of command, for a deteriorating patient, evaluated by the trends and by an in-person assessment.

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four patients at the start of the shift. Which patient does the nurse assess first?

options.text: A patient with a pain score of 8 of 10 awaiting analgesia
options.rationale: Distressing and the most emotionally compelling option on the list. Pain is urgent, and it is not airway.

options.text: A patient with a respiratory rate of 28 using accessory muscles
options.rationale: Accessory muscle use means the work of breathing has exceeded what the patient can sustain. That is the one finding on this list that can end in an arrest within the hour.

options.text: A patient with a blood glucose of 248 mg/dL due for insulin
options.rationale: Needs attention this shift. It is elevated and not an emergency, and insulin can follow the first assessment.

options.text: A patient whose family is waiting to discuss discharge plans
options.rationale: This matters to the family and it can move. Nothing deteriorates while they wait twenty minutes.

questions.takeaway: Accessory muscle use with a rate of 28 is respiratory failure in progress. Airway and breathing come before pain, glucose, and anything a family is waiting for.
questions.strategy: Pain at 8 of 10 is placed on these lists to be chosen. Rank by what kills first, not by what is most distressing.

strategies: ABCs

steps.action: Find the airway or breathing problem
Set glucose and the family aside

elimination.verdict: The patient using accessory muscles.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel report a blood pressure of 88/50 mm Hg on a patient admitted with dehydration, and add that he looks fine. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Ask the assistive personnel to repeat the measurement
options.rationale: Delegates the verification back to the same source. When delegated data is abnormal, the nurse is the one who confirms it.

options.text: Reassess the blood pressure and the patient personally
options.rationale: The nurse needs both the number and what the patient looks like, and looks fine from an unlicensed observer is not an assessment. One visit answers whether this is real.

options.text: Notify the provider of the reported reading
options.rationale: Escalating a number the nurse has not confirmed, with no assessment to report alongside it.

options.text: Review the record for the patient's baseline pressures
options.rationale: This is accurate and inert. Knowing yesterday's pressure tells you nothing about what is happening in the room right now.

questions.takeaway: Delegated data that falls outside normal gets verified by the nurse. Accountability for the outcome did not transfer with the task.
questions.strategy: Reviewing the chart feels thorough and produces no new information about the patient in front of you.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
Verify delegated data

steps.action: Cut repeating it by the same person

steps.detail: Both act before the nurse has looked.

elimination.verdict: Reassess personally.

chapters.title: Ethics, Legal Implications, and Documentation
chapters.subtitle: Ethical principles and dilemmas, standards and statutes, malpractice, informatics, and the health record

sources.title: Legal Implications in Nursing Practice
sources.label: Potter Ch. 23 · Legal Implications in Nursing Practice

questions.scenario: A nurse works on a unit where several difficult situations arise during one week.
questions.stem: For each situation, indicate which ethical principle is most directly at stake.

rows.text: A competent patient refuses a recommended amputation
rows.rationale: His right to decide for himself, even when the team disagrees with the decision.

rows.text: A nurse withholds a medication because the dose would harm the patient
rows.rationale: She is preventing harm, and the action is defined by what she stopped rather than by what she did.

rows.text: A nurse promised to return after her break and does
rows.rationale: Keeping the promises you make, which is what builds trust across a shift.

rows.text: A unit reviews whether two patients with equal need receive equal access to a scarce bed
rows.rationale: This is fairness in how care and scarce resources get distributed between people with equal claims.

rows.text: A nurse arranges additional analgesia so a patient can tolerate physiotherapy
rows.rationale: She is acting to do good rather than just to avoid harm, and that is what separates this from nonmaleficence.

rows.text: A nurse tells a patient she will pass his question to the provider today, and does
rows.rationale: Another promise kept. Fidelity appears twice because it is the principle that runs through ordinary shifts.

questions.takeaway: Autonomy is the patient deciding. Beneficence is doing good. Nonmaleficence is avoiding harm. Justice is fairness between people. Fidelity is keeping promises.
questions.strategy: Beneficence and nonmaleficence are the pair that gets confused. One adds a benefit; the other prevents a harm.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate doing good from avoiding harm
steps.detail: Adding analgesia, or withholding a dose.

steps.action: Watch for more than one person

elimination.verdict: Autonomy, nonmaleficence, fidelity, justice, beneficence, fidelity.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a patient whose family insists that aggressive treatment continue, while he has a valid advance directive declining it. The team is divided. Which type of ethical problem is this?

options.text: Moral distress, because the nurse knows the right action but cannot take it
options.rationale: The near-miss. Moral distress is knowing what is right and being unable to do it. Here the right course is genuinely contested.

options.text: A legal problem requiring the risk management department
options.rationale: Legal input may follow, and the situation is first an ethical one about whose wishes govern.

options.text: A communication failure between the team and the family
options.rationale: Communication is involved and the conflict would remain even if everyone understood each other perfectly.

options.text: An ethical dilemma, because two defensible courses of action conflict
options.rationale: A dilemma exists when there are competing legitimate claims and no option satisfies everyone. Both positions have an ethical basis.

questions.takeaway: An ethical dilemma has competing defensible options. Moral distress is knowing the right action and being prevented from taking it.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is moral distress. Ask whether the right course is unclear, or clear and blocked.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask whether the right action is known

steps.detail: That requires a known right action.

steps.action: Cut the legal and communication framings
steps.detail: Both would leave the conflict intact.

elimination.verdict: That leaves an ethical dilemma.

questions.stem: A nurse is repeatedly assigned to give treatments she believes are prolonging suffering in a dying patient. She has raised it twice and nothing has changed. She dreads her shifts. Which is she experiencing?

options.text: An ethical dilemma
options.rationale: A dilemma is uncertainty between two defensible options. She is not uncertain; she is blocked.

options.text: Moral distress
options.rationale: She knows what she believes is right and is constrained from acting on it. The repetition and the dread are characteristic.

options.text: Compassion fatigue
options.rationale: Exhaustion from prolonged exposure to suffering. Related, and it does not name the constraint she is describing.

options.text: Burnout from workload
options.rationale: Workload is not what she describes. The distress is about what she is being asked to do, not how much.

questions.takeaway: Moral distress is knowing the ethically right action and being unable to take it. An ethical dilemma is not knowing which action is right.
questions.strategy: The pair worth separating is dilemma and distress. Uncertainty against constraint.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She is clear about what she believes is right.

elimination.verdict: That leaves moral distress.

questions.stem: A nurse encounters a situation involving a disagreement about a patient's care. Place the steps of processing an ethical problem in the correct order.

options.text: Ask whether this is an ethical problem
options.rationale: First. Not every difficult situation is an ethical one, and some are clinical or communication problems.

options.text: Gather information relevant to the case
options.rationale: Gathering information is the second step, and it draws on the patient, the family, the agency and the wider social context.

options.text: Identify the ethical elements and examine your own values
options.rationale: Third. Clarify values, recognize the principles involved, and distinguish facts from opinions from values.

options.text: Name the problem in a clear, simple statement
options.rationale: Fourth. Difficult to do well, and it is what makes the final plan effective and the discussion possible.

options.text: Identify possible courses of action
options.rationale: Identifying possible courses of action is the fifth step. Ask others and be creative about what the options actually are.

options.text: Create and implement an action plan
options.rationale: Sixth. Gather support, and identify an alternative if the chosen action does not resolve it.

options.text: Evaluate the action plan
options.rationale: Seventh. Decide whether further action is needed, and what transfers to the next situation.

questions.takeaway: Seven steps: is it ethical, gather information, identify elements and examine values, name the problem, identify options, create and implement a plan, evaluate.
questions.strategy: The step people invert is naming the problem. It comes after examining values, not before, because your values shape how you name it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Is this even an ethical problem?
A clear problem statement makes the options possible.

elimination.verdict: Ask, gather, identify, name, options, implement, evaluate.

questions.stem: A nurse working through an ethical problem has gathered information from the patient, the family and the agency. Which step comes next?

options.text: Name the problem in a clear statement
options.rationale: Step four, and it comes after the elements have been identified. Naming it first risks naming it wrongly.

options.text: Identify possible courses of action
options.rationale: Step five. Options generated before the problem is named tend to answer the wrong question.

options.text: Identify the ethical elements and examine her own values
options.rationale: Step three. Clarify values, recognize the principles involved, and distinguish facts from opinion from values.

options.text: Convene the ethics committee
options.rationale: Committees support the process rather than replacing its steps, and this stage is still hers to work through.

questions.takeaway: The seven steps run in order: ask, gather, identify elements and examine values, name, options, implement, evaluate.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are later steps in the same sequence. Ask what has to happen before you can name a problem accurately.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Naming and options both come after.

elimination.verdict: That leaves identifying elements and examining values.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks which principles the profession's code of ethics identifies as key. Which are included? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confidentiality
options.rationale: Confidentiality is named, and it sits underneath every decision about what gets documented and who gets told.

options.text: Advocacy
options.rationale: Advocacy is named, and it places the nurse between the patient and everyone else in the building.

options.text: Responsibility
options.rationale: Responsibility is named, and it concerns what the nurse is obliged to do in the first place.

options.text: Loyalty to the employing institution
options.rationale: The code binds the nurse to the patient. Institutional loyalty is not a principle of it, and it can conflict with advocacy.

options.text: Efficiency in the use of resources
options.rationale: This is a legitimate organizational value and it is not among the code's key principles.

options.text: Accountability
options.rationale: Accountability is named, and it concerns answering for what you actually did.

questions.takeaway: A code of ethics is a set of guiding principles all members of a profession accept. Its key principles are advocacy, responsibility, accountability, and confidentiality.
questions.strategy: One distractor would put the institution where the patient belongs. That substitution is the reason advocacy is first on the list.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and F are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse posts on social media that she had 'a rough shift with a difficult 40-year-old motorcycle crash patient' without naming anyone. Which problem does this create?

options.text: It should have been posted to a private group of nurses instead
options.rationale: A private audience is still an audience, and the information is still disclosed.

options.text: None, because no name or medical record number was used
options.rationale: Identifiability is not limited to names. This is the misunderstanding that produces most social media breaches.

options.text: It reflects poorly on the profession but breaches no principle
options.rationale: Professional image is a real concern and the confidentiality breach is the specific problem here.

options.text: The detail may identify the patient, which breaches confidentiality
options.rationale: A specific age, mechanism and timeframe can identify someone in a small community. Removing the name does not anonymize a case.

questions.takeaway: Social media is a named contemporary ethical issue. Confidentiality is breached by identifiable detail, not only by names.
questions.strategy: One distractor states the exact reasoning that causes these breaches. Ask whether a reader could work out who this is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what a reader could piece together

elimination.verdict: That leaves potential identification.

questions.stem: A nurse strongly disagrees with a competent patient's decision to decline dialysis. Which action reflects her professional obligation?

options.text: Ensure the information is complete, then support the decision
options.rationale: Autonomy means the competent patient decides. Her role is making sure the decision is informed, not making sure it is the one she would choose.

options.text: Arrange for the provider to explain the consequences again
options.rationale: Explaining again is reasonable once. After a settled decision it becomes pressure rather than information.

options.text: Document that the patient is refusing recommended treatment
options.rationale: Documenting is necessary and it does nothing about whether the decision was informed in the first place.

options.text: Request a consultation from the ethics committee
options.rationale: Committees are for genuine dilemmas. A competent patient declining treatment is not one.

questions.takeaway: Autonomy governs when a competent patient has made an informed decision. The nurse's disagreement is not an ethical problem.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats a settled competent decision as a dilemma. Ask whether anything here is actually contested.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves informing and supporting.

questions.stem: A nurse says she thinks it is wrong to lie, and her colleague says the hospital policy requires honest disclosure of errors. Which distinction do these two statements illustrate?

options.text: Ethics are individual beliefs and morals are institutional rules
options.rationale: This reverses both terms. Morals are the personal beliefs; ethics are the shared professional standards.

options.text: Values are personal preferences and morals are professional duties
options.rationale: Reverses the relationship. Values are what a person holds important; morals are personal beliefs about right and wrong.

options.text: Morals are personal beliefs; ethics are shared professional standards
options.rationale: Her first belief is a moral position she holds. The policy expresses an ethical standard the profession and institution accept.

options.text: Both terms describe bioethics as applied to nursing practice
options.rationale: Bioethics concerns ethical questions arising in health care and the life sciences. Neither statement is specifically bioethical.

questions.takeaway: Morals are personal beliefs about right and wrong. Ethics are the standards a group or profession accepts. Values are what a person holds important.
questions.strategy: Two distractors swap the two terms. Fix which one is personal before reading the options.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves morals personal, ethics shared.

questions.stem: A unit convenes an ethics committee for a contested end-of-life decision. Which statement describes its role?

options.text: It provides a structured forum for discussion and recommendation
options.rationale: Committees support the resolution process, bringing perspectives together and helping the team work through the steps.

options.text: It determines whether the nurse acted within her legal scope
options.rationale: That is a regulatory and legal question. An ethics committee advises on the right thing to do, not on whether a license was breached.

options.text: It replaces the need to work through the ethical steps
options.rationale: The steps are how the case is prepared for and used in the discussion.

options.text: It makes the final decision when the team cannot agree
options.rationale: Committees advise. The decision remains with the patient, the surrogate and the treating team.

questions.takeaway: Ethics committees support the process of resolving ethical problems. They advise rather than decide.
questions.strategy: One distractor makes the committee the decision-maker. Ask who is left holding the decision afterwards.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the scope and replacement options
steps.detail: One is regulatory, one skips the work.

elimination.verdict: That leaves a structured forum and recommendation.

questions.stem: At an ethics committee orientation, a nurse describes how to work through an ethical problem on the unit. Which statement needs correcting?

options.text: "Naming the problem clearly makes the final plan more effective."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it is stated directly. A clearly named problem produces a better plan.

options.text: "If I feel strongly enough about it, my personal beliefs should guide the plan."
options.rationale: Examining your values is step three, and examining them means recognizing their influence rather than letting them determine the outcome.

options.text: "If the first action does not resolve it, I should have an alternative identified."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Step six includes having an alternative ready if the first action does not resolve it.

options.text: "I should distinguish among facts, opinions and values when I look at the situation."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and separating facts from opinions and values is part of step three.

questions.takeaway: Examine your own values so you know what is influencing you. That is not the same as letting them decide the outcome.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate the steps correctly. The fourth turns self-examination into justification.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Personal belief as the deciding factor.

elimination.verdict: That leaves personal beliefs guiding the plan.

questions.stem: A patient in skeletal traction develops pale, cold toes with reduced sensation. The nurse becomes occupied elsewhere and neither documents nor reports it. Two days later his leg requires amputation. Which term describes the nurse's conduct?

options.text: Negligence, which does not apply to licensed professionals
options.rationale: Malpractice is a type of negligence. The distinction is that the person held liable is a professional, not that negligence stops applying.

options.text: A quasi-intentional tort
options.rationale: Quasi-intentional torts involve no intent to harm and include breaches such as confidentiality. This is a failure to meet a standard of care.

options.text: Malpractice, which is negligence committed by a professional
options.rationale: Conduct falling below the standard of a reasonably prudent nurse, by someone acting in a professional role, causing harm.

options.text: An intentional tort
options.rationale: Intentional torts require intent. Nothing suggests she meant to harm him; she got busy and failed to act.

questions.takeaway: Negligence is conduct falling below the standard of a reasonably prudent person. Malpractice is negligence by a professional.
questions.strategy: One distractor says negligence does not apply to professionals. It does; malpractice is a subtype of it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A licensed nurse in her professional role.
Malpractice is a type of negligence.

elimination.verdict: That leaves malpractice.

questions.stem: A nursing expert is asked to testify in a case about a patient harmed on a medical unit. Against what standard will the nurse's conduct be judged?

options.text: What a reasonably prudent nurse would do in similar circumstances
options.rationale: The standard of proof, almost word for word. It is not the best possible nurse and it is not this nurse's own opinion.

options.text: What the most experienced nurse on the unit would have done
options.rationale: The standard is reasonably prudent, not exemplary. Holding everyone to the best performer would make the standard unreachable.

options.text: What the hospital's policy manual required at the time
options.rationale: Policy is evidence of the standard and does not define it. A policy can itself fall below the standard.

options.text: What the nurse believed was appropriate at the time
options.rationale: The standard is external to her. What she personally believed was appropriate does not set the bar she is measured against.

questions.takeaway: Standard of proof: what a reasonably prudent nurse would do under similar circumstances in the geographical area where the alleged breach occurred.
questions.strategy: Two distractors set the bar too high or too low. One substitutes policy for the standard itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reasonably prudent, similar circumstances, same area.
One is evidence, one is internal.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the reasonably prudent nurse standard.

questions.scenario: A charge nurse assigns work among a registered nurse, a licensed vocational nurse, and a certified nursing assistant.
questions.stem: For each task, indicate the least qualified person who may appropriately perform it.

rows.text: Recording intake and output
rows.rationale: Named on her Delegation 411 slide among the assistant's tasks, alongside vitals, ambulation, position changes, bathing and eating.

rows.text: Initial admission assessment of a newly admitted patient
rows.rationale: Assessment belongs to the registered nurse. The licensed vocational nurse may perform secondary assessment and reinforcement.

rows.text: Reinforcing teaching the registered nurse has already provided to a stable patient
rows.rationale: The vocational nurse takes secondary and reinforcing roles: assessing, teaching and monitoring stable patients, and discharge.

rows.text: Evaluating whether a patient met an outcome
rows.rationale: Evaluation is a registered nurse function. Judging whether an outcome was met takes nursing judgment.

rows.text: Assisting a stable patient with ambulation
rows.rationale: Walking a stable patient is named among the assistant's tasks, and stability is what makes it delegable.

rows.text: Caring for a patient whose condition is unstable
rows.rationale: An unstable patient is a registered nurse responsibility. Instability is what pulls the task back up the ladder.

questions.takeaway: RN: unstable patients, assessment, evaluation, teaching. LVN: secondary and reinforcing, stable patients, discharge. CNA: vitals, ambulation, positioning, bathing, eating, intake and output.
questions.strategy: Two rows are about teaching and assessment at different depths. First contact belongs to the registered nurse; reinforcement can go to the vocational nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask how stable the patient is
Ask whether it is initial or reinforcing

elimination.verdict: Two CNA, one LVN, three RN.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews what a patient must receive for his informed consent to be valid. Which elements are required? Select all that apply.

options.text: Knowledge that he may refuse without losing other supportive care
options.rationale: Named, and it removes the fear that refusing one thing costs him everything else.

options.text: The names and qualifications of those performing and assisting
options.rationale: The names and qualifications of those performing and assisting are required, and this is the element most often skipped in practice.

options.text: A description of serious harm including death, and anticipated pain or discomfort
options.rationale: A description of serious harm is required, and it must include death where death is a real possibility.

options.text: An explanation of alternative therapies and the risks of doing nothing
options.rationale: Alternatives must be explained, and doing nothing is itself an alternative with its own consequences.

options.text: A guarantee that the procedure will achieve the intended result
options.rationale: No procedure can be guaranteed, and promising an outcome would invalidate rather than strengthen the consent.

options.text: The provider's personal success rate with the procedure
options.rationale: Patients often want it and it is not a required element. Required content is the procedure, the personnel, the risks, the alternatives, and the right to refuse.

options.text: An explanation of the procedure
options.rationale: An explanation of the procedure is the first element. He has to know what is being proposed.

questions.takeaway: Informed consent requires explanation of the procedure, who is performing it, serious harm including death, alternatives and the risks of doing nothing, the right to refuse without losing other care, and the right to withdraw even after the procedure has begun.
questions.strategy: One distractor offers a guarantee. Consent describes risk honestly; it never promises a result.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Procedure, people, risks, alternatives, right to refuse.
He may refuse even after it has begun.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse stops at the scene of a road collision and provides care within her competence until paramedics arrive. Which law addresses her legal position?

options.text: The Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act
options.rationale: EMTALA governs how hospitals must treat people presenting for emergency care. It does not apply at a roadside.

options.text: Good Samaritan laws, which limit liability and offer legal immunity
options.rationale: Named directly. They protect a nurse who helps at the scene of an accident.

options.text: Her state nurse practice act, which permits emergency care
options.rationale: The practice act defines her scope. Good Samaritan laws address liability for helping outside employment.

options.text: Her employer's malpractice insurance
options.rationale: Employer coverage applies to care given in the course of employment. She stopped at a roadside on her own time.

questions.takeaway: Good Samaritan laws limit liability and offer legal immunity to a nurse who helps at the scene of an accident.
questions.strategy: One distractor is a real emergency statute that governs hospitals rather than roadsides.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: At a roadside, not at work.

steps.action: Cut the practice act and insurance
steps.detail: One is scope, one is employment coverage.

elimination.verdict: That leaves Good Samaritan laws.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse reviews the federal statutes affecting her practice.

The law requiring institutions to give patients written information about their right to refuse treatment and to formulate an advance directive is the [[1]].

The law giving patients rights over their health information and protecting employees is [[2]].

The law requiring insurers to cover mental health and substance use treatment is the [[3]].

The act prohibiting the purchase or sale of organs is the [[4]].

options.text: Americans with Disabilities Act
options.rationale: The Americans with Disabilities Act protects the rights of people with physical or mental disabilities.

options.text: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act
options.rationale: The Affordable Care Act concerns consumer protections, affordable coverage, access and quality.

options.text: Patient Self-Determination Act
options.rationale: Requires written information about the right to make decisions, refuse treatment, and formulate an advance directive such as a power of attorney or living will.

options.text: Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act
options.rationale: The Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act changed the way health care is delivered to older adults.

options.text: EMTALA
options.rationale: EMTALA governs emergency treatment and active labor, not health information.

options.text: HIPAA
options.rationale: HIPAA gives patients rights over their health information and protects employees as well.

options.text: HITECH
options.rationale: The near-miss. HITECH concerns health information technology and requires nurses to ensure protected health information is secured.

options.text: the Mental Health Parity Act
options.rationale: The Mental Health Parity Act concerns insurance coverage for mental health and substance use.

options.text: Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act
options.rationale: Requires insurers to provide coverage for mental health and substance use disorder treatment.

options.text: Americans with Disabilities Act
options.rationale: The Americans with Disabilities Act concerns discrimination and access rather than insurance coverage.

options.text: HIPAA
options.rationale: HIPAA concerns health information, not what an insurer has to cover.

options.text: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act
options.rationale: The Affordable Care Act is broader coverage and access legislation, not parity specifically.

options.text: Uniform Determination of Death Act
options.rationale: Determines actual death, cardiopulmonary or irreversible cessation of the entire brain and brain stem.

options.text: Uniform Anatomical Gift Act
options.rationale: The near-miss. It provides the foundation for the national organ donation system; the Transplant Act is what prohibits sale.

options.text: Patient Self-Determination Act
options.rationale: The Patient Self-Determination Act concerns advance directives and the right to refuse treatment.

options.text: National Organ Transplant Act
options.rationale: The National Organ Transplant Act prohibits buying or selling organs.

questions.takeaway: Self-Determination is advance directives. HIPAA is information rights. Parity is insurance coverage. Anatomical Gift builds the donation system; Transplant Act prohibits sale.
questions.strategy: Two near-miss pairs: HIPAA against HITECH, and the two organ acts. One builds the system, the other prohibits the market.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Self-Determination, HIPAA, Parity, Transplant Act.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares a medication and the vial does not look like the one she usually uses. She is behind on her round. Which action reflects the lessons drawn from the RaDonda Vaught case?

options.text: Give it and document that the appearance was unfamiliar
options.rationale: Documenting a concern is not resolving it, and the patient receives the drug either way.

options.text: Stop, verify with a drug guide or the pharmacist before proceeding
options.rationale: Pause and verify when something does not look right, particularly with high-alert medications, and use resources when in doubt.

options.text: Proceed, since she selected it from the automated cabinet under the correct name
options.rationale: An override and a confirmation error were central to that case. The cabinet is not the verification.

options.text: Ask another nurse to check it while she moves to her next patient
options.rationale: The check belongs to the person giving it. Delegating the verification does not transfer the accountability.

questions.takeaway: Follow all the rights, pause and verify when something looks wrong, use resources, avoid workarounds, and report system failures.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats the automated cabinet as the verification step. That was central to what went wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An override and confirmation error caused the harm.

steps.action: Cut delegating the check and documenting
steps.detail: Neither resolves the doubt before administration.

elimination.verdict: That leaves stopping to verify.

questions.stem: A nurse discusses a patient's diagnosis in a hospital lift where visitors can hear. She intended no harm. Which category does this fall into?

options.text: An unintentional tort
options.rationale: The near-miss. Unintentional torts arise when someone is harmed and the person knew or should have known their actions fell below the standard of practice, which describes negligence.

options.text: An intentional tort
options.rationale: Requires intent to cause the harm. She intended to speak, not to harm.

options.text: A quasi-intentional tort
options.rationale: A quasi-intentional tort is harm caused without intending it, and breach of confidentiality is the classic example.

options.text: A criminal offense under state law
options.rationale: Torts are civil wrongs. Criminal law covers felonies and misdemeanors, which this is not.

questions.takeaway: Torts are civil wrongful acts or omissions. Quasi-intentional torts involve no intent to harm. Unintentional torts arise where the person knew or should have known their conduct fell below the standard.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is unintentional tort. Both involve no intent, and they differ in whether a standard of care was breached.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One needs intent, one is a different body of law.

elimination.verdict: That leaves a quasi-intentional tort.

questions.stem: A nurse wants to reduce her personal legal risk. Which actions help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Developing and using clinical judgment to identify patient needs
options.rationale: Named directly, and sound clinical decisions are what keep practice above the standard.

options.text: Remaining aware of current issues in health care
options.rationale: Staying current is named, and standards move. What was defensible five years ago may not be now.

options.text: Documenting thoroughly and accurately
options.rationale: Named among the lessons drawn from the Vaught case, and an undocumented action is difficult to defend.

options.text: Carrying personal malpractice insurance instead of relying on the employer's
options.rationale: Insurance covers the cost of a claim. It reduces financial exposure rather than legal risk, and the question asks about the risk itself.

options.text: Declining any assignment outside the nurse's comfort level
options.rationale: Competence is the standard, not comfort. A nurse who is competent but uncomfortable still owes the care, and one who is comfortable but not competent is the actual exposure.

options.text: Becoming involved in professional organizations and committees that define standards
options.rationale: Named, and it means she helps set the standard she is judged against.

options.text: Participating in risk management and quality improvement programs
options.rationale: Risk management and quality improvement are named, and they find hazards before anyone is harmed by them.

questions.takeaway: Reducing legal risk: clinical judgment, awareness of current issues, professional involvement, risk management and quality improvement, and thorough documentation.
questions.strategy: One distractor reduces what a claim costs rather than the chance of one. Read what the question asks.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse finishes her shift and no replacement has arrived for the next shift. She leaves at the end of her scheduled hours without notifying anyone. Which concern does this raise?

options.text: Patient abandonment, because she left without handing over responsibility
options.rationale: Named among the workforce guidelines. Leaving a scheduled shift without transferring care to someone qualified is abandonment.

options.text: None, because her contracted hours had ended
options.rationale: The end of her hours does not end her responsibility until care has been transferred.

options.text: A staffing ratio violation by the employer
options.rationale: The ratio problem is real and it belongs to the employer. Her own exposure comes from how she left.

options.text: A breach of her nurse practice act's scope provisions
options.rationale: Scope concerns what she is permitted to do, not how she ends a shift. Leaving without handover is a different problem.

questions.takeaway: Nursing workforce guidelines cover staffing and ratios, assignments, patient abandonment, delegation, and nursing students.
questions.strategy: One distractor points at a genuine employer failing. The question asks what this raises for her.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the ratio and scope options
steps.detail: One is the employer's, one is unrelated.

elimination.verdict: That leaves patient abandonment.

questions.stem: At the annual risk management in-service, a nurse summarizes what creates legal exposure in practice. Which statement needs correcting?

options.text: "Malpractice is a type of negligence, and the person held liable must be a professional."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and it is the definition. Malpractice is negligence committed by someone acting as a professional.

options.text: "Risk management programs reduce legal risk by finding hazards before harm occurs."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Risk management reduces exposure by finding hazards before anyone is harmed by them.

options.text: "A nursing expert will testify about the standard of care as applied to the facts."
options.rationale: This is accurate. A nurse expert testifies about the standard of care as it applies to these particular facts.

options.text: "If I follow hospital policy exactly, I cannot be found negligent."
options.rationale: Policy is evidence of the standard, not the standard itself. A policy can fall below what a reasonably prudent nurse would do.

questions.takeaway: Policy is evidence of the standard of care, not a defense in itself. The standard is what a reasonably prudent nurse would do.
questions.strategy: Three of the four statements are accurate. The fourth treats policy compliance as complete protection.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the policy statement.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews four documentation formats used across the organization.
questions.stem: For each note component, indicate which documentation format it belongs to.

rows.text: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan
rows.rationale: Four components, and it is the only format separating subjective from objective explicitly.

rows.text: Problem, Intervention, Evaluation
rows.rationale: Problem, intervention, evaluation. The note is organized around the nursing problem rather than the patient's words.

rows.text: Data, Action, Response
rows.rationale: Data, action, response. Focus charting opens with what you found and ends with how the patient responded.

rows.text: Begins with the nursing diagnosis rather than the patient's words
rows.rationale: The P is the nursing problem, which is what makes it a nursing-focused format.

rows.text: Separates what the patient reports from what the nurse measures
rows.rationale: The S and the O are that split.

rows.text: Ends with how the patient responded to the intervention
rows.rationale: The R. PIE ends with the nurse's evaluation; DAR ends with the patient's response.

questions.takeaway: PIE: problem, intervention, evaluation. DAR: data, action, response. SOAP: subjective, objective, assessment, plan.
questions.strategy: PIE and DAR both end with a verdict, and they differ in whose. PIE ends with the nurse's evaluation; DAR ends with the patient's response.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the subjective and objective split

elimination.verdict: SOAP, PIE, DAR, PIE, SOAP, DAR.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the guidelines for quality documentation. Which characteristics should her entries have? Select all that apply.

options.text: Detailed enough to argue why each decision was made
options.rationale: Slides from recording into arguing. The entry states what was observed and done, and the reasoning belongs in the care plan rather than as justification inside the note.

options.text: Appropriate use of abbreviations
options.rationale: Using only approved abbreviations is a named guideline, and unapproved ones are a recognized source of medication error.

options.text: Accurate
options.rationale: Accurate is a named guideline, and it means exact measurements rather than words like moderate or a small amount.

options.text: Current
options.rationale: Named. Entries made long after the event lose reliability and may be questioned.

options.text: Factual
options.rationale: Factual is a named guideline. Record what you observed and what you did, not what you assumed was going on.

options.text: Persuasive in explaining the nurse's reasoning
options.rationale: Documentation records what happened. An entry written to justify rather than to record undermines its value as a legal record.

options.text: Organized
options.rationale: Named, and a reader must be able to follow the sequence of events.

questions.takeaway: Quality documentation is factual, accurate, uses appropriate abbreviations, and is current, organized and complete.
questions.strategy: One distractor turns a record into an argument. Ask what the entry is for.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Factual, accurate, abbreviations, current, organized, complete.

elimination.verdict: B, C, D, E, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A patient transfers from a clinic to a hospital. The clinic's system holds only that practice's visits, while the hospital's follows him across every facility in the network. Which distinction does this illustrate?

options.text: An electronic medical record versus an electronic health record
options.rationale: Span is the whole distinction. The medical record covers care within one practice or episode, and the health record follows the patient across facilities over a lifetime.

options.text: A paper record converted into an electronic format
options.rationale: Both of these systems are already electronic. Format is not what separates them.

options.text: A personal health record maintained by the patient
options.rationale: A personal health record is one the patient keeps and controls. Neither system in the stem is that.

options.text: A clinical data warehouse used for quality reporting
options.rationale: A data warehouse aggregates information for reporting and analysis. Neither record described is doing that.

questions.takeaway: The electronic health record is an individual's lifetime computerized record. The electronic medical record is the record for an individual health care visit.
questions.strategy: One distractor makes the difference a matter of who uses it. Ask what each one covers.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the paper and interchangeable options

elimination.verdict: That leaves lifetime against single visit.

questions.stem: A nurse receives a telephone order from a provider for a new analgesic. Which action comes first?

options.text: Read the order back to the provider for verification
options.rationale: Reading it back is the essential second step, and you cannot do it accurately from memory. Write it down first.

options.text: Write the order down as it is given
options.rationale: Writing it first is what makes read-back possible. Memory is where telephone orders go wrong.

options.text: Record that it was received as a telephone order
options.rationale: Labelling it as a telephone order is necessary, and it comes after the order has been written and read back.

options.text: Administer the medication and document it afterwards
options.rationale: This gives the drug before anyone has verified the order. That sequence is what produces the error.

questions.takeaway: Telephone orders: write it down, read it back, record it as a telephone order, administer, and obtain the countersignature within the required window.
questions.strategy: Three options are genuine steps in the sequence. Ask which one has to happen before read-back is possible.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves writing it down.

questions.stem: A nurse transfers to a unit that uses charting by exception and finds far fewer entries in each record than she is used to. Which statement describes this method?

options.text: Documentation is completed only when a patient's condition changes
options.rationale: This is close, and it leaves out that the comparison is against a defined norm rather than against the patient's own earlier state.

options.text: Only the most significant findings of the shift are recorded
options.rationale: Significance is a judgment. Charting by exception rests on defined standards rather than on what struck the nurse as important.

options.text: Only findings that deviate from a defined norm are documented
options.rationale: Its efficiency comes from the unit having agreed norms. Anything not recorded is understood to be within them.

options.text: Narrative entries replace flow sheets in this method
options.rationale: Flow sheets are central to it. They record the routine so the notes can record the exceptions.

questions.takeaway: Charting by exception documents findings that deviate from a defined norm. It depends on the norms being explicit and agreed.
questions.strategy: One distractor substitutes the nurse's judgment of significance for a defined standard. That difference is the whole method.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what the comparison is against
Cut the change-only and narrative options
steps.detail: One omits the norm, one reverses the tools.

elimination.verdict: That leaves deviation from a defined norm.

questions.stem: A nurse considers the purposes served by the health care record. Which are legitimate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Recording a nurse's concerns about unit staffing levels
options.rationale: A legitimate concern that belongs in an occurrence report or a conversation with the manager, not in a patient's record.

options.text: Facilitating communication among the interprofessional team
options.rationale: Communication is named first. The record is how everyone else follows the clinical course without asking you.

options.text: Providing a record the patient is not entitled to read
options.rationale: Factually wrong. Patients have a right of access, and nothing should be written on the assumption that they will not see it.

options.text: Supporting quality and performance improvement
options.rationale: Quality and performance improvement is a named purpose, and auditing depends entirely on what was written.

options.text: Providing a legal record of the care given
options.rationale: The legal record is a named purpose, and it is the reason the quality guidelines exist at all.

options.text: Justifying billing and reimbursement
options.rationale: Billing is a named purpose, and diagnosis-related groups draw directly on what was documented.

options.text: Serving as a resource for education and research
options.rationale: Education and research is the fifth named purpose. The record outlives the admission.

questions.takeaway: Five purposes: interprofessional communication, legal record, billing justification, quality improvement, and education and research.
questions.strategy: One distractor puts a workplace concern into a patient's record. Ask whose record it is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: B, D, E, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A patient falls while being assisted to the bathroom. The nurse completes an occurrence report. Which statement about that report is accurate?

options.text: A copy should be filed in the patient's medical record
options.rationale: The occurrence report is kept separate from the chart. Filing it in the record defeats the purpose of having it.

options.text: It replaces the need to document the fall in the patient's record
options.rationale: The fall, the assessment and the response all belong in the record. The report is additional.

options.text: The record should state that an occurrence report was completed
options.rationale: The fall and the assessment are documented in the record. That a report was filed is not.

options.text: It is an internal risk management document, not part of the record
options.rationale: Keeping it separate is what allows staff to describe system failures honestly without that account becoming part of the chart.

questions.takeaway: Occurrence reports are internal risk management documents. They are kept separate from the medical record, and the event itself is still documented in the record.
questions.strategy: Two distractors connect the report to the chart in some way. The separation is the point of it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what the report is for
Cut filing it in the chart

steps.detail: One references it, one replaces documentation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves an internal document kept separate.

questions.stem: A unit uses an acuity rating system. Which statement describes what it measures?

options.text: The number and type of nursing interventions required daily
options.rationale: The definition. It drives the hours of care and the number of staff needed for a group of patients.

options.text: The patient's risk of clinical deterioration overnight
options.rationale: Early warning scores predict deterioration. Acuity measures the nursing work a patient generates.

options.text: The severity of the patient's primary medical diagnosis
options.rationale: Medical severity and nursing workload are related and not the same. A medically stable patient can require intensive nursing.

options.text: The expected length of the patient's hospital admission
options.rationale: Length of stay is predicted by other measures. Acuity is about how much nursing care is needed per day.

questions.takeaway: An acuity rating system determines hours of care and staffing needed, based on the type and number of nursing interventions a patient requires over 24 hours.
questions.strategy: Three distractors measure something about the patient's condition. Acuity measures the work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what it is used for
Cut deterioration risk and length of stay

elimination.verdict: That leaves nursing interventions required.

questions.stem: A nurse working in home health care documents an assessment. Which data sets are used in that setting?

options.text: The Joint Commission and CMS standards
options.rationale: These are regulatory bodies that govern documentation. They are not data sets.

options.text: OASIS and the Omaha system
options.rationale: These are the two data sets used to document clinical assessment and care in home health.

options.text: Diagnosis-related groups and core measures
options.rationale: Diagnosis-related groups classify for reimbursement and core measures are clinical standards. Neither is a home health data set.

options.text: Flow sheets and charting by exception
options.rationale: These are documentation methods used across every setting rather than data sets specific to home health.

questions.takeaway: Home health uses two data sets: OASIS and the Omaha system. Documentation there is both quality control and the justification for reimbursement.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name real things from the same chapter that are not data sets.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what a data set is
steps.detail: A structured format for recording assessment.
Neither is a home health data set.

elimination.verdict: That leaves OASIS and the Omaha system.

questions.stem: A chart audit team reviews how nurses on the unit document their care. Which practice described by a nurse needs correcting?

options.text: "Findings within the defined norm are not separately recorded on this unit."
options.rationale: This is accurate for charting by exception, which is what her unit uses. Only deviations from the norm get written.

options.text: "I document what I observed and what I did, not what I assumed."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Factual is the first guideline: what you saw and what you did, not what you inferred.

options.text: “If I am busy, I can chart the whole shift at the end.”
options.rationale: Documentation must be current. Charting hours later loses accuracy and creates a record that is difficult to defend.

options.text: “I use only the abbreviations this organization has approved.”
options.rationale: This is accurate. Using only the organization's approved abbreviations is a named guideline.

questions.takeaway: Current is one of the six documentation guidelines. Charting at the end of a shift risks both accuracy and credibility.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate the guidelines correctly. The fourth trades one guideline for convenience.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Factual, accurate, abbreviations, current, organized, complete.

elimination.verdict: That leaves charting the whole shift at the end.

questions.nursesNote: 1120: Nurse reviews an entry made by a colleague earlier in the shift. Entry reads: 'Patient seemed anxious and was probably worried about the surgery. Appeared uncomfortable but refused to say much. Family member was rude to staff. Gave pain medication PRN. Will continue to monitor. BP 118/72, HR 84. Patient ambulated in corridor with assistance x1. Dressing dry and intact.'
questions.stem: Highlight the parts of this entry that do not meet the guidelines for quality documentation.

segments.rationale: Measured values recorded as measured. This is factual and accurate, which is what the guidelines ask for.

segments.text: Dressing dry and intact
segments.rationale: An observed finding stated plainly. Nothing is inferred and nothing is vague.

segments.text: Will continue to monitor
segments.rationale: This commits to nothing measurable and records no action taken. It fills space without documenting care.

segments.text: Patient ambulated in corridor with assistance x1
segments.rationale: Factual, specific about the level of assistance, and useful to the next nurse.

segments.text: Family member was rude to staff
segments.rationale: A judgment about a person rather than a record of what occurred, and it has no place in a patient's record.

segments.text: Gave pain medication PRN
segments.rationale: Not accurate or complete. No drug, dose, route, time, or response to it.

segments.text: Appeared uncomfortable but refused to say much
segments.rationale: Appeared is an impression, and refused characterizes him. Record the observed behavior and his actual words.

segments.text: Patient seemed anxious and was probably worried about the surgery
segments.rationale: Not factual. Seemed and probably are the nurse's inference. Record what he said or what she observed.

questions.takeaway: Factual means observed and done, not inferred. Accurate and complete means the drug, dose, route, time and response.
questions.strategy: Three parts of this entry are exactly right, which is what makes the rest visible. Watch for seemed, probably, appeared, and judgments about people.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No drug, dose, route or response.

elimination.verdict: s3, s5, s6, s7, and s8: empty commitment, inference, incomplete medication, impression, and judgment.

questions.stem: A team disagrees about continuing tube feedings for a patient with advanced dementia and no advance directive. The group has gathered information from the patient's family and the record, and has clarified the values and ethical principles each position rests on. In the ethical decision-making process, which step comes next?

options.text: State the problem in a clear, simple sentence
options.rationale: Naming it comes before solving it. A group that skips this argues past each other, because each member is solving a slightly different problem.

options.text: Identify every possible course of action available
options.rationale: The common skip. Generating options before the problem is named produces solutions to different questions.

options.text: Create an action plan and gather support for it
options.rationale: This is two steps early. Nothing has been named clearly and no option has been chosen yet.

options.text: Evaluate whether any further action will be needed
options.rationale: This is the last step, and it judges a plan that does not exist yet.

questions.takeaway: Gather information, clarify the values involved, then name the problem in one sentence before anyone proposes a course of action.
questions.strategy: The step everyone drops is naming the problem. When a question puts it among the options, that is usually why.

strategies: Place the group in the sequence

steps.detail: Options, plan, and evaluation all come after.

elimination.verdict: State the problem.

questions.stem: An hour after charting, a nurse realizes she entered an entire assessment on the wrong patient's paper record. Which action meets the legal guidelines for documentation?

options.text: Obliterate the entry so it cannot be misread later
options.rationale: This looks tidy and comes across as concealment. An unreadable entry in a legal record is worse than a visible correction.

options.text: Draw one line through it, label it, and initial
options.rationale: The entry stays legible, the correction is attributable, and the record shows what happened and who fixed it. That is what a court looks for.

options.text: Ask the charge nurse to remove the page entirely
options.rationale: Removing a page destroys part of the legal record, and involving someone else does not make it permissible.

options.text: Leave the entry and chart a correct note elsewhere
options.rationale: Leaves a false assessment standing in a patient's chart, where the next clinician will act on it.

questions.takeaway: Never erase, white out, or destroy. One line through, a label such as mistaken entry, your initials and the date, and the original stays readable.
questions.strategy: Anything that makes the original unreadable or removes it is wrong, however reasonable the motive sounds.

strategies: Protect the record first

steps.detail: A false entry stays in force.

elimination.verdict: One line, labeled and initialed.

questions.stem: A patient is going home after treatment for cellulitis of her lower leg. Which entry in the discharge documentation best demonstrates that teaching was effective?

options.text: Written and verbal instructions were given to the patient
options.rationale: Documents what the nurse did. It says nothing about what the patient took away.

options.text: The patient verbalized understanding of the discharge instructions
options.rationale: The most-charted phrase in nursing and the weakest. It records agreement, not comprehension, and will not hold up if the patient returns septic.

options.text: The patient described when to call about spreading redness
options.rationale: The patient produced the content back. That is evidence of learning, and it is specific enough that a reader knows exactly what the patient can do.

options.text: Discharge teaching was completed before the patient left
options.rationale: This records a task closed. Completing teaching is not the same as the patient being able to do anything with it.

questions.takeaway: Document what the patient demonstrated, not what you delivered. Verbalized understanding is a task record wearing an outcome's clothes.
questions.strategy: Three options describe nursing activity. Only one describes the patient doing something.

strategies: Ask who is the subject of the sentence

steps.action: Cut entries whose subject is the nurse
Keep the entry showing patient performance

elimination.verdict: The patient described when to call.

questions.stem: A nurse takes a telephone order from a provider to change a medication dose. Which action most directly prevents a transcription error?

options.text: Read the order back and record the provider's name
options.rationale: The read-back catches the error while the provider is still on the line, which is the only moment it can be corrected by the person who gave it.

options.text: Enter the order and ask a second nurse to verify it
options.rationale: A second nurse can confirm what was written and cannot confirm what was said.

options.text: Record it and chart it clearly as a verbal order
options.rationale: Labelling it correctly matters and it happens after the risk has passed. Documentation does not catch a dose you misheard.

options.text: Write the order and have the provider sign it later
options.rationale: Required by policy and too late to help. A countersignature days later ratifies whatever was written down.

questions.takeaway: Read-back is the step that catches the error. Labeling and countersigning are required and neither protects the patient at the moment of risk.
questions.strategy: Several options are things you must do. Only one of them happens before the error can reach the patient.

strategies: Find the step that acts in time

steps.detail: Only read-back is during the call.

steps.action: Keep read-back with the name recorded

elimination.verdict: Read back and record the name.
