options.text: Dispose of the ampule in the regular waste bin
options.rationale: Broken glass goes in the sharps container, not in regular waste where it can cut someone.

options.text: Tap or flick the top of the ampule to move fluid out of the neck before opening
options.rationale: Medication trapped above the neck is lost when the top is snapped off.

options.text: Change to a regular needle before administering the dose
options.rationale: A filter needle is for withdrawing only. You switch to a regular needle before the dose goes in.

options.text: Protect the fingers with gauze or an alcohol pad when snapping the top
options.rationale: Gauze or an alcohol pad protects your fingers, because the glass snaps at the scored neck and the edges are sharp.

questions.takeaway: Clear the neck, protect your fingers, withdraw through a filter needle, change the needle before injecting, and dispose of the glass in sharps.
questions.strategy: The filter needle is the step most often missed, and it is used in one direction only: withdraw through it, then change it before the dose goes anywhere near a patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse is to give NPH and regular insulin together in one syringe for a patient's morning dose. She has rolled the NPH vial and injected air into both vials. Which medication does she withdraw first?

options.text: The regular insulin, because it is clear and clear is drawn before cloudy
options.rationale: Drawing the clear insulin first prevents the cloudy suspension contaminating the clear vial.

options.text: Neither, because regular and NPH insulin cannot be combined in the same syringe
options.rationale: Regular and NPH may be mixed. Long-acting insulins such as glargine and detemir may not.

options.text: Either insulin may be drawn first, as long as the total volume in the syringe is correct
options.rationale: Order matters because contamination only runs one way. Getting NPH into the regular vial changes that vial's action.

options.text: The NPH, because the cloudy suspension must be resuspended and drawn before the clear insulin
options.rationale: The NPH does get rolled before you draw, but it is still withdrawn second, after the clear insulin.

questions.takeaway: Clear before cloudy. Regular is drawn before NPH, and long-acting insulins are never mixed at all. Clear before cloudy: regular insulin is withdrawn before NPH when the two are mixed in one syringe. Long-acting insulins such as glargine and detemir are never mixed with any other insulin.
questions.strategy: The rule protects the clear vial. If cloudy suspension enters it, every subsequent dose drawn from that vial is altered.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Regular is clear, NPH is cloudy.
Rolling happens before drawing; the order is unchanged.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: regular first.

questions.concept: Clear before cloudy: regular insulin is withdrawn before NPH when the two are mixed in one syringe. Long-acting insulins such as glargine and detemir are never mixed with any other insulin.

questions.stem: A nurse must combine a medication supplied in a vial with a medication supplied in a glass ampule, giving both in one syringe. Both are ordered at the same time and are compatible. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Withdraw from the ampule first, then inject air into the vial and withdraw the second medication
options.rationale: Injecting air into the vial with ampule medication already in the syringe risks pushing it into the vial.

options.text: Draw both medications without a filter needle, since they are being combined in one syringe anyway
options.rationale: The ampule still requires a filter needle regardless of what else is in the syringe.

options.text: Prepare the medication from the vial first, then use the same syringe and filter needle to withdraw from the ampule
options.rationale: The vial requires air injection before withdrawal, and doing it first avoids introducing the ampule medication into the vial.

options.text: Use separate syringes for each medication and combine the two doses immediately before injecting
options.rationale: Two syringes adds a transfer step, and every transfer is another chance for error and contamination.

questions.takeaway: Vial first, then the ampule, using the same syringe and filter needle. When mixing medications from a vial and an ampule, prepare the medication from the vial first, then use the same syringe and filter needle to withdraw from the ampule.
questions.strategy: The order follows from the mechanics: vials need air injected in, ampules do not. Whatever needs air pushed into it goes first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: The vial, because it is sealed.
Air injection with medication already drawn risks contaminating the vial.
The ampule always needs a filter needle.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the vial requires air injection before withdrawal, and doing it first avoids introducing the ampule medication into the vial.

questions.concept: When mixing medications from a vial and an ampule, prepare the medication from the vial first, then use the same syringe and filter needle to withdraw from the ampule.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews needlestick prevention with a student after a colleague on another unit sustained an injury while disposing of a used syringe. Which statements and actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Injuries occur when workers recap needles, mishandle lines and needles, or leave needles at the bedside
options.rationale: Recapping, mishandling lines, and leaving sharps loose are where most needlesticks happen, and all three are avoidable.

options.text: Needlestick injuries are the most frequent route of exposure to bloodborne disease for health care workers
options.rationale: Needlesticks are the most frequent route of bloodborne exposure for health care workers, and that is why the prevention measures are federally required.

options.text: Dispose of sharps in a puncture-proof, leak-proof container that stands upright and is labeled with the biohazard symbol
options.rationale: The container is puncture-proof, leak-proof, upright, labeled with the biohazard symbol, and never overfilled.

options.text: Recap the needle carefully with one hand before disposal
options.rationale: Recapping is a cause of needlestick injury. The needle goes straight into the container.

options.text: Use sharps with engineered sharps injury protection, such as safety syringes and blunt-end cannulas
options.rationale: Engineered sharps protection, like safety syringes and blunt-end cannulas, is required under the Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act.

questions.takeaway: Never recap. Use engineered safety devices, and dispose into an upright, puncture-proof container that is not overfilled. Needlestick injuries are the most frequent route of exposure to bloodborne disease for health care workers and occur through recapping, mishandling lines and needles, and leaving needles at the bedside. The Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act mandates sharps with engineered sharps injury protection. Sharps containers are puncture-proof, leak-proof, upright, labeled with the biohazard symbol, and never overfilled.
questions.strategy: The wrong option describes a technique taught as safer recapping. It is still recapping, which is one of the three causes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Recapping, mishandling, leaving needles at the bedside.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and E are selected.

questions.concept: Needlestick injuries are the most frequent route of exposure to bloodborne disease for health care workers and occur through recapping, mishandling lines and needles, and leaving needles at the bedside. The Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act mandates sharps with engineered sharps injury protection. Sharps containers are puncture-proof, leak-proof, upright, labeled with the biohazard symbol, and never overfilled.

questions.stem: A nurse uses the Z-track method to administer an intramuscular medication known to be irritating to subcutaneous tissue. A student asks why she displaces the skin before inserting the needle. What is the purpose of this technique?

options.text: To reduce the depth the needle must travel before reaching the muscle tissue beneath
options.rationale: The needle still goes in at 90 degrees to reach muscle. Displacing the skin does not shorten the path.

options.text: To eliminate the need to rotate injection sites between doses of the same medication
options.rationale: Sites get rotated either way, to prevent induration and abscess at one spot.

options.text: To allow a larger volume of medication to be given safely in one injection site
options.rationale: Volume limits come from the muscle mass available, not from the technique used to inject.

options.text: To keep the medication in the muscle and prevent it tracking back into subcutaneous tissue
options.rationale: Displacing the skin before injection means the tissue layers no longer line up when released, sealing the medication in the muscle.

questions.takeaway: The Z-track method keeps intramuscular medication in the muscle and prevents it tracking back into the subcutaneous tissue layer above.
questions.strategy: Medication that tracks back into subcutaneous tissue irritates it and absorbs at the wrong rate, so the technique protects both comfort and the intended action.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves D: displacing the skin before injection means the tissue layers no longer line up when released, sealing the medication in the muscle.

questions.concept: The Z-track method keeps intramuscular medication in the muscle and prevents it tracking back into the subcutaneous tissue layer above.

questions.stem: A student notices that an intramuscular antibiotic is drawn with a 21 gauge needle while an insulin dose uses a 29 gauge, and asks whether the larger number means a larger needle. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: A smaller gauge number means a finer needle, which is gentler on the dense tissue of a muscle
options.rationale: This has the relationship backwards. A smaller gauge number means a wider bore, not a finer needle.

options.text: Gauge is selected according to the patient's body weight rather than the medication being given
options.rationale: Needle length may vary with body size; the gauge follows the medication and the route.

options.text: Gauge describes the length of the needle rather than the width of its bore or lumen
options.rationale: Length is stated separately in inches. Gauge describes the width of the lumen.

options.text: A smaller gauge number means a larger bore, which thicker medications require
options.rationale: Gauge runs inversely to diameter. Intramuscular uses 20 to 25, subcutaneous 25 to 30, and intradermal 25 to 27.

questions.takeaway: Needle gauge runs inversely to bore: the smaller the number, the wider the needle. IM 20 to 25, SQ 25 to 30, ID 25 to 27. Intramuscular uses 20 to 25 gauge, subcutaneous 25 to 30, and intradermal 25 to 27.
questions.strategy: This one relationship makes the three tables coherent. The route needing the thickest medication has the lowest numbers.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Length and body size are separate considerations.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: gauge runs inversely to diameter.

questions.concept: Needle gauge runs inversely to bore: the smaller the number, the wider the needle. Intramuscular uses 20 to 25 gauge, subcutaneous 25 to 30, and intradermal 25 to 27.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old is scheduled for metoprolol 50 mg by mouth daily. At the time the dose is due the blood pressure is 88/52 and the apical pulse is 54. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose as ordered, since an order is a prescriber decision
options.rationale: An order does not transfer responsibility. The nurse who administers a medication answers for having given it.

options.text: Hold the dose, document the findings and rationale, and notify the provider
options.rationale: A beta blocker lowers both rate and pressure further. The right medication given to a patient whose condition contraindicates it is unsafe administration, whatever the order says.

options.text: Give half the dose to reduce the effect on blood pressure
options.rationale: Altering a dose is prescribing. Right dose means the dose ordered or none at all.

options.text: Give the dose and recheck the vital signs in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Monitors a problem the nurse created rather than preventing it. Both values are already below the point at which this drug is safe to give.

questions.takeaway: The ten rights are not a substitute for assessment. Right medication plus wrong patient condition equals unsafe administration.
questions.strategy: Three options proceed in some form. Ask what this drug does to a pulse of 54 and a pressure of 88/52.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves holding, documenting and notifying.

questions.note: The ten rights are patient, medication, dose, route, time, documentation, reason, response, education and the right to refuse. Slide 29 gives a different ten: drug, patient, dose, route, time, refuse, knowledge and understanding, questions and challenges, response and outcomes, advice. If she asks for the ten rights directly, answer from slide 28 and expect slide 29 wording among the distractors.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews four medication events from the past month.
questions.stem: For each event, indicate whether it is a medication error, an adverse drug reaction, or neither.

rows.text: Mild drowsiness is reported, a known expected secondary effect of the drug
rows.rationale: A side effect is an expected secondary effect of a drug given correctly. Ask: was it a mistake, and was it unintended? Neither, so it is a side effect rather than an error or an adverse reaction.

rows.text: A patient receives a dose intended for the patient in the next bed
rows.rationale: A medication error is a preventable mistake in the medication use process. Ask: did someone do something incorrectly that could have been prevented? Yes, at administration.

rows.text: A transcribed order reads 5.0 mg and is given as 50 mg
rows.rationale: Preventable, and it happened at transcription. Ask where in the process the mistake entered: ordering, transcription, dispensing, administration, or monitoring. Errors are not only bedside events.

rows.text: A rash develops after a correctly prescribed and correctly given antibiotic
rows.rationale: An adverse drug reaction is a harmful or unintended response that occurs with appropriate use. Ask: was anything done wrong? No, so it cannot be an error.

questions.takeaway: A medication error is a preventable mistake in the process. An adverse drug reaction is harm with appropriate use. A side effect is expected.
questions.strategy: Ask whether anything was done incorrectly. If nothing was, it cannot be an error however bad the outcome.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Drowsiness is a known side effect.

elimination.verdict: Two errors, one adverse reaction, one neither.

questions.stem: A nurse administers half of a prescribed opioid dose and must discard the remainder. Which action is correct?

options.text: Discard the remainder in the sharps container and document the amount
options.rationale: Named as never. A sharps container cannot be opened to verify what went in, so the dose stays unaccounted for.

options.text: Return the remaining medication to the dispensing cabinet
options.rationale: Once drawn up it cannot be returned. The running count would no longer match what is physically in the cabinet.

options.text: Have a second nurse witness the waste and both sign the record
options.rationale: A witnessed waste with two signatures is what accounts for the full dose and prevents diversion. Nobody can verify a waste they did not see.

options.text: Document the waste in the record and discard it at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Documents a waste that has not happened yet and leaves a controlled substance unsecured in the meantime.

questions.takeaway: Controlled substances: locked storage, tamper-evident syringes, running counts, documented waste witnessed by a second nurse, and never into a sharps container.
questions.strategy: One distractor is the thing that is prohibited by name. Ask what makes a waste verifiable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A second person watching it happen.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the witnessed waste.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for an oral medication has become lethargic and can no longer swallow reliably. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Crush the tablet and give it in applesauce
options.rationale: Does not fix the swallowing problem, so the aspiration risk remains. Not every tablet may be crushed either.

options.text: Give the medication with a full glass of water to help it down
options.rationale: More fluid delivered into an unsafe swallow is more aspiration risk, not less.

options.text: Document that the patient refused the medication
options.rationale: Refusing and being unable are different problems. One is a choice to respect, the other is a condition that needs a different route.

options.text: Hold the dose and contact the provider about an alternative route
options.rationale: Swallowing ability and level of consciousness are both assessed before administration. Route selection follows the patient's condition, not the order alone.

questions.takeaway: Assess swallowing ability, level of consciousness and clinical condition before administration. Route selection depends on the patient, not only on the order.
questions.strategy: Two distractors try to get the tablet down anyway. One mislabels inability as refusal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The patient can no longer swallow safely.

elimination.verdict: That leaves holding and seeking another route.

questions.stem: A nurse gives medications to an 84-year-old who takes seven drugs daily. Which factors explain why an older adult may respond differently to the same drug at the same dose? Select all that apply.

options.text: Polypharmacy
options.rationale: Each added drug multiplies the possible interactions rather than just adding one more thing to the list.

options.text: Increased sensitivity to medication effects
options.rationale: The same blood level produces a larger response, so a standard adult dose can be too much.

options.text: Changes in body composition
options.rationale: Less water and more fat alters where the drug distributes, which changes the concentration reaching the target.

options.text: Reduced gastric acid production, which prevents oral absorption
options.rationale: Gastric acid does fall with age. Ask: does less acid prevent absorption, or change its rate and extent? It changes it, which is an absorption effect already covered. Prevents is the word that makes this false.

options.text: Chronic illness
options.rationale: Named alongside multiple medications and opioid use, and it alters both the organs that clear the drug and the body it acts on.

options.text: A reduced need for medication with advancing age
options.rationale: Not a named factor and not true. Older adults typically take more medications, not fewer. The issue is how the drug behaves, not how much is needed.

options.text: Age-related changes in renal and hepatic function
options.rationale: Both clearance routes slow, so the drug stays active longer than the dosing interval assumes.

questions.takeaway: Same drug plus same dose does not mean same response. Age-related changes affect absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion.
questions.strategy: One distractor invents a reduced requirement. Everything else describes what the body does to the drug.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: ADME changes, chronic illness, multiple medications, opioid use.
Not named, and the opposite is usual.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, E, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A patient refuses an evening antihypertensive, stating only that it is not wanted tonight. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Mix the medication into pudding so the dose is received
options.rationale: Concealing medication in food is named among the things not to do, and it removes the right to refuse rather than respecting it.

options.text: Document that the patient is non-compliant with the regimen
options.rationale: Named as something not to chart automatically. Non-compliant labels the patient instead of recording what happened and why.

options.text: Find out why the patient is refusing and assess the patient's understanding
options.rationale: A refusal has a reason behind it. Finding the reason is what makes education, a timing change or a provider conversation possible.

options.text: Explain that the medication must be taken because the provider ordered it
options.rationale: An order does not override a competent patient's refusal, and it ends the conversation that would have found the reason.

questions.takeaway: Do not force, hide in food, shame, or automatically chart non-compliant. Find out why, assess understanding, educate, respect the right to refuse, notify when indicated, document.
questions.strategy: Three distractors appear on the list of things not to do. Ask what you would need to know to actually help.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what you do not know

steps.detail: Both named as not to do.

steps.action: Cut the appeal to the order

elimination.verdict: That leaves finding out why.

questions.stem: A nurse is interrupted twice while preparing medications, is working a double shift, and is caring for two patients whose drug names look alike. Which action most directly reduces the risk these conditions create?

options.text: Prepare both patients' medications together to reduce the number of trips
options.rationale: Mixing different patients' medications is named among the things to avoid. It takes the exact hazard in this stem, two similar names, and puts the two doses side by side.

options.text: Rely on the barcode scan at the bedside to catch any name mix-up
options.rationale: Scanning is one of the checks, not a replacement for the other two. A scan catches the wrong patient; it does not catch a dose that was prepared wrong and then correctly scanned to the right patient.

options.text: Record the staffing and workload conditions in a safety report at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Worth doing, and it documents the risk after the shift rather than reducing it during the shift. The medications are being given now.

options.text: Prepare medications in an interruption-free area and verify each look-alike name against the order
options.rationale: Interruptions and look-alike names are two of the named risk factors, and this addresses both at the point where the error would occur. It is the only option that changes the conditions rather than working around them.

questions.takeaway: Error risk factors: interruptions, fatigue, heavy workload, poor communication, similar names and packaging, unclear orders, incomplete history, look-alike and sound-alike drugs, multiple medications, and a poor environment. Reduce the condition, do not work around it.
questions.strategy: Three options manage around the risk. Ask which one removes the interruption and the name confusion at the point the error would happen.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Named as avoid, and it worsens the name hazard.

steps.action: Cut the scan and the report
steps.detail: One is a later check, one is after the fact.

elimination.verdict: That leaves an interruption-free area with name verification.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse reviews pharmacology with a student.

What the drug does to the body is [[1]].

How the drug enters the bloodstream is [[2]].

The desired response the drug was given to produce is the [[3]].

A response caused by an excessive amount of drug is a [[4]].

options.text: pharmacokinetics
options.rationale: Pharmacokinetics means what the body does to the drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion. Ask the same direction question and the answer reverses. This is the near-miss.

options.text: absorption
options.rationale: Absorption means the drug moving from the site of administration into the blood. It is one component of kinetics, not the whole idea.

options.text: distribution
options.rationale: Distribution means where the drug travels once it is in the blood. Also kinetics.

options.text: pharmacodynamics
options.rationale: Pharmacodynamics means the drug acting on the body: medication to target or receptor to physiologic response to therapeutic effect. Ask: which direction is the action running? Drug onto body.

options.text: absorption
options.rationale: Absorption means passage from the administration site into the bloodstream. Ask: is the drug getting in, or already in? Getting in. Affected by route, ability to dissolve, blood flow to the site, surface area, and lipid solubility.

options.text: excretion
options.rationale: Excretion is the drug leaving the body, mostly through the kidneys. That happens after it has been absorbed.

options.text: metabolism
options.rationale: Metabolism is the drug being chemically changed, mostly in the liver. That also comes after absorption.

options.text: distribution
options.rationale: Distribution happens after the drug is already in the blood, so it answers where it goes rather than how it got in.

options.text: side effect
options.rationale: A side effect is an expected secondary effect. Ask the same question: is it why the drug was ordered? No, it comes along with it.

options.text: adverse effect
options.rationale: An adverse effect is a harmful or unintended response. Nobody orders a drug for one.

options.text: toxic effect
options.rationale: A toxic effect is what happens when there is too much drug in the body, not the response you were aiming for.

options.text: therapeutic effect
options.rationale: The therapeutic effect is the desired, expected response. Ask: is this the reason the drug was ordered? Yes.

options.text: adverse effect
options.rationale: An adverse effect is harm occurring with appropriate use. Ask the same question: was there too much drug? Not necessarily, which is what separates the two. This is the near-miss.

options.text: therapeutic effect
options.rationale: A therapeutic effect is the response you wanted. This blank is about harm, so it is the opposite.

options.text: side effect
options.rationale: A side effect is expected and secondary, and it shows up at ordinary doses rather than high ones.

options.text: toxic effect
options.rationale: A toxic effect results from an excessive amount of drug, whether from the dose given, accumulation over time, or impaired clearance. Ask: was there too much drug? Yes.

questions.takeaway: Dynamics is what the drug does to the body. Kinetics is what the body does to the drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion.
questions.strategy: Two near-miss pairs: dynamics against kinetics, and adverse against toxic. One turns on direction, the other on whether there was too much drug.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Drug acting on body, or body acting on drug.

elimination.verdict: Pharmacodynamics, absorption, therapeutic effect, toxic effect.

questions.stem: A nurse scans a barcoded medication and the system displays a prompt to verify the apical pulse before giving it. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Override the prompt, since pharmacy has already verified the order
options.rationale: Pharmacy reviewed the order, not this patient's pulse. Overriding a safety prompt is the named workaround.

options.text: Assess the apical pulse and act on the finding before giving the dose
options.rationale: The prompt directs an assessment, and the ten rights do not replace assessing the patient. This is the assessment the drug itself requires.

options.text: Document that the prompt was acknowledged and administer the dose
options.rationale: Acknowledging is not assessing, and documenting it creates a record that something was checked when it was not.

options.text: Ask assistive personnel to obtain the pulse while the dose is given
options.rationale: The assessment has to precede the dose, and an apical pulse before a rate-controlling drug is a nursing assessment rather than a delegable task.

questions.takeaway: Integrate assessment, medication knowledge, labs, vital signs, clinical condition, orders and nursing judgment. A prompt that directs an assessment is not satisfied by acknowledging it.
questions.strategy: Two distractors treat the prompt as a box rather than an instruction. One delegates an assessment and loses the sequence.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the override and the acknowledgment

steps.detail: Assessment stays with the nurse, and it comes first.

elimination.verdict: That leaves assessing the apical pulse first.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked to perform a procedure that the state nurse practice act permits registered nurses to perform and that facility policy allows. The nurse has not performed it since school. Which question is most important to answer before proceeding?

options.text: Is this within my scope of practice
options.rationale: The stem states the practice act permits it. Scope sets the outer limit and says nothing about this nurse's current ability.

options.text: Is this allowed by facility policy
options.rationale: The stem states policy allows it. Policy can narrow the practice act and never widen it, but that question is answered.

options.text: Has the provider written an order for it
options.rationale: An order authorizes the intervention. It does not establish that this nurse may or can perform it, and it does not transfer responsibility.

options.text: Am I competent to perform this safely today
options.rationale: Scope and policy are both already satisfied in the stem. Competency is the remaining question, and it is the one only this nurse can answer.

questions.takeaway: Before administering: is it within my scope, within my education and competency, allowed by law, allowed by policy, and am I competent. Scope permitting something is not the same as being able to do it safely.
questions.strategy: The stem answers two of the five questions outright. The one it leaves open is the answer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves competency.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews an assignment for high-alert medications. Which are classified as high-alert? Select all that apply.

options.text: Certain intravenous medications
options.rationale: The route delivers the full dose at once and removes any chance of retrieving it.

options.text: Opioids
options.rationale: Opioids are high-alert because an error depresses respiration, and they carry a diversion risk on top of that.

options.text: Acetaminophen given by mouth for a headache
options.rationale: Not high-alert at a standard oral dose. The classification rests on how much harm an error would cause, not on how often the drug is given.

options.text: Anticoagulants
options.rationale: An error causes bleeding that may not be visible until it is substantial.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride 1,000 mL infused over 8 hours
options.rationale: A plain maintenance fluid. Ask: would an error here carry heightened risk of significant harm? No. Certain intravenous medications are high-alert; the route alone does not make a solution high-alert.

options.text: Insulin
options.rationale: High-alert means an error carries a heightened risk of serious harm. A tenfold insulin error can cause fatal hypoglycemia, so the double-check is never skipped.

options.text: Concentrated electrolytes
options.rationale: Concentrated potassium is the classic example. An error with it is immediately toxic to the heart.

questions.takeaway: High-alert medications: insulin, opioids, anticoagulants, concentrated electrolytes, and certain intravenous medications.
questions.strategy: One distractor is a common drug that is not high-alert. Ask what an error with each one would actually do.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An error carries heightened risk of harm.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F, and G are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked when the three medication checks are performed. Which answer is accurate?

options.text: Before preparation, after preparation, and after administration
options.rationale: The third check happens at the bedside before the dose is given. A check after administration cannot prevent anything.

options.text: At the start of the shift, at administration, and at handoff
options.rationale: Two of these are points where the medication is not in hand, so there is nothing to verify.

options.text: When obtaining the medication, when preparing it, and at the bedside
options.rationale: Three separate points, each verifying patient, medication, dose, route and time while there is still time to catch an error.

options.text: Once by the nurse, once by pharmacy, and once by a second nurse
options.rationale: This describes three different people checking rather than three checks by the nurse who gives the drug.

questions.takeaway: Three checks: when obtaining, when preparing, and at the bedside. Each verifies patient, medication, dose, route and time.
questions.strategy: One distractor puts the last check after administration, which is too late to prevent anything.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask when the drug is in hand

steps.detail: One is not the sequence, one describes people.

elimination.verdict: That leaves obtaining, preparing and at the bedside.

questions.stem: A nurse realizes a medication has been given to the wrong patient. Place the actions in the order they should be performed.

options.text: Assess the patient
options.rationale: Find out what state the patient is in before anything else. Every action that follows depends on what this finds.

options.text: Protect the patient
options.rationale: Protecting the patient is acting on what the assessment found: intervening if needed and monitoring afterward.

options.text: Notify the appropriate persons
options.rationale: The provider and the charge nurse, so treatment and oversight can begin. Nothing can be reported usefully before the assessment is done.

options.text: Follow facility policy
options.rationale: Following facility policy means the organization's defined steps for this kind of event, including the reporting form.

options.text: Document appropriately
options.rationale: The record of what happened and what was done about it, in the patient's chart.

options.text: Complete a safety report
options.rationale: The internal report, which is separate from the patient's record and is not referenced in it.

options.text: Continue monitoring
options.rationale: Effects can appear hours later. The sequence does not end when the paperwork does.

questions.takeaway: Assess, protect, notify, follow policy, document, safety report, continue monitoring. The patient comes before the paperwork and the monitoring outlasts it.
questions.strategy: The step people invert is putting notification or documentation first. Nothing can be reported usefully before you know how the patient is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate the chart from the report
steps.detail: One is the patient's, one is the organization's.

elimination.verdict: Assess, protect, notify, policy, document, report, monitor.

questions.stem: A nurse finishes teaching a patient about a new anticoagulant and asks whether the teaching was understood. The patient says yes. Which action should follow?

options.text: Document that the patient verbalized understanding of the teaching
options.rationale: This records a nod as evidence. The entry looks complete and establishes nothing about what he actually understood.

options.text: Provide the written medication information sheet for reference
options.rationale: Useful reinforcement, and it still does not tell you whether the teaching landed.

options.text: Ask whether the patient has any remaining questions about the medication
options.rationale: Another closed question. No questions is not evidence of understanding, and it is often evidence of confusion.

options.text: Ask the patient to explain in their own words what they will do and what to watch for
options.rationale: Teach-back makes the patient produce the content. A yes records politeness, not comprehension.

questions.takeaway: Use teach-back instead of asking do you understand. Education covers what the drug is, why it is given, how to take it, when, what to expect, and when to call.
questions.strategy: Three options accept a yes or a no as proof. Ask which one requires the patient to produce the content.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the sheet and the closed question

elimination.verdict: That leaves teach-back.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares a medication, is called away before giving it, and returns to find the syringe where it was left. Which action is correct?

options.text: Discard it and prepare a fresh dose
options.rationale: An unattended medication cannot be verified. Nobody can account for what happened to it during the time it was out of sight.

options.text: Administer it, since the nurse prepared it and recognizes the syringe
options.rationale: Recognition is not verification. Recognizing the syringe says nothing about what happened to its contents.

options.text: Label it and administer it after rechecking the order
options.rationale: Labeling it now does not establish what happened to it while it sat unattended. The order was never the problem.

options.text: Return it to the medication room and administer it at the next scheduled time
options.rationale: This keeps a dose nobody can vouch for in circulation, and it delays the medication besides.

questions.takeaway: Avoid unlabeled syringes, unattended medications, mixing different patients' medications, distractions, guessing, expired medications, and skipping the barcode scan.
questions.strategy: Three distractors find a way to use the dose. Ask what can actually be accounted for.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nothing about the time it was unattended.

elimination.verdict: That leaves discarding and preparing fresh.

questions.nursesNote: 0750: Morning medications are being prepared for a 54-year-old. The chart lists an allergy to penicillin with documented anaphylaxis. Scheduled medications are ceftriaxone, furosemide, insulin aspart and warfarin. Potassium this morning is 3.1 mEq/L. Blood glucose is 62 mg/dL. The last INR was drawn four days ago and no result appears in the chart. Blood pressure 118/70, apical pulse 72, temperature 36.9 C. The patient reports no bleeding or bruising, is alert and oriented, and swallows without difficulty.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require nursing action before these medications are given.

segments.text: Allergy to penicillin with documented anaphylaxis, with ceftriaxone scheduled
segments.rationale: Anaphylaxis means a life-threatening whole-body allergic reaction. Ask: does the scheduled drug share structure with the allergen? Ceftriaxone is a cephalosporin, closely enough related that this needs clarifying before the dose rather than after.

segments.text: Alert and oriented, swallows without difficulty
segments.rationale: Level of consciousness and swallowing are both assessed before oral medications, and both are intact here.

segments.text: Apical pulse 72
segments.rationale: Normal. Pulse is checked before rate-controlling drugs, and none of these four is one.

segments.text: Blood glucose 62 mg/dL with insulin aspart scheduled
segments.rationale: Insulin lowers glucose, and 62 is already below the normal floor of 70. Insulin is a high-alert medication, which means an error carries heightened risk of serious harm.

segments.text: Temperature 36.9 C
segments.rationale: A temperature of 36.9 C is normal, so there is nothing here to act on.

segments.text: Potassium 3.1 mEq/L with furosemide scheduled
segments.rationale: Furosemide is a loop diuretic, which means it causes potassium loss in the urine. Ask: does the drug push this value further in the direction it is already abnormal? Yes, from a level already below 3.5.

segments.text: Blood pressure 118/70
segments.rationale: A blood pressure of 118/70 is within normal limits, so nothing here delays any of the four drugs.

segments.text: Last INR drawn four days ago with no result in the chart, with warfarin scheduled
segments.rationale: INR means international normalized ratio, the measure of how long blood takes to clot on warfarin. Ask: is the value that governs this dose available? No. The absence of a result is itself the finding.

segments.text: Reports no bleeding or bruising
segments.rationale: A reassuring finding. It does not substitute for the missing INR, because bleeding appears after the level is already too high rather than before.

questions.takeaway: Assess allergies, vital signs, relevant labs, level of consciousness and swallowing before administration. A missing lab result is a finding, not an absence of one.
questions.strategy: Five findings are normal or reassuring, and two of them are placed to rule something out. The missing INR is the one people read past, because nothing abnormal is written down.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Pair each drug with its check

steps.detail: No INR result in the chart.
Pressure, pulse, no bleeding, swallowing, temperature.

elimination.verdict: s1, s4, s6, and s8: four drugs, four checks that have not been satisfied.

questions.stem: A nurse receives an order reading: metoprolol, give daily. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Administer the dose the patient was taking at home
options.rationale: Filling a gap in an order from the home regimen is prescribing, and the home dose may not be what is intended now.

options.text: Ask the pharmacist to supply the usual dose for this drug
options.rationale: The pharmacist reviews and dispenses. Neither the pharmacist nor the nurse may decide what the prescriber intended.

options.text: Document that the order is unclear and hold it until rounds
options.rationale: This records the problem instead of solving it, and a scheduled cardiac medication sits undelivered until rounds.

options.text: Contact the prescriber, because the order is incomplete
options.rationale: An order must be complete, clear, appropriate, safe, consistent with the patient's condition, and within the nurse's scope. This one has no dose and no route, so it cannot be verified against anything.

questions.takeaway: An order must be complete, clear, appropriate, safe, consistent with the patient's condition, and within the nurse's scope. An incomplete order is clarified, never inferred.
questions.strategy: Two distractors fill in the missing information from somewhere else. Neither source is the prescriber.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Home dose and usual dose are both inferences.

elimination.verdict: That leaves contacting the prescriber.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked which route gives the most rapid effect and carries the greatest risk if an error occurs. Which answer is accurate?

options.text: Intramuscular
options.rationale: Used when the oral route is not appropriate. Absorption depends on blood flow and tissue, so it is slower than intravenous and some margin remains.

options.text: Subcutaneous
options.rationale: Subcutaneous is common for insulin, limited to small volumes, and slower than intramuscular.

options.text: Intravenous
options.rationale: The dose enters the circulation immediately and in full, which is what makes it fast and what makes an error impossible to retrieve.

options.text: Oral
options.rationale: Oral is the most convenient and the slowest, and it depends on the patient being able to swallow.

questions.takeaway: Intravenous gives a rapid effect and immediate systemic availability, which is also why an error carries the highest risk.
questions.strategy: The feature that makes the route fast is the same feature that makes an error unrecoverable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nothing can be retrieved once it is in.

elimination.verdict: That leaves intravenous.

questions.stem: A preceptor listens to a new graduate discuss medication safety. Which statement requires correction?

options.text: "The ten rights do not replace assessing the patient."
options.rationale: This is accurate. The right drug given to a patient whose condition does not tolerate it is still unsafe.

options.text: "A medication error is preventable; an adverse drug reaction happens with appropriate use."
options.rationale: This is accurate, and the distinction decides which kind of event you are reporting.

options.text: "I check the medication when I obtain it, when I prepare it, and at the bedside."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Three checks, each one verifying patient, medication, dose, route, and time.

options.text: "If the order is written correctly, responsibility for the dose belongs to the prescriber."
options.rationale: An order authorizes a medication. It does not transfer responsibility, and the nurse who administers it answers for having given it.

questions.takeaway: An order authorizes a medication. It does not transfer responsibility for administering it.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate the material correctly. One moves responsibility off the nurse and onto the prescriber.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rights and assessment, error definitions, three checks.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the responsibility statement.

questions.scenario: A 67-year-old received intravenous hydromorphone 20 minutes ago and lorazepam an hour before that. The patient is now difficult to rouse, with a respiratory rate of 7, shallow effort, and an oxygen saturation of 86% on room air. Blood pressure is 104/62.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes first, the 1 problem this represents, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Stimulate the patient, support the airway, and apply oxygen
options.rationale: Airway and breathing come before everything else. Stimulation and oxygen address the immediate hypoxia while help is coming.

options.text: Document the findings and reassess in one hour
options.rationale: A rate of 7 with a saturation of 86% will not wait an hour. Documentation follows the intervention rather than replacing it.

options.text: Administer the next scheduled dose of hydromorphone on time
options.rationale: Adds opioid to a patient already in respiratory depression. The next dose is held, not given.

options.text: Call for rapid response and obtain the order for naloxone
options.rationale: Naloxone reverses opioid effect at the receptor. The patient needs it, and the nurse needs the order and the team rather than acting alone.

options.text: An adverse drug reaction to lorazepam alone
options.rationale: An adverse drug reaction is harm with appropriate use. Ask: does one drug explain this? The hydromorphone 20 minutes ago is the nearer cause, and the two together are the real answer.

options.text: An expected side effect of hydromorphone
options.rationale: A side effect is an expected secondary effect at an ordinary dose, and opioid sedation is one. Ask: is a respiratory rate of 7 with a saturation of 86% expected, or harm? Harm. This is the distractor that costs people the question, because the sedation looked expected right up to the point it stopped being safe.

options.text: A medication error in the dose administered
options.rationale: A medication error is a preventable mistake in the process. Ask whether the stem describes anything done incorrectly. Nothing was, so this is a reaction rather than an error.

options.text: Opioid-induced respiratory depression
options.rationale: Opioid-induced respiratory depression means the drug has slowed the brain's drive to breathe. Ask: is there a sedating drug on board and is the rate falling? Both, and the lorazepam compounds it.

options.text: Whether the patient can state the purpose of the medication
options.rationale: Tests teaching in a patient who cannot currently be roused, and it evaluates nothing the actions changed.

options.text: Pain score at the intravenous site
options.rationale: A real assessment, and not the one that tells you whether breathing is recovering.

options.text: Respiratory rate and depth
options.rationale: The finding that defined the problem, and the first one to improve if the reversal works.

options.text: Level of consciousness and oxygen saturation
options.rationale: Rousability and saturation together show whether oxygenation is recovering. Naloxone is short-acting, so both can fall again.

questions.takeaway: Opioids are high-alert because an error or an accumulation depresses respiration. Two sedating drugs together is additive, so the second one is the dose that declares the problem.
questions.strategy: Two sedating drugs in the history, and the question is not which one. The tempting option calls the sedation an expected side effect, which it is until the respiratory rate falls.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An opioid and a benzodiazepine, additive.

elimination.verdict: Support and reverse, for opioid-induced respiratory depression, evaluated by respiratory status and rousability.

skills.title: Personal Hygiene, Perineal Care, and Bedmaking

sources.title: Personal Hygiene, Perineal Care, and Bedmaking
sources.label: Skill · Personal Hygiene, Perineal Care, and Bedmaking

questions.stem: A nurse performs catheter care for a 53-year-old with an indwelling urinary catheter inserted three days ago. The meatus is intact with no discharge and the patient reports no discomfort. In which direction does she clean the catheter?

options.text: From the drainage tubing back toward the meatus, in one continuous motion
options.rationale: This carries organisms along the catheter toward the urinary tract, which is the direction you are trying to prevent.

options.text: From the meatus outward for about four inches, without pulling or creating friction
options.rationale: Cleaning away from the meatus moves organisms away from the entry point rather than toward it, which is the cleanest-to-dirtiest principle applied to this site.

options.text: Only at the meatus itself, leaving the catheter surface untouched
options.rationale: The first few inches of catheter carry organisms toward the meatus and are cleaned.

options.text: In a back-and-forth motion along the length of the catheter
options.rationale: Returns the cloth to the meatus after it has been soiled, and the friction irritates the tissue.

questions.takeaway: Clean from the meatus outward for about four inches. Cleanest to dirtiest, always moving away from the entry point. Catheter care: assess the meatus and surrounding skin for redness, swelling, discharge, trauma, or discomfort, perform perineal hygiene with 2% chlorhexidine cloth or mild soap and warm water, and clean the catheter from the meatus outward for about four inches without pulling or friction.
questions.strategy: The whole of hygiene runs on one principle: cleanest to dirtiest. Catheter care is that principle applied to the shortest route into the bladder.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cleanest to dirtiest means away from the meatus.
Both return organisms toward the meatus.
The proximal catheter is cleaned too.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: cleaning away from the meatus moves organisms away from the entry point rather than toward it, which is the cleanest-to-dirtiest principle applied to this site.

questions.concept: Catheter care: assess the meatus and surrounding skin for redness, swelling, discharge, trauma, or discomfort, perform perineal hygiene with 2% chlorhexidine cloth or mild soap and warm water, and clean the catheter from the meatus outward for about four inches without pulling or friction.

questions.stem: A nurse gives a bed bath to a 90-year-old who tires quickly and has fragile skin over her shoulders and sacrum. She has been in bed for four days and her daughter is visiting. Which principles apply? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use lukewarm water and mild cleansers to prevent irritation
options.rationale: Lukewarm water and mild cleansers protect the skin. Hot water and harsh soap dry it out and damage it.

options.text: Use a single basin of water for the whole bath
options.rationale: Water contaminated early in the bath is carried to every later area, including the perineum.

options.text: Encourage normal range of motion during bathing
options.rationale: Encouraging normal range of motion during the bath gets you movement that would otherwise need its own intervention.

options.text: Avoid excessive force and friction
options.rationale: Force and friction both damage skin that is already fragile in a patient who has been in bed for days.

options.text: Bathe the patient at the same time each day regardless of tolerance
options.rationale: The timing gets matched to the patient, not to the routine. This patient tires quickly.

options.text: Use hot water to improve circulation during the bath
options.rationale: Lukewarm water is the rule. Hot water damages fragile skin and risks a burn.

questions.takeaway: Lukewarm water, mild cleanser, minimal friction, assess while you bathe, encourage movement, and match the bath to the patient's tolerance. Bathing principles: clean skin when soiled and at regular intervals, use lukewarm water and mild cleansers, avoid excessive force and friction, minimize factors that dry the skin, use the bath to interact with and assess the patient, encourage range of motion, and consider a partial bath for a patient who fatigues easily.
questions.strategy: Three separate things happen during a bath: hygiene, skin assessment, and range of motion. That is why it is worth doing well rather than quickly.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A full bath regardless of tolerance ignores what the stem tells you.

elimination.verdict: A, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Bathing principles: clean skin when soiled and at regular intervals, use lukewarm water and mild cleansers, avoid excessive force and friction, minimize factors that dry the skin, use the bath to interact with and assess the patient, encourage range of motion, and consider a partial bath for a patient who fatigues easily.

questions.stem: A patient is being transferred from the emergency department by stretcher after a fall and will arrive on the unit within the hour. The bed is empty and the linen has been changed. How does the nurse prepare the bed?

options.text: As an occupied bed, with the patient already lying in it
options.rationale: An occupied bed is made with the patient already lying in it, and this bed is empty.

options.text: It does not matter, as long as the linen is clean
options.rationale: How the bed is prepared decides how easily and safely he can be moved off the stretcher.

options.text: As a closed bed, with the top sheets pulled up to the head of the bed
options.rationale: A closed bed is usually made by housekeeping after discharge and is not prepared for an arriving patient.

options.text: As an open bed, with the top sheets fanfolded lengthwise and not tucked in
options.rationale: An open bed is prepared for immediate use, and fanfolding the linen allows transfer from a stretcher without fighting tucked bedding.

questions.takeaway: Open bed: fanfolded, untucked, ready for immediate use. Closed bed: top sheets up, made after discharge. An open bed is prepared for immediate use with the top sheets fanfolded lengthwise and not tucked in, to ease transfer from a stretcher. A closed bed has the top sheets pulled up to the head and is usually made after discharge.
questions.strategy: The distinction is about the next few minutes. An open bed says someone is arriving now; a closed bed says the room is waiting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A patient arriving by stretcher within the hour.
A closed bed is for an empty room.
One requires a patient present, one ignores the transfer.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: an open bed.

questions.concept: An open bed is prepared for immediate use with the top sheets fanfolded lengthwise and not tucked in, to ease transfer from a stretcher. A closed bed has the top sheets pulled up to the head and is usually made after discharge.

questions.stem: A nurse changes the linen for a 51-year-old who cannot tolerate being out of bed after hip surgery. The bed is at its lowest position and one other staff member is available to help. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tell the patient what you are going to do before moving him
options.rationale: Communication before movement is specified, and it is what allows him to help rather than resist.

options.text: Identify how many additional people are needed before starting
options.rationale: Work out how many people you need before you start. Discovering it halfway through leaves the patient unsupported.

options.text: Work quickly without involving the patient, to shorten the procedure
options.rationale: Patient self-help is encouraged as much as possible, and it preserves both function and dignity.

options.text: Remove the pillow so the sheet lies flat
options.rationale: Taking the pillow away removes support after hip surgery and adds discomfort without making the linen change easier.

options.text: Lower the bed fully before beginning the linen change
options.rationale: The bed is raised to a comfortable working height while working, then lowered before leaving.

options.text: Keep the back straight, bend the knees, and avoid twisting
options.rationale: A straight back with bent knees puts the load through your legs, and twisting under load is what injures backs.

questions.takeaway: Plan the help, raise the bed, communicate before you move him, keep him covered, and let him help. For an occupied bed: identify how many additional people are needed, encourage patient self-help, raise the bed to a comfortable working height, keep the back straight and knees bent while avoiding twisting, keep the patient covered as much as possible, and communicate before moving the patient.
questions.strategy: Every one of these protects something different: the nurse's back, the patient's dignity, his warmth, and his sense of control over what is happening to him.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: People, height, and what you will say.
Self-help is encouraged rather than bypassed.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and F are selected.

questions.concept: For an occupied bed: identify how many additional people are needed, encourage patient self-help, raise the bed to a comfortable working height, keep the back straight and knees bent while avoiding twisting, keep the patient covered as much as possible, and communicate before moving the patient.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old reports a hard, painful stool he has been unable to pass for two days despite a stool softener. Which type of enema is indicated?

options.text: Mineral oil
options.rationale: Its action is lubrication rather than volume, which is what a hard impacted stool requires.

options.text: Medicated
options.rationale: A medicated enema delivers a drug. It does nothing about how hard the stool is.

options.text: Tap water
options.rationale: Uses volume to stimulate peristalsis and does not soften a hard stool already in place.

options.text: Soapsuds
options.rationale: Soapsuds works by volume and irritation rather than by lubricating a stool that is already hard.

questions.takeaway: Enemas promote defecation by stimulating peristalsis. Tap water flushes with volume; mineral oil coats and lubricates hard stool. An enema instills solution into the rectum and sigmoid colon and promotes defecation by stimulating peristalsis. A tap water enema flushes the colon with a large volume of plain water. A mineral oil enema coats and lubricates a hard, painful stool. Medicated enemas must be administered by a nurse.
questions.strategy: Match the mechanism to the problem. Volume moves stool that can move; lubrication is for stool that cannot.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hard, painful stool that will not pass.
Uses volume to stimulate peristalsis and does not soften a hard stool already in place.
Also acts by volume and irritation rather than by lubricating the stool.
Delivers a drug rather than addressing the consistency of the stool.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: its action is lubrication rather than volume, which is what a hard impacted stool requires.

questions.concept: An enema instills solution into the rectum and sigmoid colon and promotes defecation by stimulating peristalsis. A tap water enema flushes the colon with a large volume of plain water. A mineral oil enema coats and lubricates a hard, painful stool. Medicated enemas must be administered by a nurse.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel describe their plan for hygiene and catheter care on a unit where several patients have indwelling catheters. The AP describes how she plans to manage the drainage systems during the shift. Which statement by the assistive personnel indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will empty the bag when it is about half full."
options.rationale: This is accurate. A full bag gets heavy, and then it may rise above the bladder or pull on the catheter.

options.text: "I will hang the drainage bag on the side rail so it is easy to reach."
options.rationale: A side rail moves with position changes, which can lift the bag above bladder level or pull on the catheter. The bag is kept below the bladder and off the floor.

options.text: "I will tell the nurse if the patient's skin around the catheter looks red."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Redness, swelling, discharge, trauma, and discomfort all get reported to the nurse.

options.text: "I will clean from the meatus outward, not back toward it."
options.rationale: This is accurate. Cleanest to dirtiest means moving away from the entry point, never back toward it.

questions.takeaway: Below the bladder, off the floor, and not on anything that moves.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement optimizes for convenience, and the side rail is the one surface in the room designed to move.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A side rail is raised and lowered.
Cleaning direction, emptying, and reporting are correct.

elimination.verdict: The statement needing correction: never hang the bag on a side rail.

questions.stem: A unit introduces daily 2% chlorhexidine gluconate bathing after a rise in central line infections. Staff ask how it differs from a standard soap and water bath and what it is expected to achieve. Which statements about this practice are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Chlorhexidine is effective against a broad range of bacteria
options.rationale: It works against a wide range of bacteria, so it is used before surgery instead of plain soap.

options.text: Preoperative chlorhexidine bathing can reduce surgical site infections
options.rationale: Bathing with it before an operation lowers the bacterial load on the skin, which is where surgical site infections start.

options.text: Rinse the chlorhexidine off with clear water after bathing
options.rationale: Rinsing it off defeats the purpose. The chlorhexidine left on the skin is what keeps working.

options.text: It reduces skin bacteria and health care-associated infections
options.rationale: Reducing skin bacteria and health care-associated infections is the whole reason the unit adopted this.

options.text: Chlorhexidine cloths must be used alongside a full soap and water bath each day
options.rationale: Disposable washcloths impregnated with chlorhexidine replace soap and water baths rather than supplementing them.

options.text: Apply chlorhexidine to the face and mucous membranes
options.rationale: Chlorhexidine is kept away from the face, the eyes, and mucous membranes, where it causes irritation and can damage the eye.

questions.takeaway: Daily 2% CHG bathing reduces skin bacteria, HAIs, surgical site infections, and CLABSIs, and it replaces the soap and water bath. Daily 2% chlorhexidine gluconate bathing reduces skin bacteria and health care-associated infections, is effective against a broad range of bacteria, reduces surgical site infections when used preoperatively, reduces central line-associated bloodstream infections, and reduces exposure from infected or colonized roommates and previous room occupants. CHG-impregnated disposable cloths replace soap and water baths.
questions.strategy: The roommate and previous occupant finding is the one worth carrying. It says the risk is not only what the patient brought with them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Skin flora, HAIs, SSIs, CLABSIs, environmental exposure.
CHG cloths replace the soap and water bath.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Daily 2% chlorhexidine gluconate bathing reduces skin bacteria and health care-associated infections, is effective against a broad range of bacteria, reduces surgical site infections when used preoperatively, reduces central line-associated bloodstream infections, and reduces exposure from infected or colonized roommates and previous room occupants. CHG-impregnated disposable cloths replace soap and water baths.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old receiving anticoagulation therapy for a deep vein thrombosis asks the nurse to help him shave before his family visits. His platelet count is low and he has bruising on both forearms. Which action is correct?

options.text: Use an electric razor, because he is at risk for bleeding
options.rationale: An electric razor is used for any patient with bleeding tendencies. A blade razor risks a cut that will not stop readily.

options.text: Use a blade razor carefully with generous lather to soften the skin
options.rationale: Care and lather do not remove the risk of a cut in an anticoagulated patient.

options.text: Ask assistive personnel to shave him with a blade razor
options.rationale: Handing the task to someone else does not make the razor safer. The bleeding risk comes from the blade, whoever holds it.

options.text: Decline to shave him until the anticoagulant has been discontinued
options.rationale: This withholds routine hygiene when a safe alternative is sitting right there. The anticoagulant is treating a clot.

questions.takeaway: Use an electric razor for any patient at risk for bleeding tendencies. Review coagulation status and bleeding risk before oral care as well. Use an electric razor for any patient at risk for bleeding tendencies, and obtain consent before cutting or shaving hair.
questions.strategy: Bleeding risk changes the equipment for two hygiene tasks: shaving and oral care. Both involve tissue that bleeds readily and is easy to nick.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Technique does not remove the risk.
One withholds care, one transfers the same risk.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: electric razor.

questions.concept: Use an electric razor for any patient at risk for bleeding tendencies, and obtain consent before cutting or shaving hair. Review coagulation status and bleeding risk before providing oral care.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares oral hygiene for a patient four days after a stroke who has a reduced gag reflex and a saturation of 94%. He is currently lying supine. Which position is appropriate?

options.text: Flat supine, with the head turned to one side
options.rationale: Lying flat lets fluid pool at the back of the throat, and his gag reflex is already reduced.

options.text: Prone, to protect the airway
options.rationale: Not a workable position for oral care and does not protect the airway here.

options.text: Head of the bed raised 30 to 45 degrees
options.rationale: Elevating the head of the bed positions the patient so that fluid drains away from the airway rather than toward it.

options.text: Trendelenburg, so secretions drain out
options.rationale: Head-down positioning sends fluid toward the airway instead of away from it, which is the opposite of what you want.

questions.takeaway: During oral hygiene, position the patient to avoid aspiration by keeping the head of the bed raised 30 to 45 degrees. Observe for bleeding of the oral mucosa or gums, reported pain, and changes in the oral mucosa.
questions.strategy: Oral care puts fluid in the mouth of someone who may not be able to protect the airway. Position is the intervention that makes the rest of it safe.

strategies: Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: Weakness plus a reduced gag reflex.
Both let fluid reach the airway.
Not a position for oral care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: 30 to 45 degrees.
